1	update lr_explanation_steps t set body=v.nb, label=case when v.nl='' then t.label else v.nl end from (values
2	('1797f203-7405-4af3-b631-02670691d960'::uuid,'11d53cd0483de31691e97a51f3a20044','Antonio:
3	1. One can live a life of moderation by never deviating from the middle course.
4	2. But never deviating has a cost: you lose the joy of spontaneity and miss the opportunities that come to people who occasionally take great chances or go too far.
5	
6	Marla:
7	1. Someone who never risks going too far is actually failing to live a life of moderation.
8	2. Reason: one must be moderate even in one''s moderation.','Antonio / Marla','Antonio and Marla'),
9	('1ad1e6b3-76c4-4914-ae71-a90f8924b362'::uuid,'fcc14f2192ad76164d677b3469b68c86','Go claim by claim and ask: does Marla disagree?
10	
11	Antonio''s claim 1: never deviating from the middle course is a way to live a life of moderation. Marla says the opposite. A person who never risks going too far is "failing to live a life of moderation." That''s a direct clash.
12	
13	Antonio''s claim 2: never deviating means missing out on spontaneity and opportunity. Marla doesn''t push back. If anything, Marla''s view leaves room for the occasional risk too, since moderation itself has to be practiced in moderation, which means sometimes stepping off the middle course.
14	
15	So they mostly agree that some risk is worth taking. Where they split is the definition. Antonio thinks unbroken middle-course living still counts as a life of moderation, even if it''s a dull one. Marla thinks it doesn''t count at all.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
16	('f06da175-a31e-4b96-a95e-1f79bbad878b'::uuid,'79a81c63d7c11222863a5a1b656d0aab','Lutsina:
17	1. Futuristic science fiction doesn''t need to represent current social realities.
18	2. So its writers can envisage radically new social arrangements.
19	3. Conclusion: it has the potential to be a richer source of social criticism than conventional fiction.
20	
21	Priscilla:
22	1. Science fiction writers envisage new technologies more skillfully than new social arrangements.
23	2. That shows writers'' imaginations are constrained by current realities.
24	3. Conclusion: the most effective social criticism comes from faithfully presenting current social realities, as conventional fiction does.','Lutsina / Priscilla','Lutsina and Priscilla'),
25	('fc040d7f-1735-467c-bfe3-f4d7ac1ce2c0'::uuid,'75231962662860b30d111e97669fdde1','Line the conclusions up. Lutsina says futuristic science fiction has the potential to be a richer source of social criticism than conventional fiction. Priscilla says the most effective social criticism comes from conventional fiction. Those two claims rank the same two genres in opposite order on the same job. That''s the disagreement.
26	
27	Now check the support. Lutsina''s reason is freedom: science fiction can leave current realities behind. Priscilla answers that the freedom is less real than it looks, because writers stay constrained by current realities. Notice what Priscilla doesn''t say. Priscilla never claims science fiction writers can''t envisage new social arrangements, only that they do it less skillfully than they envisage new technology. So don''t expect the answer to be about whether anyone has succeeded. Expect it to be about which genre is the better source of social criticism.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
28	('c8c0fd62-38a4-45af-ac32-f074fd153498'::uuid,'1d4acdeb9ff4a2fcc142d06d1876f93c','Graham:
29	1. A computer defeated the world''s chess champion.
30	2. So any type of human intellectual activity governed by fixed principles can be mastered by machines.
31	3. So a truly intelligent machine will inevitably be devised.
32	
33	Adelaide:
34	1. The computer was simply an extension of the people who programmed it.
35	2. It was the programmers'' successful distillation of the principles of chess that let them defeat the champion using a computer.','Graham / Adelaide','Graham and Adelaide'),
36	('4c5204e4-b044-4185-b590-9f832ae67e34'::uuid,'2e744ddd0e8fe2d60a33999aeeac6c11','Graham and Adelaide disagree about whether the computer itself deserves the credit for beating the chess champion. Graham treats the win as the machine''s achievement: the computer mastered chess, so machines can master any fixed-principle activity. Adelaide says Graham is "overlooking" who did the work. The computer was "simply an extension of the people who programmed it," and the people beat the champion "using a computer."
37	
38	Notice what Adelaide doesn''t say. Adelaide never says a truly intelligent machine is impossible, and never disputes that the champion lost. Adelaide only moves the credit from the machine to the programmers, which takes away the evidence Graham was relying on.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
39	('9eb122d6-e8fc-476e-a270-ea0bc6b652d5'::uuid,'b618336255b669d9e03bd13ff846d116','Wong and Tate disagree about whether some countries are better off as autocracies. Wong says "all countries are better off as democracies." Tate never uses the words "better off," but Tate says material needs are "more important" than the freedom and autonomy democracy brings, and that some countries meet those needs better as autocracies. If the more important thing goes better under autocracy, those countries are better off as autocracies.
40	
41	Notice what Wong concedes. A "transitional autocratic stage" is sometimes required. That''s a claim about the path to democracy, not about which system is better. Wong still thinks every country is better off once it''s a democracy, so the concession doesn''t soften the clash.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
42	('1065ffe0-ba4e-4097-bc0b-700539237a92'::uuid,'4283c73959835aeb5c80bb4b9c673d69','On libertarian principles, I oppose the proposed smoking ban.
43	*Does Pankaj say the ban should not be opposed?*
44	
45	No, nothing definitive. Pankaj pushes back against Ana''s opposition, but that doesn''t mean Pankaj supports the ban. On the LSAT, it''s common for someone to disagree with the reasoning behind position X without disagreeing with X itself.','Ana''s 1st Claim','Ana''s 1st Claim'),
46	('ca6d1705-3f5c-4664-8d1c-488a1a167d09'::uuid,'93e39c48ce70e6eb061425a8285107a3','It isn''t the government''s business to prevent people from doing things that harm only themselves.
47	*Does Pankaj say that it* **is** *the government''s business sometimes to prevent people from doing things that harm only themselves?*
48	
49	No. Pankaj doesn''t say anything about the government or what its role is.','Ana''s 2nd Claim','Ana''s 2nd Claim'),
50	('86bd2159-9263-434f-8549-6e0e40e2259d'::uuid,'0da8b37d1ece2beaf5106be77d0ee5f9','Since Pankaj didn''t disagree with any of Ana''s explicit claims, ask what Ana was *assuming*. Maybe Pankaj is disagreeing with an assumption.
51	
52	Ana''s two sentences only connect if the proposed smoking ban is trying to prevent people from doing things that harm only themselves. Otherwise the libertarian principle doesn''t reach the ban.
53	
54	Does Pankaj disagree with that? Yes. Pankaj points out that people "could still smoke all they want in private." So the ban isn''t stopping smokers from harming themselves. It applies only to smoking in public places, which is where smoke reaches other people. Pankaj is hinting that the ban targets harm to others, which puts it outside Ana''s principle.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
55	('e43489ef-03d0-4a44-80c9-b80959f7ed81'::uuid,'9ff132236d0769e3493cc9e695124a48','1. no comment
56	2. potentially agrees
57	3. potentially agrees
58	4. disagrees
59	
60	For claim #3, by saying, "Klein''s policies have been effective," Soltan is potentially agreeing with Bell that Klein''s policies avoided an impending catastrophe. And for claim #2, by saying Klein will lack "the political support to make them," Soltan potentially agrees that Klein''s policies are unpopular. Neither of these are definite, but at best they would be points that both speakers **agree** on. We''re being asked for their point of disagreement, and there''s no evidence that they disagree about claim #2 or claim #3.','Evaluate Soltan''s Responses','Evaluate Soltan''s Responses'),
61	('b498406b-c557-42f7-8ae9-4e69832345d3'::uuid,'caaa9066dc41643bc0e70484f545e581','Look for an answer about Klein''s future role: whether Klein should keep making important decisions or step down. Bell wants Klein making those decisions; Soltan wants Klein out. Beware of answers that describe claim #2 or #3, which are potential points of agreement, not disagreement.','Goal','Goal'),
62	('56e60690-b422-443c-a616-309f3e170f8c'::uuid,'2d7bbd72ed0f0cfc91133bc4d857f912','  1. Disagrees (implied: Ayla wants Carl''s views aired at the forum)
63	  2. Partly agrees: Ayla treats Carl''s views as false; no comment on dangerous
64	  3. Disagrees: Ayla thinks public scrutiny will expose the views, not legitimize or spread them
65	  4. No comment, possibly agrees','Ayla''s Responses','Ayla''s Responses'),
66	('14e65ffc-ff69-48f5-87a5-9db90da71be2'::uuid,'26693089d8b9eb6e256b196b333227c5','Ayla never says outright that Carl should be invited, but the whole reply supports it. Public challenge is "the best way to combat false views," and the forum is where that challenge would happen. So Ayla is on the other side of Bernard''s first claim.
67	
68	The sharper friction is Bernard''s third claim. Bernard says giving Carl''s views a hearing would legitimize them and help spread them. Ayla predicts the opposite effect: under public scrutiny, "people will see them for what they are."
69	
70	Now look at what they share. Both treat Carl''s views as false, and neither wants people to adopt them. They agree on the goal. They disagree about the method: does airing false views in public help defeat them or help spread them?
71	
72	One vocabulary note: "promulgate" means to spread or make widely known. If you guessed that from context, that''s enough.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
73	('22f33113-9385-489e-80e2-f4528e96a978'::uuid,'9f8543da20ddfa7e0364b18d8975e8e4','Look for an answer about method: whether letting false views be expressed in public is a good way to fight them. Bernard says no; Ayla says yes. That covers both claim #1 and claim #3.','Goal','Goal')

Beware of answers that describe claim #2 or #3, which are potential points of agreement, not disagreement.','Goal','Goal'),\n('56e60690-b422-443c-a616-309f3e170f8c'::uuid,'2d7bbd72ed0f0cfc91133bc4d857f912','  1. Disagrees: Ayla thinks public scrutiny will expose the views, not legitimize or spread them\n  4. No comment, possibly agrees','Ayla''s Responses','Ayla''s Responses'),\n('14e65ffc-ff69-48f5-87a5-9db90da71be2'::uuid,'26693089d8b9eb6e256b196b333227c5','Ayla never says outright that Carl should be invited, but the whole reply supports it. Public challenge is \"the best way to combat false views,\" and the forum is where that challenge would happen. So Ayla is on the other side of Bernard''s first claim.\n\nThe sharper friction is Bernard''s third claim. Bernard says giving Carl''s views a hearing would legitimize them and help spread them. Ayla predicts the opposite effect: under public scrutiny, \"people will see them for what they are.\"\n\nNow look at what they share. Both treat Carl''s views as false, and neither wants people to adopt them. They agree on the goal. With neither speaker taking a side, this can''t be the disagreement.'),\n('b15dece1-1bf2-4de9-83bc-ab861887f325'::uuid,'14369ce2d6b9eacb78d70fcdc51e3fc7','Lutsina AGREES: science fiction \"has the potential to be a richer source of social criticism than is conventional fiction.\" \"More promise\" is another way to say Lutsina''s \"potential to be a richer source.\" Priscilla DISAGREES: \"the most effective social criticism results from faithfully presenting the current social realities,\" which is what conventional fiction does. Priscilla puts conventional fiction on top.\n\nThe move: find each speaker''s conclusion and ask whether they answer the same question. When two conclusions rank the same two things in opposite order, look for an answer that restates that ranking in new words.'),\n('171dfb5e-e82b-4267-8bb2-9e438d2b4fcf'::uuid,'ba1626dd4f178e41e534485f46cb7dee','Priscilla probably agrees, since Priscilla treats the gap between technologies and social arrangements as a \"limitation.\" But Lutsina never mentions technology. Lutsina only says science fiction writers can envisage new social arrangements, which says nothing about whether favoring technology is a weakness. One speaker with a view isn''t enough; a disagreement needs both.'),\n('62d11c09-7ae9-462c-86c2-6fd324aa47ac'::uuid,'1fb5db3fc0a14aa9dd1695daa246fd3a','This is the trap. Lutsina would likely disagree with it, because Lutsina thinks imagining radically new arrangements makes science fiction a richer source of criticism. But does Priscilla say such criticism is \"not effective\"? No. Priscilla says the most effective criticism comes from presenting current realities. Calling one approach the most effective doesn''t make the other ineffective. Second place isn''t zero. Without Priscilla on the agree side, there''s no disagreement.'),\n('23c2f278-4af7-4e3c-b15c-8e1d31e197a2'::uuid,'87da74beed70e84459cba6147dae15f2','\"Best\" is a ranking, and neither speaker ranks chess against other activities. Graham uses chess as one example supporting a broad claim about activities governed by fixed principles. Adelaide only talks about how the chess win happened. With no position from either speaker, this can''t be the disagreement.'),\n('f0b601f8-a1ad-4d2c-8fda-0b24c1d47fc9'::uuid,'e1a8ffb4dc7dd9db4145c276a1f17a84','Neither speaker says whether chess is typical of what humans usually do. Graham only needs chess to be an activity \"governed by fixed principles,\" not a typical one. Adelaide talks about the programmers'' work, not about how chess compares with everyday human thinking. No positions, no disagreement.'),\n('bd8b3976-1153-4505-bd61-b01c60bd8c8b'::uuid,'ab1488bcaaf26428ff5a3f35f9114708','Graham AGREES: the computer''s win \"shows\" that machines can master fixed-principle activities, so Graham counts the win as the machine''s accomplishment. Adelaide DISAGREES: the computer was \"simply an extension of the people who programmed it,\" and the programmers defeated the champion \"using a computer.\" The credit goes to the people.\n\nAdelaide''s reply opens with \"you are overlooking.\" That tells you Adelaide is attacking how Graham reads the evidence, not the conclusion directly. So look for the disagreement in the evidence itself: who actually beat the champion.'),\n('379db44e-a024-4912-b720-af13ef49f92a'::uuid,'02dde599846689050fda9d60c5627739','Graham might accept this, since Graham moves from mastering fixed-principle activities to a \"truly intelligent machine.\" But Adelaide doesn''t take the other side. Adelaide never says that performing by fixed principles fails to show intelligence, only that the intelligence behind this win belonged to the programmers. Adelaide could accept D and still credit the people.'),\n('f3541d8a-33eb-407d-85e2-562b1e58d1d6'::uuid,'070b67213efbcce33809afb7a094dc24','Graham says machines can master these activities, which goes further than aiding them, so Graham would likely accept that tools can help. Adelaide treats the computer as an extension of its programmers, basically a tool, but says nothing about \"any\" fixed-principle activity. Neither speaker denies this, so there''s no disagreement.'),\n('129a49b3-bfdf-4aa7-a83c-5f5720b45195'::uuid,'b2c1dae622c8aa73fce1527c27203668','Tate AGREES: material needs matter more than freedom and autonomy, and some countries meet those needs better as autocracies. Put those together and those countries are better off as autocracies. Wong DISAGREES: \"all countries are better off as democracies.\" One exception is enough to contradict an \"all\" claim, and A asserts exactly that exception.\n\nWhen one speaker makes an \"all\" claim, check whether the other speaker supplies a counterexample. That''s often the cleanest disagreement on the page.'),\n('17499598-763f-4132-9589-4c6c984dae87'::uuid,'eed32fd5f227d3195154a2695e0c6895','Tate disagrees: the \"simple material needs of people are more important\" than freedom and autonomy. But Wong never ranks freedom and autonomy against anything. Wong says countries are better off as democracies without saying why, so we can''t put Wong on the agree side. An answer only one speaker addresses can''t be their disagreement.'),\n('bebfb802-e001-40c5-be87-2afd037cd852'::uuid,'5bf35a53b6c059d936e2b5c9710e5873','Tempting, because Wong mentions countries that aren''t democratic yet. But Wong says a transitional stage is required \"before a country can become democratic,\" which describes a delay, not an impossibility. Wong never says some countries can''t make it. Tate doesn''t address whether countries can become democracies at all. No positions, no disagreement.'),\n('b3cb96cf-5c96-44c9-ad5c-16ac358f867e'::uuid,'64dedafeae95b2875c2fb5ed0917e344','Tate says this word for word: freedom and autonomy \"are of genuine value.\" Wong doesn''t object. If anything, someone who thinks every country is better off as a democracy likely values what democracy provides. Agreement, or at most silence, isn''t a disagreement.'),\n('c0cf5f4d-61e8-4033-9956-1eab3bbac7f4'::uuid,'08fd09f3ecc2f57c7f80af01cb6db64e','Tate says some countries \"can better meet these needs as autocracies,\" which is a comparison. A democracy can meet those needs and still meet them less well than an autocracy, so Tate doesn''t have to deny this. And Wong never talks about material needs. Neither speaker takes a clear position.'),\n('e6e3674d-1b5b-4e8a-bab7-82c680153aa8'::uuid,'e558e6b16eb7ad8f38a66bb91a7be115','Ana says it is not the government''s business to prevent people from doing things that harm only themselves. Pankaj never says what the government''s business is; Pankaj only describes where the ban applies. Pankaj could fully accept Ana''s principle and still object, because the objection is about whether the ban falls under it.'),\n('0ac01bec-dc9d-45df-bbe7-cc2615ebf4af'::uuid,'de3acb1c80c9ce5f404bdba615ad67f8','Ana appeals to libertarian principles, but Pankaj never challenges them. Pankaj''s reply doesn''t say government should ignore those principles. It says the ban isn''t the kind of thing they forbid. Arguing that a rule doesn''t apply is different from rejecting the rule.'),\n('c40a32c3-0ce4-4b22-a830-6fc26f568985'::uuid,'10641cbc02edd7d3be850b794f6751e9','Ana AGREES, by assumption. Ana opposes the ban by citing a principle about things \"that harm only themselves.\" That principle only reaches the ban if the ban is aimed at harm to smokers alone.\n\nPankaj DISAGREES. The ban applies only in public places, and people \"could still smoke all they want in private.\" A ban meant to protect smokers from themselves would leave a strange gap there. A ban meant to protect other people from smoke fits it exactly.\n\nWhen the second speaker doesn''t touch any explicit claim, look for the assumption that holds the first speaker''s argument together. That''s often where the disagreement lives.'),\n('c9c7d3fd-6a1d-4bbb-a8c5-5d180dd7bb40'::uuid,'bbb2757ce41d19e745544ad3d9304b96','Pankaj clearly agrees, saying the ban \"would apply only to smoking in public places.\" Can we put Ana on the other side, believing the ban would not prohibit smoking in public places? No. Ana says nothing about where the ban applies and may well assume it covers public places. Pankaj''s point rests on the word \"only,\" and this answer leaves it out.'),\n('b9cbdb41-4d2c-47ee-a0db-3a1c53b6085c'::uuid,'673463a72988de2f8ac3f28d288dc79f','Soltan AGREES: Soltan''s conclusion is that Klein \"should step down.\" Bell DISAGREES: Klein \"is just the person we need making important decisions in the future.\" Someone who should keep making the big decisions shouldn''t step down.\n\nNotice how much the two speakers share: the policies worked, and important decisions are coming. They split only on what to do about Klein. When speakers agree on the facts, look for the disagreement in their conclusions.'),\n('248a8c74-1ec6-40b3-93ae-a1e217b4b75e'::uuid,'5382124857e813efaac224975686264d','\"Always\" makes this too strong to pin on Bernard, whose argument is about Carl''s case, not every view in every situation. And even if Bernard held the general rule, Ayla could accept it too. Ayla doesn''t think the forum would legitimize Carl''s views at all; Ayla thinks it would expose them. The dispute is about what the forum would do, not about whether legitimizing bad views is acceptable.'),\n('6d3a9470-f5b7-4dae-9568-a74e25ebcdfe'::uuid,'d2873dfaa9d8d918899b6988471362bc','\"Every\" makes this too strong for Ayla. Ayla says this forum will provide convincing arguments against Carl''s views and people will see them for what they are. That''s one case, not a claim about every dangerous idea. And Bernard never says what happens when people hear forceful counterarguments. Without clear positions on both sides, this isn''t the disagreement.'),\n('b068e848-36fb-4c3c-b345-001bd0e9d697'::uuid,'2d532659124e790c9d1a865f16d81cd2','Ayla AGREES almost word for word: \"The best way to combat false views is to challenge them in public.\" Challenging views in public means letting them be expressed in public. Bernard DISAGREES: giving Carl''s views a platform would \"legitimize them\" and \"help to promulgate them,\" which is the opposite of fighting them.\n\nThe move: when two speakers share a goal (nobody wants Carl''s views adopted), look for the disagreement in the means. Then match the answer''s general words to the case. \"Erroneous ideas\" stands in for Carl''s false views, and \"allowing the public expression\" stands in for inviting Carl to the forum.'),\n('69dafa2e-e158-440c-baeb-409d650dd4ec'::uuid,'b8846b73545540c45710fc2593de2628','Bernard calls Carl''s views \"false, and worse, dangerous,\" but that''s about Carl''s views, not a general claim that people with false views tend to endanger society. And Ayla never says whether false views make their holders dangerous. Without a clear position from either speaker, this can''t be the point at issue.'),\n('e766b047-89e1-46ff-aa38-4a6214ed3601'::uuid,'71c7ef49a1326595b99b498a4f2e99c7','Both speakers seem to agree, so it''s not a disagreement. Bernard wants to avoid anything that would support the adoption of Carl''s views. Ayla wants to combat those views so people \"see them for what they are.\" Neither wants Carl''s views adopted. Ayla never calls them \"dangerous,\" but nothing Ayla says supports encouraging their adoption either.')\n) v(id,ob,nb) where t.id=v.id and md5(t.body)=v.ob returning t.id;"}

3	('b1263c88-23c0-4741-b8db-d358aca86a38'::uuid,'d0c541810b81496af94848989e808dff','On Main Conclusion, read with one expectation in mind: the conclusion usually arrives before its support. Most of the time it is the first sentence or the sentence right after a pivot like "however."
4	
5	So test the first sentence. It is a prediction: encryption "will bring the writing of biographical history virtually to an end." Nobody can observe the future, so a prediction is an opinion, and an opinion needs support. Ask: why should we believe that? The rest of the paragraph answers. 6	
7	Notice the chain has two levels. The "so" claim (historians will lose the revealing material) is itself a conclusion, supported by the encryption premise. But the argument does not stop there. 9	
10	Expect traps that restate the encryption premise or the "so" claim about historians losing access. Both sit on the path to the conclusion, but neither is where the argument ends up.','Goal','Goal'),

Yet there is an abundance of radioactive elements in the universe today.','Evidence','Evidence'),
12	('45dbc0d9-a286-424f-a410-af0ebba07c3e'::uuid,'f14c81b3b5a374fdad0d680b2f157c46','On Main Conclusion, expect the conclusion before its support. It is usually the first sentence or the sentence after a pivot.
13	
14	The first sentence hedges: radioactive elements "may have been created when the universe began." Here that "may" claim is a concession, not something the author sets out to prove. Then the pivot: "However, even if this occurred, these elements are clearly still being created in the universe today." "Clearly" marks the author''s own view. Check it with the support test: why should we believe new radioactive elements are being created?
15	
16	The rest of the paragraph answers that question. Most radioactive elements decay within a few million years. So if none had been made since the beginning, almost none would be left. But there are plenty left. Lined up:
17	
18	No new elements created after the beginning → almost none left today
19	Not almost none left (there is an abundance)
20	So: new elements have been created
21	
22	That is the contrapositive at work, and it lands exactly on the second sentence.
23	
24	The final sentence starts with "So," which tempts us to call it the conclusion. It is a conclusion, but an intermediate one: it is drawn from the decay premise and then used to prove the second sentence. On Main Conclusion, the last sentence is rarely the answer, so check it before you trust it.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
25	('700bf360-94ed-427f-8d38-5d5c17e0cfcf'::uuid,'f2aae07c3fb60c19801696d97dbd4b24','Look for a meaning match for the second sentence: "these elements are clearly still being created in the universe today." Swap the pronoun for what it refers to: radioactive elements are still being created today. The answer does not need "clearly" or the "even if" clause.
26	
27	Expect traps built from the "So" sentence, the decay premise, and the opening concession.','Goal','Goal'),
28	('9f682a5c-e6e2-4a79-a868-713cb9886c6d'::uuid,'3ff85f01eaec964f7130cff3ec3aa687','On Main Conclusion, expect the conclusion to come before at least some of its support. Most of the time it is the first sentence or a rebuttal after a pivot.
29	
30	This one is the rebuttal. The first sentence is a fact: people are debating what caused the recession. Nothing supports it, and nothing needs to. Then the pivot: "It is a mistake, however, to assume..." That is the columnist taking a side.
31	
32	To confirm, run the support test: why should we believe that answering the cause question is not essential? The next sentence opens with "after all," a support indicator, and gives a reason. Corrective lenses treated myopia well before anyone knew the cause was genetic. So a problem can be treated without knowing its cause.
33	
34	The four support indicators to listen for are for, after all, because, and since (FABS). When one of them opens a sentence, the claim right before it is usually what it supports.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
35	('f8fa244a-1b9a-4460-9863-0be7715e6e60'::uuid,'13ce34ae2e47d5f3dda100706bdc578d','When we have rebuttal-style conclusions, take an extra second to state the author''s position in the words of the position being rebutted. For example, if we hear, "Some people think that ketchup is a vegetable. However, they''re wrong," then the conclusion is "Ketchup is not a vegetable."
36	
37	Here the opposing position is: "We need to figure out what caused the current recession in order to improve the economy. It''s essential." The columnist says that is a mistake. It''s not essential. You could improve the economy even if you never figured out what caused the recession.
38	
39	Notice what kind of claim that is. "Essential" means required, so the columnist is saying knowing the cause is not necessary for improvement. Find the answer that says knowing the cause is not required, and nothing stronger.','Goal','Goal'),
40	('483bda78-e7ed-4f1e-a8b7-047836ea4211'::uuid,'c4faa171371e6907cbba61c063ea4c5a','Railroads rely increasingly on automation. Since fewer railroad workers are needed, operating costs have been reduced. The chief competitor of railway shipping is shipping by truck, and no reduction in operating costs is predicted for the trucking industry.','Evidence','Evidence'),
41	('5fd7255e-a2d2-42b3-9ba9-1cfa1f76ea10'::uuid,'c130a8f40fbb7ec8c7a305ee6ed4b49c','On Main Conclusion, expect the conclusion before at least some of the evidence. Usually it is the first sentence or a rebuttal after a pivot.
42	
43	This one breaks the usual pattern. The first sentence is a plain fact about automation, and nothing argues for it. The second sentence is a claim about costs, supported by the worker reduction ("Since fewer railroad workers are needed"). The third sentence is the first one that sounds like the author looking ahead: "This means that we can expect the volume of freight shipped by rail to grow." "We can expect" is a prediction, and "This means that" tells us it is drawn from what came before.
44	
45	Run the support test. Why should we believe rail freight will grow? Because rail''s costs went down. Then the last sentence adds a second reason after the conclusion: trucking, the main competitor, is not getting cheaper. So the conclusion sits in the middle, with support on both sides.
46	
47	Phrases like "this means that," "this shows that," and "this suggests that" can mark a main conclusion just as well as "therefore." Don''t assume the conclusion has to be the first or last sentence.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
48	('a44ddbaa-7d85-4d10-90b1-628b7856ef8c'::uuid,'986195cd4763cf85c1e430735f845b46','Find the answer that matches the third sentence: rail freight volume is expected to grow. Watch for answers that restate the cost claim or the trucking premise. They are reasons for the prediction, not the prediction.','Goal','Goal'),
49	('16dc0f84-9a71-46ad-b41d-fd85cadbad55'::uuid,'5faf56195adcd505c8d93e2400ed1161','Whenever we do Main Conclusion (or Role), we remind ourselves that 90% of the time, the conclusion will be the first sentence or it will be a rebuttal.
50	In this argument, the first sentence is clearly factual, not the author''s opinion, so it''s not a First Sentence Conclusion.
51	And when the second sentence begins with an attribution, "Some scientists claim", we would anticipate a Pivot into a Rebuttal.
52	Sure enough, we get "However, this conclusion is far from justified". The last sentence provides factual support. We can tell the last claim is factual because it is prefaced by "it is known that".
53	
54	Confirm with the support test: why should we believe the scientists'' conclusion is far from justified? Because natural cycles of ocean temperature can last 60 years or more, so a 15-year warming trend could be part of one. That is a reason to doubt the scientists'' explanation, not proof that it is false. So the climatologist''s conclusion is about the evidence: the human-pollution explanation has not been established.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
55	('040f7ebc-2ab8-4f5d-a00f-e1748dd5dc72'::uuid,'40c8ae0e2245a562b159d77895f46e14','Rossi states a general principle ("It is undemocratic for people to live under a government in which their interests are not represented") and applies it to children: since children''s interests are sometimes different from their parents'', children should have the right to vote.','Rossi''s argument structure','Rossi''s Argument'),
56	('64ff2094-a2ad-452d-b663-2ae8fe80efbf'::uuid,'71b24f58affa375a5e462c627508f952','The stem asks only about Rossi, so Smith''s reply is background here. Read Rossi''s two sentences as conclusion plus evidence.
57	
58	Conclusion: children should have the right to vote.
59	Evidence: it is undemocratic for people to live under a government that does not represent their interests, and children''s interests are sometimes different from their parents''.
60	
61	Now characterize the evidence. The first sentence is not about children at all. It is a broad rule about all people: if your interests are not represented, your situation is undemocratic. The second sentence plugs children into that rule. Their interests can differ from their parents'', so the parents'' votes do not fully represent them, so by the rule children need a vote of their own.
62	
63	That is one of the standard Method moves: state a general principle, then apply it to a specific case. Other common moves are analogy, counterexample, ruling out alternatives, and raising an overlooked consideration. None of those fits Rossi. There is no comparison case, no exception, and no rival explanation.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
64	('9ed8ab00-1856-4758-ac73-2673fa84fbef'::uuid,'300b0778f7dac6a8e42871cf0b4e8a82','Look for an answer saying Rossi relies on a general principle, or applies a broad rule to a specific group. Check every answer against Rossi''s argument only. Smith''s reasoning is the source of at least one trap.','Goal','Goal'),
65	('da224888-545e-40ea-91c7-476774fdb2d6'::uuid,'7d53604392010fbdaab9af8dc96760dc','The ad''s structure is an analogy: pride causes Austin Stables to outperform competitors in horse racing; Barr has the same tradition of pride; therefore Barr should outperform its competitors in cars. The ad reaches its conclusion by drawing a parallel between two different industries based on a shared trait.
66	
67	The sentence "Such a tradition of pride is not only found in the business of horse racing" is the bridge. It tells us the ad wants pride''s payoff in one business to carry over to another. That is how an analogy works: what is true of one case is claimed for a similar case.
68	
69	On Method, run the "argues X by Y" test on every answer: X has to match the conclusion and Y has to match the evidence. Here X is that Barr will beat its competitors, and Y is a comparison to a stable whose pride made it a winner. An answer that gets either half wrong is out.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
70	('a317e1e5-ab37-4e5b-bbab-d8b82a2d5887'::uuid,'a19b42b50b23ea070d39db288d13638d','Pointing out that the correlation (people tend to gesture less when they talk about abstract rather than physical concepts) is far from universal is not enough reason to reject the researchers'' claim.','Conclusion','Conclusion'),
71	('19f9c71a-58b8-411d-8e59-a606c1293ce5'::uuid,'2040fcc203ec7348999a5321a051346a','Some people perceive words like "comprehension" as expressing a physical action, like grasping something, rather than a state of understanding, which is abstract.','Evidence (because)','Evidence (because)'),
72	('cf1bccc3-eaff-40dc-85d7-d20d5fbc952f'::uuid,'1d92c7c8b2e296ca774c1443d6e0aea7','Start with what the author is responding to. Researchers say people tend to gesture less when they talk about abstract concepts. A critic could point out exceptions: people who gesture while discussing something abstract. The author says exceptions like that are not enough to throw out the claim.
73	
74	Why not? Because some of the exceptions may not be exceptions at all. Take someone who gestures while talking about comprehension. That looks like a strike against the researchers, since comprehension, as a state of understanding, is abstract. But if that person thinks of comprehension as grasping something, a physical action, then the person is talking about a physical concept, and gesturing is exactly what the researchers'' claim predicts.
75	
76	So the author keeps the generalization and explains away the counterevidence. The cases that seem to break the pattern are reclassified using a fact about how people perceive words. Notice that the author never says the correlation is universal and never brings in new support for it. The job is defensive: show that the apparent exceptions do not hurt the claim.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
77	('d4decaa6-f9e5-49e7-9cc9-94df1d943950'::uuid,'b5f5d21b4076f1128e9c49137023cdbe','Use "argues X by Y" on every answer. X should match the conclusion: the researchers'' claim survives the objection that the correlation is far from universal. Y should match the evidence: a fact about how some people perceive certain words.
78	
79	In Method terms, the author answers a counterexample by giving it an alternate explanation that fits the rule. So look for something like: "uses a fact about how people perceive words to show that apparent exceptions are consistent with the generalization."','Goal','Goal')

Why should we believe rail freight will grow? Because rail''s costs went down. Then the last sentence adds a second reason after the conclusion: trucking, the main competitor, is not getting cheaper. So the conclusion sits in the middle, with support on both sides.\n\nPhrases like \"this means that,\" \"this shows that,\" and \"this suggests that\" can mark a main conclusion just as well as \"therefore.\" Don''t assume the conclusion has to be the first or last sentence.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),\n('a44ddbaa-7d85-4d10-90b1-628b7856ef8c'::uuid,'986195cd4763cf85c1e430735f845b46','Find the answer that matches the third sentence: rail freight volume is expected to grow. Watch for answers that restate the cost claim or the trucking premise. They are reasons for the prediction, not the prediction.','Goal','Goal'),\n('16dc0f84-9a71-46ad-b41d-fd85cadbad55'::uuid,'5faf56195adcd505c8d93e2400ed1161','Whenever we do Main Conclusion (or Role), we remind ourselves that 90% of the time, the conclusion will be the first sentence or it will be a rebuttal.\nIn this argument, the first sentence is clearly factual, not the author''s opinion, so it''s not a First Sentence Conclusion.\nAnd when the second sentence begins with an attribution, \"Some scientists claim\", we would anticipate a Pivot into a Rebuttal.\nSure enough, we get \"However, this conclusion is far from justified\". The last sentence provides factual support. We can tell the last claim is factual because it is prefaced by \"it is known that\".\n\nConfirm with the support test: why should we believe the scientists'' conclusion is far from justified? Because natural cycles of ocean temperature can last 60 years or more, so a 15-year warming trend could be part of one. That is a reason to doubt the scientists'' explanation, not proof that it is false. So the climatologist''s conclusion is about the evidence: the human-pollution explanation has not been established.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),\n('040f7ebc-2ab8-4f5d-a00f-e1748dd5dc72'::uuid,'40c8ae0e2245a562b159d77895f46e14','Rossi states a general principle (\"It is undemocratic for people to live under a government in which their interests are not represented\") and applies it to children: since children''s interests are sometimes different from their parents'', children should have the right to vote.','Rossi''s argument structure','Rossi''s Argument'),\n('64ff2094-a2ad-452d-b663-2ae8fe80efbf'::uuid,'71b24f58affa375a5e462c627508f952','The stem asks only about Rossi, so Smith''s reply is background here. Read Rossi''s two sentences as conclusion plus evidence.\n\nConclusion: children should have the right to vote.\nEvidence: it is undemocratic for people to live under a government that does not represent their interests, and children''s interests are sometimes different from their parents''.\n\nNow characterize the evidence. The first sentence is not about children at all. It is a broad rule about all people: if your interests are not represented, your situation is undemocratic. The second sentence plugs children into that rule. Their interests can differ from their parents'', so the parents'' votes do not fully represent them, so by the rule children need a vote of their own.\n\nThat is one of the standard Method moves: state a general principle, then apply it to a specific case. Other common moves are analogy, counterexample, ruling out alternatives, and raising an overlooked consideration. None of those fits Rossi. There is no comparison case, no exception, and no rival explanation.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),\n('9ed8ab00-1856-4758-ac73-2673fa84fbef'::uuid,'300b0778f7dac6a8e42871cf0b4e8a82','Look for an answer saying Rossi relies on a general principle, or applies a broad rule to a specific group. Check every answer against Rossi''s argument only. Smith''s reasoning is the source of at least one trap.','Goal','Goal'),\n('da224888-545e-40ea-91c7-476774fdb2d6'::uuid,'7d53604392010fbdaab9af8dc96760dc','The ad''s structure is an analogy: pride causes Austin Stables to outperform competitors in horse racing; Barr has the same tradition of pride; therefore Barr should outperform its competitors in cars. The ad reaches its conclusion by drawing a parallel between two different industries based on a shared trait.\n\nThe sentence \"Such a tradition of pride is not only found in the business of horse racing\" is the bridge. It tells us the ad wants pride''s payoff in one business to carry over to another. That is how an analogy works: what is true of one case is claimed for a similar case.\n\nOn Method, run the \"argues X by Y\" test on every answer: X has to match the conclusion and Y has to match the evidence. Here X is that Barr will beat its competitors, and Y is a comparison to a stable whose pride made it a winner. An answer that gets either half wrong is out.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),\n('a317e1e5-ab37-4e5b-bbab-d8b82a2d5887'::uuid,'a19b42b50b23ea070d39db288d13638d','Pointing out that the correlation (people tend to gesture less when they talk about abstract rather than physical concepts) is far from universal is not enough reason to reject the researchers'' claim.','Conclusion','Conclusion'),\n('19f9c71a-58b8-411d-8e59-a606c1293ce5'::uuid,'2040fcc203ec7348999a5321a051346a','Some people perceive words like \"comprehension\" as expressing a physical action, like grasping something, rather than a state of understanding, which is abstract.','Evidence (because)','Evidence (because)'),\n('cf1bccc3-eaff-40dc-85d7-d20d5fbc952f'::uuid,'1d92c7c8b2e296ca774c1443d6e0aea7','Start with what the author is responding to. Researchers say people tend to gesture less when they talk about abstract concepts. A critic could point out exceptions: people who gesture while discussing something abstract. The author says exceptions like that are not enough to throw out the claim.\n\nWhy not? Because some of the exceptions may not be exceptions at all. Take someone who gestures while talking about comprehension. That looks like a strike against the researchers, since comprehension, as a state of understanding, is abstract. But if that person thinks of comprehension as grasping something, a physical action, then the person is talking about a physical concept, and gesturing is exactly what the researchers'' claim predicts.\n\nSo the author keeps the generalization and explains away the counterevidence. The cases that seem to break the pattern are reclassified using a fact about how people perceive words. Notice that the author never says the correlation is universal and never brings in new support for it. The job is defensive: show that the apparent exceptions do not hurt the claim.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),\n('d4decaa6-f9e5-49e7-9cc9-94df1d943950'::uuid,'b5f5d21b4076f1128e9c49137023cdbe','Use \"argues X by Y\" on every answer. X should match the conclusion: the researchers'' claim survives the objection that the correlation is far from universal. Y should match the evidence: a fact about how some people perceive certain words.\n\nIn Method terms, the author answers a counterexample by giving it an alternate explanation that fits the rule. So look for something like: \"uses a fact about how people perceive words to show that apparent exceptions are consistent with the generalization.\"','Goal','Goal')\n) v(id,ob,nb,ol,nl) where t.id=v.id and md5(t.body)=v.ob returning t.id;"}

2	('4d006c9f-2adb-4b45-ad0a-c61058ef5e47'::uuid,'e2632d05168ef65add8ae905acc978f3','Line up what the psychologists studied against what the author concludes.
3	
4	The research is about one schedule. Children in nine-month schools forget a significant amount during summer breaks. That''s it. Nothing in the evidence is about the twelve-month schedule. Yet the author claims that schedule "will insure" students do not forget during their breaks.
5	
6	Where does that guarantee come from? The author is assuming forgetting is a problem of the nine-month schedule only. But the twelve-month schedule still has breaks. Three of them, each a month long.
7	
8	Given that kids forget over a long summer, how could we argue the twelve-month plan is no better? Maybe kids forget plenty in a month, too. If a month away wipes out most of what a summer away does, the twelve-month schedule could mean three rounds of forgetting instead of one.
9	
10	So the gap is in the comparison. The evidence shows a bad result in one situation, says nothing about the other, and the author treats the other as free of it.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
11	('730ec4b7-2e8c-497f-b24e-11ad4b771c51'::uuid,'0fc0d08152cad15a92f7806b20bb18e5','Look for an answer saying the argument assumes, without evidence, that forgetting during breaks happens only under the nine-month schedule. A "fails to consider" version would also work: the argument fails to consider that students might forget during month-long breaks too. Either way, the answer should point at the missing evidence about the twelve-month schedule.','Goal','Goal'),
12	('aac5aeae-90fe-4f43-975e-7342189649ab'::uuid,'d2efdc0e0e243e46187ca775840d0b4a','Watch the word "crime" change jobs between the evidence and the conclusion.
13	
14	The evidence is about classification. Vagrancy laws turn "innocuous everyday occurrences" into crimes. Acts that were legal yesterday are illegal today.
15	
16	The conclusion is about amount. Vagrancy laws "increase crime." The columnist sets this against the laws'' purpose of reducing "criminal activity," which makes it sound like people are now doing more harmful things.
17	
18	Picture a park where twenty people nap on benches every week. A vagrancy law passes. The same twenty people nap on the same benches. On paper, the town now has twenty crimes a week that it didn''t have before. Has anyone''s behavior changed? No. The count went up because the label changed.
19	
20	So the evidence supports only "more acts are now called crimes." The conclusion needs "people are committing more crime." The columnist slides from one claim to the other as if they were the same.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
21	('e242526d-7b83-4e28-97dd-4583986280a8'::uuid,'704cb2b38b8e165d060e6de25fc7444a','Look for an answer saying the argument confuses relabeling acts as crimes with an actual increase in criminal activity. It might say the argument fails to distinguish the two, or that it uses "crime" in two different senses.','Goal','Goal'),
22	('be542e31-fdb8-4f27-9efd-47a6c021fbd1'::uuid,'a06f0987e29377977b61d5e19435ecad','The evidence is a conditional. Fresh okra is required for the best seafood gumbo:

24	best gumbo → fresh okra
25	
26	Its contrapositive tells us what happens without fresh okra:
27	
28	no fresh okra → no best gumbo
29	
30	That''s what the evidence supports. Now read the conclusion closely. Without reliable fresh okra, customers could not count on good gumbo:
31	
32	no fresh okra → no good gumbo
33	
34	"Best" became "good." Those are different standards. A gumbo can be good without being the best. Without fresh okra, Chris might still serve a very good gumbo that just isn''t the best one possible.
35	
36	So the critic takes a requirement for the top level of quality and treats it as a requirement for a merely good level. Given the evidence, how could we argue customers can still count on good gumbo? Say good gumbo doesn''t need fresh okra at all.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
37	('bdf29502-171b-4a69-a682-dcb73b880d1c'::uuid,'235d486bb690f455d35341a4ec31d444','Start with the first sentence, because the whole argument rests on it: people "can either fight for anarchy or they can tolerate totalitarian government control."
38	
39	Those are the two extremes. Anarchy means no government at all. Totalitarian control means government controls "all facets of human life." What about everything in between? A government that runs the courts and the roads but leaves your personal life alone is neither one.
40	
41	Now look at the support. The evidence attacks only total control: it destroys the spirit and makes life miserable. Fine. Given that, how could we still argue against fighting for anarchy? Point to a third option. If limited government is available, rejecting totalitarian control doesn''t push us to anarchy. It could just as easily push us to the middle.
42	
43	The argument works only if those two options are the only ones. That''s a false choice: two options presented as if nothing else exists.
44	
45	Notice the flaw sits in a premise. We usually accept premises as true, but when an argument reaches its conclusion by knocking out one side of an either/or, the right answer can point out that the either/or was never complete.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
46	('dbf4f7ad-6583-4e0a-a7da-bcc3bbe42768'::uuid,'b9813e0033fc0f564281be79b1c0a3b2','The evidence is about words. We call a web page a "site," and we talk about "visiting" it. Those words also describe land.
47	
48	The conclusion is about law. Trespass law, which protects land, should be extended to protect property in cyberspace.
49	
50	The bridge between them is an analogy: web sites resemble real estate, so they should be treated like real estate. But what resemblance has been shown? Only that we use some of the same words. That''s a similarity in vocabulary, not in anything that matters to the law.
51	
52	Test it with another shared word. We "drive" traffic to a web page. Should traffic laws apply to web pages? Of course not. Shared vocabulary doesn''t show that two things are alike in the ways a law cares about, such as how they can be entered, damaged, or used without permission.
53	
54	Given the evidence, how could we argue against the conclusion? Point out that a web site might share nothing with land except the words we use for it.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
55	('3d7044df-b611-43ef-bc37-d1034be5d990'::uuid,'c8e909be97700ddd3541556b8ff79b32','Start with the curious fact. The Swahili and the Oromo both built tombs with large pillars and paneled facades, and no other people in contact with the Swahili built them.
56	
57	The historian''s explanation: Oromo culture influenced Swahili culture. That''s a claim about direction. The style traveled from the Oromo to the Swahili.
58	
59	What evidence points that way? None. The evidence shows the two cultures share the style. It dates the Swahili tombs to the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, but gives no date at all for the Oromo ones.
60	
61	Given that, how could we argue the Swahili were not influenced by the Oromo? Flip the arrow. Maybe the Swahili built these tombs first and the Oromo picked up the style from them. Everything in the evidence fits that story just as well. (The two cultures could even have arrived at the style independently.)
62	
63	For the Oromo to have influenced the Swahili, the Oromo must have had the style first. The historian takes that for granted.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
64	('85f2aa0c-b959-4739-b2cd-80f2eb60e896'::uuid,'bf573070a99270505867345cb28f4a1f','Look for an answer saying the historian assumes the Oromo built these tombs before the Swahili did. A "fails to consider" version works too: the argument fails to consider that the Swahili may have influenced the Oromo.','Goal','Goal'),
65	('492f384f-6a7a-4799-a551-2ca7ac5c336a'::uuid,'cee5e26ae533844193dffe6e0bd8376d','Sort the celestial objects in this galaxy into three groups. Stars generate light. Planets don''t; they only reflect it. And there are "many other celestial objects" that are neither.
66	
67	The conclusion says some of those other objects generate light. Why? The evidence never says whether the other objects generate light. The author seems to reason: planets don''t generate light, these objects aren''t planets, so some of them do. Here is the shape:
68	
69	planet → does not generate light
70	some objects are not planets
71	so, some of those objects generate light
72	
73	That''s an illegal negation. The rule tells us what is true of something that is a planet. It tells us nothing about things that aren''t planets. The author is treating planets as if they were the only objects that don''t generate light, and nothing supports that.
74	
75	Given the evidence, how could we argue the conclusion is false? Suppose every one of those other objects is dark, like a planet. Then there are many objects that are neither stars nor planets, and none of them generates light.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
76	('c7d28d53-3548-4654-945d-960ddbd4e443'::uuid,'1ec64aaf4ba494f821f52d9ef8358e16','The stem says "fails to consider," so look for a possibility that would wreck the conclusion. The best one: objects other than planets might also fail to generate light. The answer might put it exactly that way: planets are not the only objects that do not generate light.','Goal','Goal'),
77	('3763d81a-64c3-4fb9-ae0a-a4bc3c7a30cc'::uuid,'0abbc95396f34a9f9f4a1f32eeab6e23','Among patients who received less than six weeks of PT, about 31% showed major improvement, whether they were treated by a general practitioner or by a specialist. Among patients who received PT for longer, about 50% showed major improvement, again regardless of whether they were treated by a general practitioner or by a specialist.','Evidence','Evidence'),
78	('cb8adb6d-d0e9-4940-b968-8cdcd4c6227b'::uuid,'451b16dc66ad940bf4561180bc5ec3e7','The conclusion is about one patient''s choice: picking a specialist or a general practitioner won''t change your odds of major improvement. The evidence is about whole groups: across all patients, the two kinds of practitioner get the same rates.
79	
80	Can equal group rates hide real differences? Try numbers. Suppose there are two kinds of injury, sprains and fractures, and each practitioner sees as many of one as the other. General practitioners get major improvement in 50% of sprains and 12% of fractures. Specialists get 12% of sprains and 50% of fractures. Both average 31%, the same figure the records show for short treatment. The records look identical.
81	
82	Now you have a fracture. Does your choice matter? Very much: 50% with a specialist, 12% with a general practitioner. The equal totals hid the fact that each practitioner is better at a different injury.
83	
84	So given the evidence, how could we argue the choice does matter? Point out that the overall numbers could be an average of very different results for different injuries.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
85	('db1f7ed4-5792-4923-90d8-a4c6f39f24ae'::uuid,'464f5a334e02cfdc7742389271abfffa','Look for an answer saying the argument overlooks that the two kinds of practitioner might do better with different kinds of injuries or patients. Then equal overall rates would not mean equal odds for any one patient.','Goal','Goal')
86	) v(id,ob,nb,ol,nl) where t.id=v.id and md5(t.body)=v.ob returning t.id;

2	('e34d0838-18d8-4ccd-8b0d-337355c43b69'::uuid,'015f118d9aba35d7caec6c561e823e14','The argument never weighs academic against nonacademic learning. It limits itself on purpose: the twelve-month schedule is preferred "insofar as academic learning is concerned." Test the presumption: if academic and nonacademic experiences were worth exactly the same, would the argument lose anything? No. It needs no view about their comparative worth.'),
3	('3549c011-a0fb-4d8c-a7fc-5134a91b642c'::uuid,'87e03991eaade35120dff6bd3051b4ee','The two groups here, children on a nine-month schedule and children on a twelve-month schedule, differ in exactly the way the argument cares about: how the breaks are arranged. That distinction is the subject of the argument, not an arbitrary line. The problem is what the author assumes about one side, not where the line is drawn.'),
4	('abf5c035-ed10-43f4-80e2-0a928c7019d1'::uuid,'f82a6cd5a82303244c2d2290de63db38','This matches the prediction in formal words. The "two situations" are the two schedules. The "undesirable result" is forgetting schooling over a break. The evidence ties that result to the nine-month schedule, and the author takes for granted that it belongs to that schedule alone, so the month-long breaks are assumed to be safe.
5	
6	When a comparison has evidence about only one option, check whether the argument quietly assumes the other option is free of the problem. That unstated "only" is what an answer like this one names.'),
7	('5e9e56b6-b330-429a-a95c-1978c233a16e'::uuid,'653a4aadac0c1a76d1592bea47c6cf31','Questioning the sample attacks the one part of the argument that has evidence behind it. The research only needs to describe children in nine-month schools, and nothing suggests it doesn''t. Grant that the data is perfectly representative and the argument still fails, because no one has shown that month-long breaks avoid the same forgetting.'),
8	('0e57e7f7-876d-47a4-86e7-37a3d9d78a20'::uuid,'ca8bcd00c1fb88d9b67cd06bdcf2efff','The author accepts the psychologists'' finding and uses it as the main evidence. That view is never rejected later in the argument. If anything, the argument leans on the research too far, by stretching a finding about summer breaks into a promise about month-long breaks.'),
9	('32e01438-bb80-4728-81ee-0a40814e08e8'::uuid,'699b6e128479874c1493b4ce8a40b18d','The columnist calls these occurrences "innocuous," which means harmless. The whole complaint is that harmless acts get treated as crimes. So the argument presumes the opposite of this answer: it treats the occurrences as not harmful.'),
10	('0d6f50c3-bbf9-4503-879d-0310cf72cd97'::uuid,'02d66b588d488920601bb03bfa42e3e1','The columnist never says vagrancy laws produce more innocuous occurrences. The occurrences stay the same; only their legal status changes. This answer invents an increase in the occurrences and then criticizes a causal inference the argument never makes.'),
11	('9a7649fd-02d9-45ac-9956-c066c97c575e'::uuid,'e2a39a136a473d1df894c86f45d74ffd','Ask whether naming the occurrences would fix anything. Suppose the columnist listed them: napping on a bench, standing on a corner. The argument would still slide from "more acts count as crimes" to "more criminal activity." The vagueness isn''t what breaks the argument.'),
12	('83218fb4-db52-490b-8e73-95df524be292'::uuid,'c52784f6e1fe090028e9fa43f9d35164','On a "fails to consider" answer, ask whether the idea would weaken. Suppose crime would rise even without vagrancy laws. That says nothing about whether the laws themselves add to the count, which is the columnist''s claim. Other causes of crime leave the argument untouched.'),
13	('ce414672-98b3-4b32-8fdd-fb51629899a8'::uuid,'0c86ef2a3b7af05aec370eccd92d0ef2','This names the slide we predicted. "An increase in criminal activity" is what the conclusion claims. "The reclassification of certain occurrences as crimes" is all the evidence shows.
14	
15	When a conclusion reuses a word from the evidence, check whether the word means the same thing in both places. If it doesn''t, the right answer says the argument fails to distinguish the two meanings, just as this one does.'),
16	('1177d3b7-2e6d-4096-8dd2-a3876ba58b4e'::uuid,'5d53023ab7080102e072aa17510ec7db','The critic never relies on the competitor being right. The argument only says what would follow "If this claim were true." A biased source can still make a claim, and a hypothetical about that claim stands or falls on its own logic. The bias never touches the reasoning.'),
17	('cf58bda1-3e22-45e9-8c00-3387c0935a20'::uuid,'0f406637165eb9f86dcb0d3d8f310b43','This describes a quality passing from an ingredient to the dish: stale okra, so stale gumbo. The critic does something different. The okra lacks freshness, and the critic concludes the gumbo lacks goodness. Those are two different qualities, so this isn''t the error. The real error is the shift from "best" to "good."'),
18	('b4c437ea-852d-4294-9b3f-193db0fa2049'::uuid,'d339331c61ceecc10faff7547a32fdf0','This is the tempting one, because it uses necessary and sufficient language and mentions both "best" and "good." Check what the argument does with fresh okra. It treats fresh okra as required for good gumbo: no fresh okra, no good gumbo. That''s treating it as necessary, not sufficient.
19	
20	To confuse it with a sufficient condition, the critic would have to argue that fresh okra guarantees good gumbo. The critic never says that. The error is a necessary condition moved from one standard to another, not a necessary condition flipped into a sufficient one.'),
21	('2be07b0a-184d-41e2-b0ea-8a07fb664d5f'::uuid,'2876324e0be5b1c4a70efbcd83882cd3','This matches the prediction. The evidence says fresh okra is necessary for the best seafood gumbo. The conclusion uses fresh okra as if it were necessary for good seafood gumbo.
22	
23	When a conclusion leans on a requirement from the evidence, check that the requirement is attached to the same thing. Here it moved from "best" to "good," and that move is the flaw this answer describes.'),
24	('6c2276ea-19e0-4752-90b1-72fb354b9a8b'::uuid,'67760a348e6ad050379a9bab2d336191','The critic''s hypothetical already allows for this. A supplier who "cannot reliably supply" fresh okra may still deliver it on some days, and customers still couldn''t count on getting it. Considering the possibility changes nothing, and it never touches the jump from "best" to "good."'),
25	('6bd57511-0dfa-420c-aa04-c0e0b4b6f9a6'::uuid,'a9e8e4cd282727e0b6dacb531bb8d9b7','The argument does give a reason anarchy beats total control. Total control "destroys the spirit," while anarchy "allows each individual the freedom to pursue a personal course of happiness." So the claim that the argument makes no attempt to explain this is false. The answer misdescribes the argument.'),
26	('9a25312d-531c-44b2-a51d-c7257f7d3f3c'::uuid,'cbd72b76eac4bd6e9b2160b6290966c2','The argument names tolerating totalitarian control as an option and then recommends against it. 27	('65454df0-03b0-42b4-87eb-f21bec5477f7'::uuid,'9a3e4ca2f9139a2199beaccb8745e032','This reverses the direction. The evidence is that totalitarian control makes life miserable, and the conclusion is that people should fight for anarchy. Check any "infers X from Y" answer: Y must match the evidence and X the conclusion. Here they are swapped.'),
28	('af5d9a8a-1e44-4e4d-8c0d-cef7451d55e2'::uuid,'01cd6fe6ae8abb96e1261a8f75dcbcc3','The anarchist says "history shows" that total control destroys the spirit. 29	('d0611d74-d9d1-49f8-9d07-278fbd372de1'::uuid,'50de1e31d51437477fabdb3da72da527','This is the false choice. The first sentence offers only two paths, and the argument needs that to be true: rejecting one path proves the other only when nothing else is available.
30	
31	When an argument gets to its conclusion by eliminating one option, check whether it has shown the options were the only ones. If it hasn''t, an answer like this one names the flaw.'),
32	('41e3ba86-2046-4d3c-9b7a-714a6e694947'::uuid,'2215c6290ea81e424900c4ab06c812d4','The argument never claims that people consider cyberspace property to be real estate. It claims only that some words for web sites "evoke ideas" of real estate. And even if many people did consider it real estate, that would be one more fact about how we talk and think, not a reason the law should treat the two alike.'),
33	('6f96cb51-1680-43fd-8f72-8af700bdecd4'::uuid,'a50a9ebfeecb46d40a045aa46f11b34c','Circular reasoning needs a premise that already assumes the conclusion. Check the premises: some words for web sites evoke real estate, and trespass law usually applies to real estate. Neither says trespass law should cover cyberspace. The conclusion goes beyond them, which is the opposite of circular.'),
34	('fe327f4b-d92b-4be6-96ac-a884624d6bdb'::uuid,'de248182e38d1b609e8ba546f2d470ae','The tempting part is the first sentence: most lawyers think copyright law is the best protection for web site owners. 35	('a7470bc8-e738-4186-b44e-458bb387b295'::uuid,'db546d94e43b09d3151d6c927a5a4e3f','This matches the prediction. The "similarities that constitute the analogy" are the shared words "site" and "visiting," and "merely verbal" names exactly what''s wrong with them.
36	
37	When an argument concludes that two things should be treated alike, ask what similarity it has actually shown, and whether that similarity matters for the treatment it recommends. Here the only similarity is in vocabulary.'),
38	('d4be0d8a-be23-47f8-ae49-c2fba22756a1'::uuid,'1c7a2c4a40bc55aaba2fdbb26371d78c','The argument mentions expert opinion only to move away from it. 39	('c69683a6-ec91-4a15-b1c8-a5746f49625d'::uuid,'7d1a1c1f58a33b23164c8d3b92d9a6fa','The historian''s point is about a building style: large pillars and paneled facades. 40	('cf285e65-f822-4053-843f-f3b576dafbdd'::uuid,'227304ea380dc9755565ff35690c1eb2','This flaw needs a timeline: A came before B, so A caused B. The historian gives no such timeline. 41	('d06b0378-d8ef-4185-800a-2801b0e1d690'::uuid,'feb779386e332b7e86f994e5617d58f1','Drawing a narrower conclusion than your evidence allows is caution, not a flaw. 42	('6f1a46ce-d1db-4c3b-8e24-c0b2510aeb64'::uuid,'159130c2e0ddded9afe210c95115fe27','This sounds like the classic alternative-explanation answer, so test it. 43	('138c0180-b00d-4676-860d-88f4ea869bb7'::uuid,'b7f584339feeb2577e93b6bb58572215','This is the prediction. Influence runs in a direction, and the conclusion picks one: Oromo to Swahili. 44	
45	Whenever a conclusion says one group influenced another, ask what establishes the order. If nothing does, the assumption that the source came first is the gap.'),
46	('a87522a7-6533-4cec-b41e-6c51f40708b2'::uuid,'75ba073b8ce5c65c08981476ecea07b1','Run the "fails to consider" test: would this weaken? Suppose planets are the only objects that reflect light. 47	('ed5d2a49-4bf1-4e6b-adf3-482e4502c131'::uuid,'2bd1fe7a53f6bd7cc6a2397caebf364f','The argument is only about this galaxy. 48	('a4752c56-4624-429c-ad28-17383d439f91'::uuid,'0d42f7d963567a92fdad6913f21d2fa0','Objects in other galaxies are outside the argument. 49	('8665cb3c-f38c-41f1-95a7-55b53b5c32a9'::uuid,'7651f4579fc0f462a5ab4852c8afa976','The argument never says light is the only difference between stars and planets. 50	('222e83dd-8235-489b-b1b9-52331375ef09'::uuid,'a60fae19557389355d5a4aee3120a1f2','This names the overlooked possibility. 51	
52	On a "fails to consider" answer, ask whether the idea would weaken the argument. This one opens exactly the gap the argument skipped.'),
53	('25055e28-603e-41ba-a038-2e99a1c467d8'::uuid,'a51006d8832df05bce966458697b7c9b','The argument never mentions "any improvement." Its evidence and its conclusion are both about major improvement. 54	('d55ccc72-2bc7-40b2-b69f-5b0b79b48d53'::uuid,'d8687bf0c27c6c6acfeb92cc9c5531b3','The argument doesn''t need to know which injuries need short treatment and which need long. 55	('50ac8dfa-b0b7-402f-af44-9c90e7836fcf'::uuid,'3fa6b315ffe6138c1e96b9f3fbe6a73d','The evidence is records of whether patients "showed major improvement." 56	('d719533f-d6de-486c-9cd6-90c1a21059da'::uuid,'302aa41f8373de18f925b50ede56d541','Percentages already account for group size. If 31% of 100 general-practitioner patients and 31% of 1,000 specialist patients improved, the rates are still equal. 57	('5cdd5e95-22eb-4381-8fdc-7e784071f139'::uuid,'d42647904370260310c396490ab69329','This is the hidden-subgroup problem from the numbers above. 58	
59	Whenever an argument moves from equal group results to "the choice won''t matter for you," check whether the group could split into parts where the results differ.')
60	) v(id,ob,nb) where t.id=v.id and md5(t.body)=v.ob returning t.id;

And a patient could feel more warmly about a specialist while the records still show the same improvement.'),\n('d719533f-d6de-486c-9cd6-90c1a21059da'::uuid,'302aa41f8373de18f925b50ede56d541','Percentages already account for group size. If 31% of 100 general-practitioner patients and 31% of 1,000 specialist patients improved, the rates are still equal. 18	('faeec81a-8f99-4993-b190-fdb631d6d733'::uuid,'9c7a82eee8d8bb9bac6710d9e1be18d1','The reason is that reforms are generally undertaken early in a new government.
19	(*why should we believe that?*)','Intermediate Conclusion','Intermediate Conclusion'),
20	('17884611-816c-465a-97e6-8a2062b1a24f'::uuid,'129beca1aa6c5fed133bba8ce0f54e8a','If leaders don''t act quickly to solve a problem and it becomes an issue later, they must either deny there is a problem or deny that anything could have been done about it. Otherwise, they have to admit responsibility for the problem persisting. Waiting puts leaders in that bind, which is why reform tends to come early.','Evidence','Evidence'),
21	('37b696bf-f5fe-452b-80bb-a04d449faf90'::uuid,'ef9b4386c4a3146c2eaefd26a4b41ef2','Whenever we''re doing Main Conclusion, we prime our brain before reading the paragraph: "Remember, on Main Conclusion and Role, the conclusion usually appears **earlier** than its support."
22	
23	For these questions, the conclusion is usually
24	- the first sentence
25	or
26	- a rebuttal
27	
28	When we read this first sentence, we''re asking ourselves, "Is this the author''s conclusion? Does it sound like the pundit''s opinion?"
29	
30	The normative language "it is good to X" tells us that the first sentence is an opinion. If the rest of the paragraph tries to support that claim, then we''ll know that the first sentence was the main conclusion.
31	
32	The second sentence telegraphs that support is being provided by saying "the **reason** is that ..."
33	
34	The third sentence explains why reforms come early. A leader who waits on a problem has to deny the problem, deny anything could have been done, or admit responsibility for it. Each layer supports the one above it, and the first sentence supports nothing else. That is the main conclusion.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
35	('dd7d6e60-de99-4bde-b1b3-11fb9b0bbfd8'::uuid,'d00ecbdf54239996a386d4b9502acf76','Find an answer that says the same thing as the first sentence: it is good for national leaders to be voted out of office after a few years. Watch for answers that restate the support about reforms coming early, or that invent new claims about motivation or time in office.','Goal','Goal'),
36	('3709b645-473e-4c56-9f12-87e7130f8a61'::uuid,'fbefa5ef6f436d44d4e74063e3c7bb04','Many people with access to the Internet express a longing for emotional connection to a global human community, which often leads them to use the Internet to learn about other cultures.','Opposing Ideas','Context'),
37	('1a438dd8-b976-47a9-9499-c31e240741a1'::uuid,'44539ecb91ddb89bfc3c06feeff56e4d','This argument follows a pattern you will see often on Main Conclusion: setup, pivot, conclusion, reason.
38	
39	The first two sentences describe what many people do: they long for a connection to a global community, so they use the Internet to learn about other cultures. Then "However" turns the paragraph. The columnist doesn''t dispute that people do this; the claim is that it probably won''t work. "for" then introduces the reason: the Internet is used mainly for acquiring information, not for developing feelings of interconnectedness.
40	
41	Check with the support test. Why believe that learning about other cultures online won''t satisfy the longing? Because the Internet is mainly an information tool. The reason fits, so the sentence between "However" and "for" is the conclusion.
42	
43	Keep its boundaries in mind: it is about learning through the Internet, it is hedged with "probably," and it is about the longing for emotional connection.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
44	('1f6ab750-57ee-49a9-b386-eb84a74794c1'::uuid,'c87f97d8fcd30c41d8866ddda6714419','Expect the correct answer to say that, for people who long for emotional connection to a global community, learning about other cultures through the Internet probably won''t satisfy that longing. Keep the hedge and the Internet setting.','Goal','Goal'),
45	('33828dbe-43ee-4861-b7df-b175a3adf075'::uuid,'065088003de8a7e4c9018dd8109dbe82','Banking industry visionaries foresee a bright day in the near future when customers will be able to transact all their financial business by means of computers or telephones from the comfort of their own homes.','Opposing Evidence','Opposing Point'),
46	('094f289f-7210-494a-85ae-098afcfce9b5'::uuid,'a943bcce0cc14025bd11f253e33ef7a5','As banks eliminate their branch offices and customer-service employees, customers will have to serve as their own tellers, and pay more transaction fees for their efforts.','Evicence','Evidence'),
47	('34c9d326-a55d-4f8d-a204-c0e5e8a6d76c'::uuid,'5f6d7d4002474afbaf7f54adc2bd31e1','Main Conclusion paragraphs often open with someone else''s view and then push back. This one does. The first sentence belongs to the banking industry visionaries, who see home banking as a bright day. Then "But" turns the paragraph: that may be more of a paradise for banks than for their customers. That sentence is the author''s own view.
48	
49	Run the support test. Why believe home banking helps banks more than customers? Because banks will cut branches and staff, and customers will do the tellers'' work and pay more fees for it. The last sentence answers the question, so it is evidence, and the sentence after "But" is the conclusion.
50	
51	Notice the claim is a comparison (banks more than customers) and it is hedged with "may."','Goal','Evaluate'),
52	('a78e131c-aa9f-4d01-977d-4b3d44c056fa'::uuid,'8377cb46f26d7ae7832362c690f59b7c','This is a three-layer argument, and the indicator words map it for us.
53	
54	"After all" means the sentence that follows supports the one before it. So the first sentence is the main conclusion, and the claim that social movements have adopted popular music is support for it. Inside that sentence, "since" adds a deeper layer: movements adopt popular music because it can help convert nonmembers, raise morale and express solidarity.
55	
56	Music can convert, raise morale, express solidarity
57	→ Social movements have adopted popular music to express their viewpoints
58	→ Popular music has been used for religious and political messages, which many listeners don''t realize
59	
60	Now look at what the support actually proves. Social movements using music to express their viewpoints shows that popular music does more than entertain. It shows nothing about what listeners realize. So the part of the conclusion the evidence backs is this: popular music has been used for something besides enjoyment. Expect the right answer to state that core in its own words.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
61	('9499c2a9-a70b-48aa-bf1c-d84142bcc9b2'::uuid,'6052306e4744d9ce5ae2a3f63b0bc15a','Look for an answer that captures the point of the first sentence: popular music has served purposes beyond simple enjoyment, such as carrying religious and political messages. Does it sound like the pundit''s opinion?\"\n\nThe normative language \"it is good to X\" tells us that the first sentence is an opinion. If the rest of the paragraph tries to support that claim, then we''ll know that the first sentence was the main conclusion.\n\nThe second sentence telegraphs that support is being provided by saying \"the **reason** is that ...\"\n\nThe third sentence explains why reforms come early. A leader who waits on a problem has to deny the problem, deny anything could have been done, or admit responsibility for it. Each layer supports the one above it, and the first sentence supports nothing else. That is the main conclusion.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),\n('dd7d6e60-de99-4bde-b1b3-11fb9b0bbfd8'::uuid,'d00ecbdf54239996a386d4b9502acf76','Find an answer that says the same thing as the first sentence: it is good for national leaders to be voted out of office after a few years. Watch for answers that restate the support about reforms coming early, or that invent new claims about motivation or time in office.','Goal','Goal'),\n('3709b645-473e-4c56-9f12-87e7130f8a61'::uuid,'fbefa5ef6f436d44d4e74063e3c7bb04','Many people with access to the Internet express a longing for emotional connection to a global human community, which often leads them to use the Internet to learn about other cultures.','Opposing Ideas','Context'),\n('1a438dd8-b976-47a9-9499-c31e240741a1'::uuid,'44539ecb91ddb89bfc3c06feeff56e4d','This argument follows a pattern you will see often on Main Conclusion: setup, pivot, conclusion, reason.\n\nThe first two sentences describe what many people do: they long for a connection to a global community, so they use the Internet to learn about other cultures. Then \"However\" turns the paragraph. The columnist doesn''t dispute that people do this; the claim is that it probably won''t work. \"for\" then introduces the reason: the Internet is used mainly for acquiring information, not for developing feelings of interconnectedness.\n\nCheck with the support test. Why believe that learning about other cultures online won''t satisfy the longing? Because the Internet is mainly an information tool. The reason fits, so the sentence between \"However\" and \"for\" is the conclusion.\n\nKeep its boundaries in mind: it is about learning through the Internet, it is hedged with \"probably,\" and it is about the longing for emotional connection.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),\n('1f6ab750-57ee-49a9-b386-eb84a74794c1'::uuid,'c87f97d8fcd30c41d8866ddda6714419','Expect the correct answer to say that, for people who long for emotional connection to a global community, learning about other cultures through the Internet probably won''t satisfy that longing. This one does. The first sentence belongs to the banking industry visionaries, who see home banking as a bright day. Then \"But\" turns the paragraph: that may be more of a paradise for banks than for their customers. That sentence is the author''s own view.\n\nRun the support test. Why believe home banking helps banks more than customers? Because banks will cut branches and staff, and customers will do the tellers'' work and pay more fees for it. The last sentence answers the question, so it is evidence, and the sentence after \"But\" is the conclusion.\n\nNotice the claim is a comparison (banks more than customers) and it is hedged with \"may.\"','Goal','Evaluate'),\n('a78e131c-aa9f-4d01-977d-4b3d44c056fa'::uuid,'8377cb46f26d7ae7832362c690f59b7c','This is a three-layer argument, and the indicator words map it for us.\n\n\"After all\" means the sentence that follows supports the one before it. So the first sentence is the main conclusion, and the claim that social movements have adopted popular music is support for it. Inside that sentence, \"since\" adds a deeper layer: movements adopt popular music because it can help convert nonmembers, raise morale and express solidarity.\n\nMusic can convert, raise morale, express solidarity\n→ Social movements have adopted popular music to express their viewpoints\n→ Popular music has been used for religious and political messages, which many listeners don''t realize\n\nNow look at what the support actually proves. Social movements using music to express their viewpoints shows that popular music does more than entertain. It shows nothing about what listeners realize. So the part of the conclusion the evidence backs is this: popular music has been used for something besides enjoyment. Expect the right answer to state that core in its own words.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),\n('9499c2a9-a70b-48aa-bf1c-d84142bcc9b2'::uuid,'6052306e4744d9ce5ae2a3f63b0bc15a','Look for an answer that captures the point of the first sentence: popular music has served purposes beyond simple enjoyment, such as carrying religious and political messages.
