41	('9f4ef585-edda-41b5-b5ea-61fc558935a1'::uuid,'0f3dd48fd9ff9df6759c1a9bc53b6891','Chain the two rules: virtue requires excellence, and excellence requires repeatedly overcoming inclinations to do wrong. So every virtuous person has overcome such inclinations, and you can''t overcome an inclination you never had.
42	
43	The move to repeat: when two "only" rules share a term, connect the outer ends, then ask what the final requirement itself presupposes. The right answer here states that presupposition.'),
44	('9bf9af78-c1ff-4171-8855-60df2e39885f'::uuid,'ed5cae321750368076a01c683c2fe1b3','Nothing in the report counts against small screens. It says unlimited tiles can be joined, not that a screen needs many tiles. A compound screen of just a few bright tiles fits everything we''re told.'),
45	('39a9401b-5cd4-4c88-ae7f-5858da4e7447'::uuid,'101abb4c5ddd848e4dae857a69bbc618','The report is about what the technology can do, not what buyers want. Test it: every sentence could be true even if nobody wanted to buy one of these sets. Demand is a new topic.'),
46	('3094c624-6649-4953-a36b-6587ea8759fb'::uuid,'ed4cd6ea44cc9148d4f1d8b64b815933','The report describes size and brightness at one fixed thickness: "a set of this thickness." It never changes the thickness, so it can''t tell us what a thicker set does to brightness. C invents a second relationship from a sentence that held thickness constant.'),
47	('15f1e9c6-1913-4426-b843-71cb92a57ccb'::uuid,'b62d7d0ffd3a59c1b4227ec5dfccf863','This is the problem and the fix put together. Noncompound screens in thin sets get dimmer as they grow. Compound screens are thin, each tile is bright, and unlimited tiles can be added without losing brightness or adding thickness. So a thin set can now have a screen that''s both bright and very large.
48	
49	The move to repeat: when a stimulus states a limitation and then says "however" and "moreover" about a new approach, the inference is usually that the new approach gets past that limitation.'),
50	('9071ab01-af53-4183-b3f6-ba3609cf6036'::uuid,'282ddd0fd083ad0f64e02b3497ee225f','The report lists advantages. It never says those are the only differences. Cost, resolution or durability could all be worse with compound screens, and nothing in the report rules that out. Silence about disadvantages doesn''t prove there are none.'),
51	('79776865-8d4b-4b95-bf94-665de1d5b8b4'::uuid,'2ec27b383d884592baecf2ab71d4a06f','The stimulus proves the opposite for some beliefs. The beliefs in the second sentence aren''t grounded in observable evidence, yet they come from a reliable source and so are reasonable. A belief can lack observable evidence and still be reasonable.'),
52	('5ac3e540-b9bb-4d34-920e-33fcea124682'::uuid,'94dd89528a9246a806f4bf0eab0adc71','The second sentence directly contradicts this. It describes beliefs that are based on a reliable source and are not self-evident. One counterexample is enough to sink an "all" claim, and the stimulus hands us that counterexample.'),
53	('6b221977-e312-4303-8fab-e3861fa7b159'::uuid,'b462f419ece11dd33b3e57b17905b5f1','The rule runs reliable source → reasonable. C runs it backward: reasonable (with no observable evidence) → reliable source. A reliable source is one way to make a belief reasonable, not the only way. A reasonable belief could rest on something else entirely.'),
54	('df219328-2674-438e-9f17-2b4ff1f8a6af'::uuid,'1f8554d206c3295b5f70ef4b36b260ad','This turns a "some" fact into a rule. The second sentence shows some beliefs lack both traits, but a group that lacks both doesn''t prove that lacking one forces lacking the other. Nothing rules out a belief that is self-evident yet not grounded in observable evidence.'),
55	('21b9fc7c-c685-4555-9802-c12811a5ff77'::uuid,'eb758e50ed392baedea71c902b2f3b42','Run the beliefs from the second sentence through the rule. They''re based on a reliable source, so they''re reasonable. They''re also not self-evident and not grounded in observable evidence. So among reasonable beliefs that aren''t self-evident, some aren''t grounded in observable evidence.
56	
57	The move to repeat: when a "some" fact triggers a rule, the rule''s result attaches to that group, and you can pair it with any other trait the group has. The right answer is often a "some" statement built from those traits.')
58	) v(id,ob,nb) where t.id=v.id and md5(t.body)=v.ob returning t.id;

Buying a competing package is still investing in computer modeling technology, so the requirement would be met. And meeting a requirement doesn''t guarantee anything, so we can''t say the predicament would have stayed unresolved.'),\n('5880ae4a-e75e-4d9e-87a7-1b8d3b654680'::uuid,'a1bcd3c5abbaecac54e97f363ee2e07b','This is the chain with the middle link removed. So no investment means no resolution.\n\nThe move to repeat: when two conditionals share a term, line them up so the shared term is the result of one and the trigger of the other, then connect the outer ends. Check the direction too. B keeps the \"not\" on both sides in the same order the rules give them, so it follows.'),\n('857f0842-9bec-472d-a187-7738d81adba7'::uuid,'47632ed0a408edb695cafb503a0052f6','The stimulus only tells us about rush-hour flow. When a chain has a weak link, the right answer keeps that weakness in its wording.'),\n('82131486-4dbf-4f30-8846-a80cdceb4c08'::uuid,'3b1c74e33e6b46ae4e7286e0dae03638','\"Most nurseries\" is a claim about the whole industry. {"project_id": "53b9a6f2-aba7-4ae4-8dd1-fa5b8aab4d76", "sql": "insert into lr_explanation_steps (explanation_id,position,label,body) select v.e,v.p,v.l,v.b from (values\n('cbdecbe8-ae3b-4bf8-8309-586d3c924c8c'::uuid,1,'Evaluate','Both sentences are conditionals, and they share one idea: the increase in rush-hour traffic flow. When two rules share a term, try to chain them.\n\nThe increase is the result in the first rule and the trigger in the second:\nno investment → no increase in rush-hour flow → predicament not resolved\n\nRead it forward: without the computer modeling investment, there''s no increase, and without the increase, the predicament stays unresolved. Or read the contrapositive: resolving the predicament required the increase, and the increase required the investment.\n\nEach link is a requirement. The investment was needed; nothing says it was enough. So the safe inferences are about what could not have happened without something, not about what was guaranteed to happen.'),\n('cbdecbe8-ae3b-4bf8-8309-586d3c924c8c'::uuid,2,'Goal','Look for the two ends of the chain joined together. Something like: if the city had not invested in computer modeling technology, the financial predicament would not have been resolved. The contrapositive version (resolving the predicament required the investment) would work just as well.'),\n('ac2194b1-6d03-4995-b8f9-556aa1f12fa4'::uuid,1,'Evaluate','Each sentence picks up where the last one ended: sewage leads to overnutrified water, overnutrified water leads to algae, and algae can lead to a fish kill. When causes and effects line up end to end like this, connect the first cause to the last effect.\n\nWatch the word \"sometimes\" on the last link. The algae don''t always feed toxic microorganisms. So the chain doesn''t prove that sewage always kills the fish. It proves that it can.'),\n('ac2194b1-6d03-4995-b8f9-556aa1f12fa4'::uuid,2,'Goal','Look for a softly worded answer that joins the start of the chain to the end: overnutrifying an estuary with sewage can lead to most of its fish dying. An answer that says this \"will\" happen goes past the \"sometimes\".'),\n('ef68a7e2-3ce5-47c5-9918-a96762181a53'::uuid,1,'Evaluate','We have one rule and one fact. The rule works on a variety''s suitability. The fact is about one variety: some nurseries call every Stark Sweet Melody tree \"miniature.\"\n\nCan we fire the rule? Only if we know whether Stark Sweet Melody is suitable for a tub or pot, and we''re never told. So we can''t say anyone is mislabeling outright.\n\nWhat we can do is put the inference in conditional form. Suppose Stark Sweet Melody is not suitable. Then none of its trees can be correctly labeled \"miniature.\" But some nurseries label them \"miniature.\" So those nurseries are mislabeling.\n\nAlso notice what the rule doesn''t give us. Suitability is required for a correct \"miniature\" label, but it isn''t enough. Even a suitable variety might not be miniature.'),\n('ef68a7e2-3ce5-47c5-9918-a96762181a53'::uuid,2,'Goal','Look for an answer that keeps the unknown as a condition: \"If Stark Sweet Melody is not suitable for a tub or pot, then some nurseries are mislabeling it.\" It might be phrased with \"unless,\" which means \"if not.\"'),\n('4e360875-0755-4a5a-850a-ef5d076a133c'::uuid,2,'Goal','Look for an answer built on the \"at most one exception\" idea: if there are two or more new courses, at least one has a prerequisite. Another safe version: any new course that didn''t come from Dean Wilson''s proposal has a prerequisite. Reject answers that assume a proposal gets approved, or that stretch the prerequisite rule past upper-level courses.'),\n('92043ea4-ffbd-42ba-b249-6faaf3768e45'::uuid,2,'Goal','Look for the fix stated as a capability: thin television sets can now have screens that are both large and bright. The \"However\" and \"Moreover\" tell us the report is building toward exactly that. Reject answers about what people want, what''s wrong with the new screens, or how thickness changes brightness.')\n) v(e,p,l,b) where not exists (select 1 from lr_explanation_steps x where x.explanation_id=v.e and x.position=v.p) returning id;"}

Here the bridge is "lemur." The only primates native to Madagascar are lemurs, and lemurs are lower primates. Put those together: every primate native to Madagascar is a lower primate.
10	
11	Now ask what that rules out. Lower primates and higher primates are two separate groups, so a lower primate is not a higher primate. That means no primate native to Madagascar is a higher primate. Not a diurnal one, not a nocturnal one, not any kind.
12	
13	The last sentence is the tempting one, because it looks like it chains with the lemur sentence. 18	('bc3a398f-5239-4954-85b8-150de15bb487'::uuid,'ff0c24f92cdbc2a82e8786f81369feb7','Match up the parts of the sociologists'' response. The sociologists object that a complex phenomenon cannot be caused by a simple phenomenon.
19	
20	That objection only lands if Y is a simple phenomenon. If voters'' economic decisions were themselves complex, the sociologists'' rule would not touch the theory. So the sociologists apparently assume that Y is simple.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
21	('47832198-bd32-4ead-ae25-2ab4f3e8e78b'::uuid,'3cac3607eb855e85ea3599bb155829aa','Look for an answer saying the sociologists treat voters'' economically driven decisions as a simple phenomenon, or at least as something that isn''t automatically complex.

24	('9257949a-230b-4b41-a4c4-abd07679c010'::uuid,'c9a998b9e12adcb03ecffd9cb25966bb','The citizen predicts a chain: a major tax cut for upper-income citizens, then a correspondingly large increase in investment, then new jobs. 25

27	
28	So the citizen needs, at a minimum, that the tax-cut money can go toward investment. It''s a small requirement, but the whole plan rests on it.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
29	('2ba7efc6-5622-4ad3-8663-b4ca174d2aea'::uuid,'ecb824d3b71df012431583a3964da8a9','Expect a defender: an answer that rules out the objection "the tax-cut money can''t end up as investment." 30	('f1ab5847-6ef7-4571-97c9-15d2dac5a986'::uuid,'9be7417684d2b25aab48dc45a98b0b74','The scientist argues by analogy. Selective breeding is a crude form of genetic engineering, and people have done it for millennia, so genetic engineering is not unethical.
31	
32	What has to be true about selective breeding for that to work? It has to be acceptable. If selective breeding were itself unethical, showing that genetic engineering resembles it would only put genetic engineering in bad company. The millennia of practice don''t settle that question either. A practice can be very old and still wrong.
33	
34	There''s a second gap: is choosing which animals breed really the same kind of thing as directly manipulating genetic codes? The scientist treats them as one category, and a critic could dispute that. But the first gap is the one the argument can''t do without. The scientist never says selective breeding is ethical.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
35	('e81c2c4a-d249-4334-b88c-446aad548525'::uuid,'3eb152713dcbfce68a168c3bc9da2de0','The answer will most likely protect the base of the analogy: selective breeding itself is not unethical. It could also defend the comparison, saying breeding and genetic-code manipulation are relevantly alike. 36	('7b91f97d-2de9-4390-ab49-d7c537e4a795'::uuid,'089fe55cad76fef3e04cb2314b3b1417','The evidence gives a trade-off. Presoaking saves time. Skipping it gives plumper beans. The conclusion says that when quality matters more than speed, skip the soak.

39	
40	So the author has to assume that plumper beans make for a better dish.','Evaluate','Evaluate')

2	('d09bbec0-51eb-49df-89af-535df224ddeb'::uuid,'202bca7fd1ee26a02c56a48c4228f2ad','This treats the ancestral species as a lemur. 3	('d64c48e3-e2d5-4ae0-991c-bb04e630db40'::uuid,'f938d591ee4ed832f38d825bd99cb4d2','This is the chain from the Goal. Lemurs are the only primates indigenous to Madagascar, and lemurs are lower primates, so every primate native to Madagascar is a lower primate and none is a higher primate. 4	
5	The move to carry forward: when an answer adds a qualifier to a "none" statement you''ve proven, check whether the qualifier only shrinks the group. A smaller slice of an excluded group is still excluded.'),
6	('e667bfa1-7239-4f50-87cf-0a48170a4d22'::uuid,'199d8ea367675614c6dfc7fa8433458c','The passage describes the ancestor, not the descendants. 7	('ea62f47c-ca93-4465-a834-b51fde78e899'::uuid,'a74d53ada6c69dfc6007263adcbc5cba','This is the belief the objection runs on. The sociologists reject the theory because a complex phenomenon can''t be caused by a simple one. That only counts against rational-choice theory if the cause the theory names, voters'' economically motivated decisions, is simple. 8	
9	The move: when a group rejects a theory by citing a general rule, ask which category the rule must put the theory''s key idea in. That classification is something the group has to believe.'),
10	('91303727-b979-40ca-97e8-03e3c45302de'::uuid,'75dd551d62e04ed1f735e69a88af93ba','The sociologists'' rule only rules one thing out: a simple cause can''t produce a complex result. It says nothing about how many causes a complex phenomenon has, or that each of them must be complex. A single complex cause would fit their rule just as well. "Many complex causes" adds a claim about number that we can''t trace to anything the sociologists said.'),
11	('d0fbbc49-2a5e-41dc-b342-a1693f9f0d03'::uuid,'17262829941900edf0f13b28582e746a','The sociologists never say what does cause popular support for parties. 12	('d598225c-6950-457b-9118-8100a31a6498'::uuid,'cd809889ee9c0da2c82b1dd337fae737','This is the reverse of what they believe. Their rule is about complex phenomena, so the objection only applies if popular support for parties is complex. If they thought it was never complex, their own rule wouldn''t touch the theory and the objection would collapse.'),
13	('96c1bf06-f611-4656-8b35-6f3266092de7'::uuid,'26d95a27dd8c2122b490206b8c826812','The sociologists don''t deny that voters care about economic advantage. They deny that those decisions are enough, by themselves, to explain something as complex as the rise of a political organization. Someone can agree that voters chase economic advantage and still think it''s too simple a cause.'),
14	('8087806a-c139-4f86-9acd-24154744ec16'::uuid,'3f03e59b3b68ca9507116c34dcc9726d','The citizen says unemployment is the highest ever, not that the recession is the worst ever. Negate A: this recession is not the worst in the country''s history. The tax-cut plan still works exactly as described, and record unemployment is still a reason to act quickly.'),
15	('8df43ddc-caab-4df4-94c0-f741a2a344e0'::uuid,'0d6ec3a7aa0572a73b059d388036d123','B is a sliding scale: the bigger the cut, the more likely people invest. 16	('0b839eed-266d-4c14-b984-dff421bb2429'::uuid,'6b5df403e978be9eb8637e1be697b7e9','Negate it: upper-income citizens could not use the tax-cut money in any way that increases investment. 17	
18	Notice how little D claims. It doesn''t say they will invest, only that they could. That''s typical of a correct Necessary Assumption answer: the argument doesn''t need a guarantee, but it can''t survive if the outcome it predicts is impossible.'),
19	('bbc83bd7-a43f-448d-8303-87715ee990a2'::uuid,'21ae306bfc3504d47bb1897d69841bbf','"Never" is far more than the argument needs. The scientist''s evidence is about one kind of manipulation, selective breeding. Negate A: some manipulation of genetic codes is unethical, say, manipulation done to cause harm. The scientist can accept that and still argue that genetic engineering, like selective breeding, is not unethical.'),
20	('24dabea0-eb2c-4347-b6c6-43e836b49b17'::uuid,'c1c716604c8c7c5d5fb37b1f93cea360','B is tempting because it sounds like a defense of genetic engineering. But the scientist''s evidence is selective breeding, something people did, not something nature accomplished. Negate B: some things nature accomplishes would be unethical to accomplish with science. The comparison between breeding and genetic engineering is untouched.'),
21	('9d05888d-1674-455d-9d01-37cd5e465428'::uuid,'3b256c75c1027e5f163d5dd03c3a7513','Negate it: "selective breeding for desired traits is unethical." Then the analogy turns against the scientist. Showing that genetic engineering is like selective breeding only puts it next to something unethical, and the millennia of practice just mean we''ve been doing something wrong for a long time. The conclusion falls.
22	
23	The move: in an argument by analogy, the conclusion borrows a property from the comparison case. The argument has to assume the comparison case actually has that property.'),
24	('710820c3-cac8-4ec5-95cc-9d798666d4e0'::uuid,'d0adadacb4b64104fff6ece2db79dd3f','The argument is about ethics, not usefulness. Negate D: selective breeding is not important for human survival. 25	('7ca72712-983a-4b7c-9943-b462ce4f7f8c'::uuid,'2c07322d7a891ac13efe90b80109a01f','E makes two sweeping claims: science can do only what is natural, and nothing natural is unethical. 26	('ab7be3d8-c1dd-47b3-b2ff-b9d7d4a150fc'::uuid,'a5dbbceecf1ea96b8f3e2319a1f2362c','This is the link from the Evaluate step. Negate it: plumper beans do not enhance the quality of a dish. Then skipping the soak buys nothing on the quality side, and the conclusion has no support.
27	
28	The pattern to repeat: find the idea that appears only in the conclusion (quality), find the idea it replaced in the evidence (plumper beans), and look for the answer that connects them.'),
29	('0c6d5556-a811-4bc3-baf7-ce13b161f6d5'::uuid,'d60c4389778910fc971ba3ad8597493a','A reverses the relationship the scientist needs. The argument needs ample food and little exercise to be capable of making animals unhealthy. A instead says a restricted diet and plenty of exercise guarantee health. Negate A: animals on that regimen could still be unhealthy for some other reason. The lab conditions could still harm them and skew results, so the argument is untouched.'),
30	('9afe9cb1-0652-4a44-948f-90b0bac54314'::uuid,'4492bc470b55a0b27eb55bb449170a35','Negate it: "these conditions *cannot* be unhealthy for the animals." Then the animals are healthy, the studies'' assumption holds, and there is nothing to skew the results.
31	
32	The move: when the evidence describes a condition and the conclusion says it skews results, the argument has to assume the condition actually affects what the studies take for granted. Here, that''s the animals'' health.'),
33	('9659c2e3-53c6-426d-b6e9-c52b170844b2'::uuid,'11af3bca50681334df5b466b208f1c50','The scientist''s claim is about lab animals and the studies that use them. 34	('141cd8cd-9fab-4f13-bc3a-c50ea68c1e6d'::uuid,'7e89bd89045844e58438d9be3d6be2d8','D says some studies already account for differences in living conditions. 35	('4cfc1100-804b-40eb-a325-b3203c009063'::uuid,'2c87ca9e85c3fc4746976babe8aa6420','E is about how consistent the animals'' eating is from day to day. 36	('250d31d6-6ab0-47cb-b1c0-b63dde4f4320'::uuid,'f3730786483c118843c8a0836f9a969a','The argument is about what highly profitable corporations can do, not about how many corporations do it now. 37	('c171f899-2ed0-4c1e-b522-b4c733420709'::uuid,'e1aa9ae1fb09d7f61b98b8b0ad54a306','B explains why savings would happen: if bonuses save money, it''s because they cut monitoring time. The conclusion still holds, since it only says the corporations can save money.'),
38	('d59a0789-6a22-45b1-aff3-e95dbc75ce67'::uuid,'d736be7fef8e830db03501d2ca7bf74e','C is about whether these corporations actually have managers monitor much. 39	('e18b806d-1d05-4ac2-9543-4cccf8e88403'::uuid,'01a77ae1a7d03ba65e28c7e218a5edba','This connects the two terms the argument swaps. The evidence says these corporations can save money by reducing monitoring, as long as employees get strong incentives. The conclusion says they can save money by giving expensive bonuses. Then the evidence''s condition isn''t met, and nothing in the argument shows the bonuses save any money.
40

42	('831eb0ef-227b-4cbb-9206-4d01df108da7'::uuid,'de018f71bbad7c1780f590bde8bd8d93','E is too strong. "Only if" makes expensive bonuses a requirement for any savings from reduced monitoring. 43	('98fb449c-dbe4-4f1b-8241-fcb4e09160e5'::uuid,'53052901acd8da4763ae35330bca20e4','The argument doesn''t care how people come to take a reasoned approach. The conditional conclusion is untouched, so the argument doesn''t need A.'),
44	('cab48aae-47a5-4fa6-a1d7-78a31f45233d'::uuid,'dad8e84af35036d648f0687bbb542f73','B is about a cost of government doing its job: does it get in the way of people pursuing their own welfare? The argument never weighs that cost. Negate B: government can''t serve its purpose without diminishing people''s ability to promote their welfare. The link between reasoned people and less need for government is unaffected.'),
45	('873db1a2-d32b-47b8-aa8b-77575bbd7d64'::uuid,'e4cd7c8fe8931e47025b1122cd16d39c','This is the link the Goal predicted. Government exists to prevent people from injuring others. Negate C: people who take a reasoned approach are just as likely to injure others as anyone else. Then a reasoned population needs government''s protection just as much, and the case for less power falls apart.
46	
47	The move: find the idea that appears only in the conclusion (a reasoned approach) and the idea it needs to connect to in the evidence (injuring others). The answer that ties them together is usually the required assumption.'),
48	('a0f691c3-1168-408d-b794-e568158be582'::uuid,'17ee827111702354df4ee794c511c91e','D is about what happens to people who injure others afterward: do they get the same treatment back? 49	('125cc63e-93fe-4f81-81ab-cbb50d35287a'::uuid,'cda480f947fce01b3e4625218815def8','E is about the risk of being injured, not of injuring others. It also ties that risk to how much interest people have in their own welfare, not to whether they take a reasoned approach. Negate E and the argument is untouched: the theorist''s case still turns on reasoned people injuring others less.')

Then the evidence''s condition isn''t met, and nothing in the argument shows the bonuses save any money.\n\nThe move: when the conclusion names a specific tool (expensive bonuses) and the evidence names a general requirement (strong incentives), the argument assumes the tool meets the requirement.'),\n('831eb0ef-227b-4cbb-9206-4d01df108da7'::uuid,'de018f71bbad7c1780f590bde8bd8d93','E is too strong. \"Only if\" makes expensive bonuses a requirement for any savings from reduced monitoring. The argument needs bonuses to be one way to supply strong incentives, not the only way. Negate E: a corporation could cut monitoring and save money using other incentives, like promotions. Bonuses could still work too, so the argument stands.'),\n('98fb449c-dbe4-4f1b-8241-fcb4e09160e5'::uuid,'53052901acd8da4763ae35330bca20e4','The argument doesn''t care how people come to take a reasoned approach. Its conclusion only says what should follow once most of them do. Negate A: governments alone can convince people to be reasonable. The conditional conclusion is untouched, so the argument doesn''t need A.'),\n('cab48aae-47a5-4fa6-a1d7-78a31f45233d'::uuid,'dad8e84af35036d648f0687bbb542f73','B is about a cost of government doing its job: does it get in the way of people pursuing their own welfare? The argument never weighs that cost. Negate B: government can''t serve its purpose without diminishing people''s ability to promote their welfare. The link between reasoned people and less need for government is unaffected.'),\n('873db1a2-d32b-47b8-aa8b-77575bbd7d64'::uuid,'e4cd7c8fe8931e47025b1122cd16d39c','This is the link the Goal predicted. Government exists to prevent people from injuring others. The conclusion says government should have less power when most people take a reasoned approach. That only follows if reasoned people injure others less. Negate C: people who take a reasoned approach are just as likely to injure others as anyone else. Then a reasoned population needs government''s protection just as much, and the case for less power falls apart.\n\nThe move: find the idea that appears only in the conclusion (a reasoned approach) and the idea it needs to connect to in the evidence (injuring others). The answer that ties them together is usually the required assumption.'),\n('a0f691c3-1168-408d-b794-e568158be582'::uuid,'17ee827111702354df4ee794c511c91e','D is about what happens to people who injure others afterward: do they get the same treatment back? The argument is about whether reasoned people need government to stop them from injuring others in the first place. Negate D: people who injure others are not eventually treated the same way. Nothing in the argument changes.'),\n('125cc63e-93fe-4f81-81ab-cbb50d35287a'::uuid,'cda480f947fce01b3e4625218815def8','E is about the risk of being injured, not of injuring others. It also ties that risk to how much interest people have in their own welfare, not to whether they take a reasoned approach. Negate E and the argument is untouched: the theorist''s case still turns on reasoned people injuring others less.')\n) v(id,ob,nb) where t.id=v.id and md5(t.body)=v.ob returning t.id;"}

Tool result:
1	update lr_explanation_steps t set body=v.nb, label=case when v.nl='' then t.label else v.nl end from (values
2	('53fcb575-8e3c-4cd6-861b-eb92df5bceae'::uuid,'3eff3679ce513f8907ef0d7923298971','The study measured two things. Speed at processing new information went up. Integrating new information with past information went down. The premise tells us integration matters more to management than speed, so the psychologist reads the trade as a loss.
3	
4	But the conclusion is about overall management ability. Is managing only speed and integration? Hardly. Think about attention to detail, staying calm with a difficult client, or energy late in the day. And even on the two measured abilities, "integration matters more" does not tell us how big each change was.
5	
6	Given that extra coffee hurt integration, how could we argue that it still did not impair overall management ability? Suppose the extra coffee also made those managers far more alert and focused in ways the study never measured. Or suppose the speed gain was huge and the integration loss was tiny. Either way, the gains could outweigh the integration loss, and overall ability would hold steady or even improve.
7	
8	The psychologist jumps from two measured changes to a verdict about overall ability. That jump only works if nothing the coffee did in the experiment made up for the integration loss.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
9	('b78d8539-5163-430b-b27f-22a233ace4ee'::uuid,'06b969dc897f74c3b9e84455e61e9c95','Look for a Defender: an answer ruling out the possibility that the extra coffee produced benefits, from the faster processing or from abilities the study did not measure, large enough to outweigh the integration loss. Negate the right answer and you should get our objection back: the extra coffee helped overall management in some way that more than made up for the loss.','Goal','Goal'),
10	('0e76c443-a2c4-4adc-9310-3cfe1103fc78'::uuid,'a106551545830b94e0aaf5c6eb4b8958','The information introduced by the chorus in a play is sometimes not consistent with the rest of the information in the play.','Evidence (since)','Evidence (since)'),
11	('64cfec38-2b0e-4301-8b93-4b272a491c89'::uuid,'3f7d9215c804b859beede4195b8ca4a1','Most of this stimulus is background. Chorus and narrator share a lot: each brings in a point of view not tied to any character, and each lets the author comment on the action and supply context. Then the pivot, "However," brings the actual argument: since the chorus sometimes introduces information inconsistent with the rest of the play, the chorus is not equivalent to the narrator.
12	
13	That shape is "X and Y are not the same, since X does thing A." What has to be true for that to work? Y must not do thing A. If I said, "Max owns a Lebron jersey, so Max and Karen are not equally big Lebron fans," I would be assuming that Karen does not own one too. If Karen also owned one, the jersey would be something they share, not a difference.
14	
15	Same here. The author is Assuming a Difference. If narrators can also introduce inconsistent information, inconsistency is a shared trait and cannot prove the two are different.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
16	('3541bb89-c5f4-4fc9-b95a-6e01d01cc757'::uuid,'d59dfeed6324c3b9a3399e007c46ca0a','So let''s look for an answer saying that a narrator in a novel does not introduce information that is inconsistent with the rest of the novel. Negated, it should say narrators can do the same thing the chorus does.','Goal','Goal'),
17	('b2e8e91b-42f7-4831-b9ad-7c235b408b34'::uuid,'c2ee21d51f4a4d1a871b65ef79178f81','We could predict a Linking assumption like, "If transporting basic materials through space would be extremely costly, then it won''t be economically feasible to colonize Mars." But this argument is practical and real world, so the answer is more likely to defend against an objection than to spell out a link.
18	
19	So let''s argue with it. Given that a colony needs tremendous quantities of basic materials on site, and that shipping those materials through space would cost a fortune, how could we argue that colonizing Mars could still be economically feasible?
20	
21	We can''t get around the need for the materials. Can we get around shipping them through space? What if we find usable materials on Mars itself, so nothing has to make the trip? What if some future technology moves materials without conventional space transport?
22	
23	Now accept that the materials really must be shipped at great cost. Is there still a way? Maybe the colony would pay for itself. Suppose Mars held a mineral so valuable that companies would gladly cover the shipping bill to mine it. Expensive is not the same as unaffordable when the payoff is big enough.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
24	('11335347-84c9-48bf-8f02-a4104a507262'::uuid,'64b4e158506d1427a71edad4990bc636','Look for a Defender answer that shuts down one of these objections, saying something like:
25	
26	"Mars cannot supply the materials itself."
27	"There is no cheaper way to get the materials there."
28	"The colony would not produce enough value to cover the cost."
29	
30	Negate the right answer and it should hand us one of those objections.','Goal','Goal'),
31	('2112e6d7-0f77-4cc5-a82a-ad44bd21084d'::uuid,'f2d8d6193d9823cebe1477743c883927','If two stars are in the same distant galaxy, the difference in their distances from Earth is negligible.','Evidence','Evidence'),
32	('f8974692-c638-4c6e-8e57-5237e9b6455f'::uuid,'d98916752848e78f8029859c7274bc46','There are two moves here, so we can test each one.
33	
34	Move one goes from the premise that the stars in one distant galaxy are all about the same distance from us to the claim that any significant difference in their apparent brightness comes from how brightly each star is actually burning. The distance part is reasonable. If one star is 10,000,000 light-years away and another is 10,000,050, the gap barely matters. But is distance the only thing that can make a star look dimmer? A cloud of dust in front of one star could dim it. Another star sitting right behind it, along our line of sight, could make it look brighter. So this move has some wiggle room.
35	
36	Move two goes from that claim to the conclusion that we can find how actual brightness correlates with other characteristics by studying these stars. A correlation needs two things to compare. We now have a way to rank the stars by actual brightness. What do we compare that ranking with? Some other characteristic, such as color or size. And we have to be able to observe that characteristic from Earth, because that is where the study happens. If no other characteristic of these distant stars can be seen from here, we have brightness figures and nothing to line them up against.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
37	('80145eb7-c868-4f62-a13a-49b7e59bc156'::uuid,'290d45f486cedcc70566318bcbaa80be','The answer could target either move. For move one, look for a Defender such as, "Nothing other than distance and actual brightness significantly affects how bright a distant star appears." For move two, look for an answer saying we can observe, from Earth, at least some characteristic of stars in distant galaxies besides their brightness. Negate that one and the plan has nothing to correlate brightness with.','Goal','Goal'),
38	('02d6150a-f77b-4cc0-915a-b5d1cd17553a'::uuid,'57a4313438ad6f31e06c611eee240326','These bovines were found in an arid region with people and no other large mammals. If there had been a natural source of water available to these bovines, then there would have been other large mammals in the area.','Evidence','Evidence'),
39	('24d6aff9-8e44-4be2-8be9-9fde247f1c8c'::uuid,'911bb055b6cde97804ecdab6fdee3549','There is a small inference to make with the premises first. We have a conditional:
40	```
41	Natural source of water available → other large mammals in the area
42	```
43	And we are told there were no other large mammals in the area. By the contrapositive, there was no natural source of water available to these bovines.
44	
45	So the bovines were living in an arid region with people around and no natural water. The author concludes the bovines were domesticated: people were keeping them and bringing them water. That sounds like early herding, so the people were no longer only hunting and gathering.
46	
47	How could we argue otherwise? Given that there was no natural water, how could wild bovines still have been there? Maybe bovines can go a long time on very little water, getting moisture from plants. Maybe the remains are of animals that wandered in during a drought and died, which would explain why remains were found at all. If wild bovines could plausibly be there without natural water, their presence proves nothing about domestication.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
48	('28fcdfc5-cf41-4456-8dd5-1651a8049d7f'::uuid,'5805699fe83bd12f0c0ab65b772e998c','The argument makes a Linking move: no natural water, yet bovines were there, so people must have been keeping them. Look for an answer saying wild bovines would not be found in a region without natural water. That same answer defends against our objection; negate it and wild bovines could have been there on their own.
49	
50	The second half of the conclusion also assumes that people who domesticated bovines were not exclusively hunter-gatherers, but that step is close to a definition.','Goal','Goal'),
51	('c0b527ac-8c98-416c-9627-6bf94d203b8a'::uuid,'47ea47258ea970ff9dbbd9c54fe640bf','The troubles from which a patient seeks relief do not have purely internal causes. They result in part from the patient''s relationships with other people.','Evidence','Evidence'),
52	('cb1ac25c-0240-4bce-9f4b-2cfe240c85b0'::uuid,'991caa71a863a8e4bd416d18df8ebe9f','The logic seems to be: since the troubles are partly caused by relationships, the patient can''t heal unless the therapist focuses on changing those relationships. So the author is assuming something like, "If a problem is partly caused by X, then solving it requires addressing X."
53	
54	Is that true? Not always. A headache might be partly caused by a noisy office, yet a painkiller can still end it without anyone touching the noise. Given that the troubles are partly relational, how could we argue the therapist doesn''t have to focus on relationships? Maybe working on the internal causes alone, such as raising self-esteem or easing anxiety, does enough good that the patient heals, even though the relationships never changed.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
55	('ea1ad4ea-d0c6-4783-b43d-fa8052cf888b'::uuid,'77045f73e9c48559d80e2eec1c76b45a','Whenever a conclusion says, "to get X, you must do Y," the author is assuming that nothing other than Y will get you X. Here, that means no route to healing skips the relationships. So look for an answer saying something like, "A patient can''t be healed by working on the internal causes alone." Negate it and you get our objection back.
56	
57	Be careful with the reverse idea, that Y is guaranteed to work. A "must" claims Y is required, not that Y is enough.','Goal','Goal'),
58	('5958ba1d-859e-46a3-a562-d3538f2c49e6'::uuid,'fa5dae2db9fd5d625df28bb969188ef4','We have a new term in the conclusion: "decreased revenues." The evidence never mentions revenue. It only talks about a ratings drop for first-run episodes. So there is a missing link: a ratings drop for first-run episodes can lead to decreased revenues for the network.
59	
60	Picture how this works. A hit comedy airs new episodes on its network every Sunday night. The producers sell reruns to other stations while the show is still running, and they make a lot of money doing it. But now fans can get their fix from reruns any night of the week, so fewer of them tune in on Sunday for the new episode. Ratings for the first-run episodes drop.
61	
62	Why would that hurt the network''s revenue? Presumably because the network earns money from its audience, through advertising, and fewer viewers means less money. The argument never says so. It also assumes the network doesn''t share in the big payout the producers get from syndication, since that money could make up for the loss.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
63	('c93cd3b3-9ed0-4e7b-b363-08ecd0638710'::uuid,'1aa00929acac613870a4e8d23a21f82e','There is no reason to believe that the hypothesis is correct. Rephrase: there is no reason to believe that an invisible "light-absorbing medium" exists in outer space.','Conclusion','Conclusion'),
64	('27f74a90-b4a4-4956-8be0-9736b1a2056a'::uuid,'77ea45713caa053cea745e55ba665a3c','The professor''s reasoning: the scientists'' support for the medium is that it would explain the low visibility of other star systems. But relativity already completely explains that low visibility. So the support is gone.
65	
66	The author seems to be thinking,
67	```
68	low visibility completely explained by relativity → no reason to believe the medium hypothesis
69	```
70	Let''s argue with it. Given that relativity completely explains why other star systems are hard to see, how could we argue that there is still some reason to believe in the medium?
71	
72	One way: maybe relativity''s explanation isn''t separate from the medium at all. Suppose relativity''s account of the low visibility only works if the medium exists. Then the more convincing relativity is, the more reason we have to believe in the medium. Think of two witnesses, Eddie and Laura. If Eddie''s complete account of what happened includes Laura''s key detail, Eddie''s account doesn''t make Laura''s detail unnecessary. It confirms it.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
73	('74beed47-7cac-4105-b985-6c63de8b7eb3'::uuid,'61b2a3f005abe769a03e4739fcad7308','Look for a Defender that rules out this overlap: relativity''s explanation does not depend on the medium. Negate it and relativity becomes a reason to believe in the medium. Or look for the principle behind the reasoning, something like, "If one theory completely explains X on its own, X gives no reason to believe a rival hypothesis."','Goal','Goal')
74	) v(id,ob,nb,ol,nl) where t.id=v.id and md5(t.body)=v.ob returning t.id;

The distance part is reasonable. If one star is 10,000,000 light-years away and another is 10,000,050, the gap barely matters. But is distance the only thing that can make a star look dimmer? A cloud of dust in front of one star could dim it. Another star sitting right behind it, along our line of sight, could make it look brighter. So this move has some wiggle room.\n\nMove two goes from that claim to the conclusion that we can find how actual brightness correlates with other characteristics by studying these stars. A correlation needs two things to compare. We now have a way to rank the stars by actual brightness. What do we compare that ranking with? Some other characteristic, such as color or size. And we have to be able to observe that characteristic from Earth, because that is where the study happens. If no other characteristic of these distant stars can be seen from here, we have brightness figures and nothing to line them up against.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),\n('80145eb7-c868-4f62-a13a-49b7e59bc156'::uuid,'290d45f486cedcc70566318bcbaa80be','The answer could target either move. For move one, look for a Defender such as, \"Nothing other than distance and actual brightness significantly affects how bright a distant star appears.\" For move two, look for an answer saying we can observe, from Earth, at least some characteristic of stars in distant galaxies besides their brightness. Negate that one and the plan has nothing to correlate brightness with.','Goal','Goal'),\n('02d6150a-f77b-4cc0-915a-b5d1cd17553a'::uuid,'57a4313438ad6f31e06c611eee240326','These bovines were found in an arid region with people and no other large mammals. If there had been a natural source of water available to these bovines, then there would have been other large mammals in the area.','Evidence','Evidence'),\n('24d6aff9-8e44-4be2-8be9-9fde247f1c8c'::uuid,'911bb055b6cde97804ecdab6fdee3549','There is a small inference to make with the premises first. We have a conditional:\n```\nNatural source of water available → other large mammals in the area\n```\nAnd we are told there were no other large mammals in the area. By the contrapositive, there was no natural source of water available to these bovines.\n\nSo the bovines were living in an arid region with people around and no natural water. The author concludes the bovines were domesticated: people were keeping them and bringing them water. That sounds like early herding, so the people were no longer only hunting and gathering.\n\nHow could we argue otherwise? Given that there was no natural water, how could wild bovines still have been there? Maybe bovines can go a long time on very little water, getting moisture from plants. Maybe the remains are of animals that wandered in during a drought and died, which would explain why remains were found at all. If wild bovines could plausibly be there without natural water, their presence proves nothing about domestication.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),\n('28fcdfc5-cf41-4456-8dd5-1651a8049d7f'::uuid,'5805699fe83bd12f0c0ab65b772e998c','The argument makes a Linking move: no natural water, yet bovines were there, so people must have been keeping them. Look for an answer saying wild bovines would not be found in a region without natural water. That same answer defends against our objection; negate it and wild bovines could have been there on their own.\n\nThe second half of the conclusion also assumes that people who domesticated bovines were not exclusively hunter-gatherers, but that step is close to a definition.','Goal','Goal'),\n('c0b527ac-8c98-416c-9627-6bf94d203b8a'::uuid,'47ea47258ea970ff9dbbd9c54fe640bf','The troubles from which a patient seeks relief do not have purely internal causes. They result in part from the patient''s relationships with other people.','Evidence','Evidence'),\n('cb1ac25c-0240-4bce-9f4b-2cfe240c85b0'::uuid,'991caa71a863a8e4bd416d18df8ebe9f','The logic seems to be: since the troubles are partly caused by relationships, the patient can''t heal unless the therapist focuses on changing those relationships. So the author is assuming something like, \"If a problem is partly caused by X, then solving it requires addressing X.\"\n\nIs that true? Not always. A headache might be partly caused by a noisy office, yet a painkiller can still end it without anyone touching the noise. Given that the troubles are partly relational, how could we argue the therapist doesn''t have to focus on relationships? Maybe working on the internal causes alone, such as raising self-esteem or easing anxiety, does enough good that the patient heals, even though the relationships never changed.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),\n('ea1ad4ea-d0c6-4783-b43d-fa8052cf888b'::uuid,'77045f73e9c48559d80e2eec1c76b45a','Whenever a conclusion says, \"to get X, you must do Y,\" the author is assuming that nothing other than Y will get you X. Here, that means no route to healing skips the relationships. So look for an answer saying something like, \"A patient can''t be healed by working on the internal causes alone.\" Negate it and you get our objection back.\n\nBe careful with the reverse idea, that Y is guaranteed to work. A \"must\" claims Y is required, not that Y is enough.','Goal','Goal'),\n('5958ba1d-859e-46a3-a562-d3538f2c49e6'::uuid,'fa5dae2db9fd5d625df28bb969188ef4','We have a new term in the conclusion: \"decreased revenues.\" The evidence never mentions revenue. It only talks about a ratings drop for first-run episodes. So there is a missing link: a ratings drop for first-run episodes can lead to decreased revenues for the network.\n\nPicture how this works. A hit comedy airs new episodes on its network every Sunday night. The producers sell reruns to other stations while the show is still running, and they make a lot of money doing it. But now fans can get their fix from reruns any night of the week, so fewer of them tune in on Sunday for the new episode. Ratings for the first-run episodes drop.\n\nWhy would that hurt the network''s revenue? Presumably because the network earns money from its audience, through advertising, and fewer viewers means less money. The argument never says so. It also assumes the network doesn''t share in the big payout the producers get from syndication, since that money could make up for the loss.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),\n('c93cd3b3-9ed0-4e7b-b363-08ecd0638710'::uuid,'1aa00929acac613870a4e8d23a21f82e','There is no reason to believe that the hypothesis is correct. Rephrase: there is no reason to believe that an invisible \"light-absorbing medium\" exists in outer space.','Conclusion','Conclusion'),\n('27f74a90-b4a4-4956-8be0-9736b1a2056a'::uuid,'77ea45713caa053cea745e55ba665a3c','The professor''s reasoning: the scientists'' support for the medium is that it would explain the low visibility of other star systems. But relativity already completely explains that low visibility. So the support is gone.\n\nThe author seems to be thinking,\n```\nlow visibility completely explained by relativity → no reason to believe the medium hypothesis\n```\nLet''s argue with it. Given that relativity completely explains why other star systems are hard to see, how could we argue that there is still some reason to believe in the medium?\n\nOne way: maybe relativity''s explanation isn''t separate from the medium at all. Suppose relativity''s account of the low visibility only works if the medium exists. Then the more convincing relativity is, the more reason we have to believe in the medium. Think of two witnesses, Eddie and Laura. If Eddie''s complete account of what happened includes Laura''s key detail, Eddie''s account doesn''t make Laura''s detail unnecessary. It confirms it.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),\n('74beed47-7cac-4105-b985-6c63de8b7eb3'::uuid,'61b2a3f005abe769a03e4739fcad7308','Look for a Defender that rules out this overlap: relativity''s explanation does not depend on the medium. Negate it and relativity becomes a reason to believe in the medium. Or look for the principle behind the reasoning, something like, \"If one theory completely explains X on its own, X gives no reason to believe a rival hypothesis.\"','Goal','Goal')\n) v(id,ob,nb,ol,nl) where t.id=v.id and md5(t.body)=v.ob returning t.id;"}

3	
4	Do we know the test leads to dangerous operations? Close enough. It finds polyps so early that it is generally unclear whether they are malignant, and in most cases doctors have such polyps surgically removed anyway. The researcher tells us that removal is a dangerous process.
5

17	('bc066e4f-d952-412f-8416-94a29eb59057'::uuid,'a68683aed69450e294e84c9502bc4f02','Look for an answer saying historians don''t date the Sumerians'' first literature before the Egyptian tablets, in other words, not earlier than about 3300 B.C. 18	('d768c294-1f6a-4632-bd81-f82cb8c3e736'::uuid,'736216bd0ab089122a11c0fc5b0394c1','We''re told there''s something worse / life-shortening about living in captivity.
19	
20	So if the odds of reaching max life expectancy are the same for captive vs. wild, then we need to hear one of these:
21	- something good / life-elongating about captivity
22	- something bad / life-shortening about the wild
23	- these fatal diseases that become a risk in captivity are not actually shortening the lives of very many leatherbacks','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
24	('97b26917-cf91-49c0-b5de-1a4234051d82'::uuid,'266d5a8653b3de2a0e87fbee6f0b0fbe','Honey adds bacteria, and bacteria cause the infections that slow healing. So honey should have slowed healing. Instead, honey wounds beat two other groups, and the answer has to explain both wins.
25	
26	Honey vs. cleaning alone: honey must do something good enough to make up for its own bacteria. Maybe it stops bacteria from growing, or its bacteria are harmless.
27	
28	Honey vs. antibiotic ointment: the ointment kills bacteria, so even if honey controls bacteria too, why does it do better? Something must be holding the ointment back, or honey must help healing in some other way.
29	
30	Look for an answer that covers both comparisons. An answer that explains only one of them leaves half the result a mystery.','Evaluate / Goal','Evaluate / Goal'),
31	('fd7cc7f3-0c52-4d37-aaf8-7873a2088d60'::uuid,'90e4ff78e5ab4b14edbe75c009c74d60','The historians'' rule says significant intellectual advances generally occur where the political system is stable. "Generally" leaves room for exceptions, so Athens doesn''t refute the rule. What we need is an explanation for why Athens turned out to be an exception.
32	
33	The cleanest way to reconcile a rule with a counterexample: find the reason the rule usually holds, then show that reason didn''t apply in this case. Why would stability usually matter for intellectual work? Maybe unrest cuts off money, safety, or time to think. If something in Athens kept thinkers supplied with whatever unrest normally takes away, Plato and Aristotle become an explained exception.
34	
35	Look for an answer that names something instability usually destroys and shows Athens had it anyway.','Evaluate / Goal','Evaluate / Goal'),
36	('110085b7-403b-4786-bc1e-5c7e106e110a'::uuid,'39282fc5c693703e0081e4310f0c5c93','The stimulus closes the obvious escape route. 37	
38	So how does a zebra survive with them? Seeing a zebra isn''t the same as catching one. The stripes could protect zebras in some way other than hiding, for example during the chase. Or zebras could have some other protection that makes up for being easy to spot.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
39	('9756593d-f136-4fa9-8aec-908d9706c158'::uuid,'fe291a93a58bb05742ffa2cedadd9ae9','Look for an answer showing that the stripes help zebras survive in some way other than making them hard to see, such as making them harder to catch once a lion attacks. 40	('d6a66e7b-c8bf-42d7-aef8-bced3c92abbd'::uuid,'b28795bb62cf6a9c21dabe2e4d3ab997','We need a way to explain how rain, or something that accompanies rain, is adding pollution to Crystal Bay. Who knows. Let''s just find some way to connect heavy rainfall to pollution in the Bay.','Evaluate / Goal','Evaluate / Goal')

1	update lr_explanation_choice_notes t set body=v.nb from (values
2	('445761f0-a033-44dd-8f8a-e9fe3f314c29'::uuid,'961f46d57ad6f70f8eddb4042696eaea','The argument is about medical necessity, not ethics. Negate A: a dangerous operation can be ethically justified even when the condition it treats is not more dangerous. The researcher can accept that and still say some of these polyp removals were not medically necessary, so the argument survives.'),
3	('e67dd86c-ba1d-401c-ba7a-3776c1f4d704'::uuid,'b68bd82bbd7e369a41dae6fe4afde755','The evidence says some removed polyps turn out not to be malignant. The conclusion says some of the operations were not medically necessary. B is the bridge between those two terms: removing a nonmalignant polyp is not always medically necessary.
4	
5	Negate it: surgical removal of nonmalignant polyps detected by the test is always medically necessary. Now every operation the test prompts was needed, malignant or not, and the conclusion has nothing left to stand on. The negation wrecks the argument, so the argument requires B.
6	
7	Notice the soft wording. "Not always" only asks for some unnecessary removals, which is exactly as much as "can prompt" in the conclusion needs. On a necessary assumption question, a modest answer that connects the evidence''s term (not malignant) to the conclusion''s term (not medically necessary) is the shape to look for.'),
8	('aa811b8e-a357-4266-a385-36a5328c0e36'::uuid,'375b8b86439fd66d2e8564f99f009742','C tells us what to do about the test: stop using it or change it. The argument stops earlier, at the claim that the test can prompt unnecessary operations. Negate C: even if the test encourages unnecessary operations, it should still be used as is. The conclusion is untouched, because it never said what to do next.'),
9	('9b3bb964-6578-4b8e-9880-6cbdc1c8948e'::uuid,'bc20d17faa504007635282dc23ca7d39','D is about malignant polyps, and the gap is about the ones that are not malignant. Negate it: some malignant polyp found by the test should not be removed. That tells us nothing about whether removing a nonmalignant polyp is necessary, so the argument is unaffected.'),
10	('fdb97b9a-5be5-4229-a810-01eed8999bc1'::uuid,'387abc0446e8ea05fb662a9f3236d967','The argument never measures how useful the test is. Negate E: the test is medically useful even when it finds polyps that need no treatment. The researcher can agree and still say the test can prompt unnecessary surgery. "Only when" makes E a strong claim the argument has no use for.'),
11	('fb81a85d-efc2-4013-8e8e-475141d39573'::uuid,'6be9b36f3b2cd4ba77b4095ae1812c15','The argument already has its literary tablet: one translated tablet appears to contain literary writing. Negate A: most of the untranslated tablets do not contain literature. That one literary tablet is still there, so the challenge stands. More literary tablets would help, but the argument doesn''t need them.'),
12	('f5bd9ec2-65c5-4bda-af59-74139fd9e2f6'::uuid,'540ee70b237f96f94c79467a5eb0a500','B links tax records to other kinds of writing, but the argument never reasons from the tax records. It has direct evidence: a tablet that appears to contain literary writing. Negate B: some civilization kept tax records and nothing else. The argument loses nothing, because it rests on the literary tablet.'),
13	('074cc8b5-fcb8-4e6c-89c5-0507d8cd9401'::uuid,'71c79a98e514bc1ee68f08052c964120','C fills the gap we predicted. The evidence dates the literary tablet to between 3300 and 3200 B.C. The conclusion says this challenges the belief that the Sumerians were first. That only works if historians don''t already place Sumerian literature earlier than the tablet.
14	
15	Negate C: historians generally believe the Sumerians did create literature earlier than 3300 B.C. Then the Egyptian tablet comes second on the historians'' own timeline, and it challenges nothing. The argument falls apart, so C is required.
16	
17	The move to repeat: when the conclusion brings in something the evidence never mentioned (here, the Sumerians), the assumption usually connects that new term to the evidence. Ask what must be true about the new thing for the evidence to matter.'),
18	('07960647-5b03-4694-9b3e-62e2f4c098a7'::uuid,'4bc0330cad87c851ff2320b97eea2071','D would hurt the argument, not hold it up. Negate it: no historians are skeptical about the tablets'' authenticity. That only makes the evidence look better. A necessary assumption is something whose denial damages the argument, and denying D helps it.'),
19	('c8acb044-6f0a-4456-a01e-f6eaa7094bb2'::uuid,'b3998989ba890c5cf5d46bc0dc72d1b1','E dates when Sumerian civilization arose, but the belief in question is about when the Sumerians first created literature. A civilization can exist for centuries before anyone writes literature. Negate E: the civilization arose at some other time, say 4000 B.C. The argument still works as long as Sumerian literature came after the tablet.'),
20	('95b813da-ad0e-4942-9f81-60b5d11defc3'::uuid,'ed8091ad012201688a86f76d39d7ed56','A compares leatherbacks with other large aquatic reptiles. The surprise is a comparison between captive leatherbacks and wild ones. Fewer diseases attacking leatherbacks would be true in both places, so it creates no difference between captivity and the wild that could offset the captivity diseases.'),
21	('1bf3ba6b-8337-4212-bff8-746ce5757312'::uuid,'278d6840af6718315a8b26762d1ac973','B compares sea turtles with other marine animals, which is the wrong comparison. Even if sea turtles live long in general, that is true of captive and wild leatherbacks alike, so it doesn''t explain why the extra diseases in captivity fail to lower the captive odds.'),
22	('86782073-ac68-4ac1-9494-90dac1b164f1'::uuid,'69abc902fb9ab7ed173e878e384ea73c','This is the something-bad-about-the-wild answer we predicted. Captive leatherbacks face diseases the wild ones never meet. Wild leatherbacks face predators, and C tells us predators kill most of the wild ones that perish. Captive turtles are presumably safe from predators. So each setting has its own main danger, and the odds of reaching full life expectancy can come out about the same.
23	
24	The move to repeat: when two groups end up equal even though one has an obvious disadvantage, look for a disadvantage on the other side that balances it.'),
25	('6629b443-0328-4197-ab72-cbc19c170594'::uuid,'db1ea5b45e96e054f9d17d0a090a446f','D deepens the paradox. If few zoologists know how to build an environment that is good for captive leatherbacks, captivity sounds even worse for them. That is one more reason to expect captive turtles to die younger, which is the opposite of what we need.'),
26	('a6695012-35bf-4641-b9ab-e8501b6b6f52'::uuid,'f080be4c342f511c5fd3b3f19b1f5866','E might tempt you if you suspect the life-expectancy figures are measured badly. But nothing in E says the error affects captive and wild turtles differently. If size is a poor guide to age everywhere, it gives no difference between the two settings, so the surprise remains.'),
27	('8431f89a-1c8e-4cef-83bf-891a618b49f4'::uuid,'81f6fe2f4470e158f847a3c18023bf42','A gives us a similarity: many of the same doctors work at Woodville and at the nearby hospitals. We need a difference that gives Woodville''s patients the benefit of private rooms. Shared doctors are the same on both sides, so they can''t explain why a hospital with only semiprivate rooms keeps up with hospitals that are mostly private.'),
28	('c6089d54-79b2-469d-b09e-cc79015781f3'::uuid,'c17b186ca100d3dc7a34d50aaf783f49','We want a reason Woodville''s semiprivate rooms do as well as other hospitals'' private rooms, and this gives it.
29	
30	If Woodville puts one patient in each semiprivate room whenever it can, then in practice many of its patients get a room to themselves. So Woodville gets the benefits of private rooms without having any, and the surprise goes away.'),
31	('b31dce01-5a21-4d11-95a9-6bacb7aa43f9'::uuid,'9349fdf74abc01cfee45c7673ee62035','E does give a difference, location, but nothing ties being downtown to fewer infections or shorter stays. To make E work we''d have to invent that link ourselves, so the surprise is still standing.'),
32	('8ace9c8d-0dcb-4137-b6fe-d80674b2b36d'::uuid,'71b3c0b1d1e2b8d2af56ffc845705df8','A compares the two groups that didn''t get honey: cleaned-only wounds beat ointment wounds. That might explain why ointment came last, but it says nothing about honey. Honey still adds bacteria, and we still don''t know why honey wounds beat the cleaned-only ones.'),
33	('48fec1a8-becb-40f9-be8c-58f5125db904'::uuid,'7599ff4501156c01e31a7abd99773a97','B makes honey''s bacteria sound less dangerous, since there are fewer of them than in an infected wound. Fewer is still more than zero. At best honey hurts less than we feared; nothing in B makes it help. The second half, that ointment rarely kills all the bacteria, explains why ointment isn''t perfect, not why honey beats it.'),
34	('ff6dc1a3-f0d7-4571-bdfd-e1ad449f330f'::uuid,'e647665535e2ee61a8d965fe6bbbd854','C answers both comparisons we set up.
35	
36	First half: honey inhibits the growth of bacteria in wounds, including the bacteria the honey contains. So honey wounds get less bacterial growth than wounds that were only cleaned. That explains why honey beat cleaning alone.
37	
38	Second half: antibiotic ointments damage sensitive wound tissue, which slows healing. So the ointment pays a price that, as far as we''re told, honey doesn''t. That explains why honey beat the ointment.
39	
40	The move to repeat: when a result beats more than one comparison group, check each answer against each group separately. The correct answer here has two parts because the surprise has two parts.'),
41	('e1db0eda-d40e-41d4-a5c8-e5b02526fd04'::uuid,'b55fb7eedcaa3219d51532afa166f1f3','D is the trap, because it gets halfway. The sugar in honey inhibits the growth of bacteria in wounds, including its own, which explains why honey wounds beat wounds that were only cleaned.
42	
43	Now check the other comparison. The ointment kills bacteria too. D gives honey a bacteria advantage over plain cleaning, but no advantage over ointment, which already handles bacteria. Nothing in D explains why ointment wounds healed more slowly than honey wounds. C has this same first half plus the reason ointment falls behind.'),
44	('aaa983bb-69f4-4402-98e6-d532088837aa'::uuid,'b4e3573b3c709d0532b6d77810d493f2','E explains why ointment falls behind: it damages sensitive tissue. It also says honey doesn''t do that to cleaned wounds. But not causing tissue damage doesn''t make honey better than plain cleaning, and honey still brings in bacteria. E gives no reason honey wounds would heal faster than cleaned-only wounds.'),
45	('8d97cdea-36ea-4dd2-95b4-bd89a455d48e'::uuid,'88815b8b8dd9fe9c3097eaa91a70aed8','A compares Athens with political systems that came later. The puzzle is inside Athens: how did great work happen there during unrest? Knowing that later systems differ tells us nothing about what let Plato and Aristotle work through the turmoil.'),
46	('5b963036-0097-4c78-a61f-1aeaa43de10b'::uuid,'2a000870d162361f3f519552315dda2c','B is tempting because esteem sounds like encouragement. But the rule is about political stability, and B never connects esteem to instability. Citizens can admire thinkers in stable cities too. Ask: does B tell us what unrest normally takes away from thinkers, and how Athens kept it? It doesn''t, so the exception is still unexplained.'),
47	('114e83fd-ab48-4085-a287-8e874670d1ac'::uuid,'55b621adda66a53a650beee0aa2810ae','C does both jobs we predicted. First, it gives the reason the rule usually holds: in unstable political environments, financial support for intellectual endeavors is typically unavailable. Second, it shows why Athens escaped that: wealthy citizens provided the support anyway.
48	
49	Now the rule and the counterexample fit together. Stability usually matters because of the money. Athens had the money without the stability, so Plato and Aristotle could keep working.
50	
51	The move to repeat: to reconcile a general rule with an exception, look for an answer that explains why the rule normally holds and shows that the reason was missing in the exception.'),
52	('8e0e9495-513d-4b9a-9400-ac34ec7c33eb'::uuid,'6baf70077de9812cd933acdae621012c','D runs the other direction: advances sometimes lead to stability. That doesn''t explain how the advances happened in Athens while it was unstable. If anything it raises a new question, since Athens had unparalleled progress and still had great unrest.'),
53	('d7fec877-56bb-4d30-b311-5ae90dd30d8e'::uuid,'0a8b3400b82fd28f16dd84eb848802f5','E adds more Athenian thinkers to the list. That makes the counterexample bigger, not smaller: now a whole group did great work during unrest. We still have no reason why any of them could.'),
54	('8c79fefe-6411-48d4-86e0-698e02c11705'::uuid,'606fc1cf424c2da0df69c1971b56afd8','A tells us true camouflage would have to change with the seasons. Zebra stripes don''t change, so A only confirms that zebras aren''t camouflaged. It says nothing about how a zebra that stands out still survives.'),
55	('953c973f-0f8b-486d-a405-81877d62e2ae'::uuid,'18573c441aa5c0a7f8380cb1bc598def','B says zebras can tell which lions are preparing to hunt and ignore the others. That might save some wasted running, but it doesn''t make a zebra any harder to catch once a lion does hunt, and the lion still spots the zebra easily. Any prey animal could have this skill, so B gives no reason a zebra this visible gets away.'),
56	('1c6dd25f-9550-4d8a-84a4-f9839dfa1ca7'::uuid,'0a82200b659c3694f9ad7367c69b9c72','C makes things worse for zebras. Lions blend in with dry vegetation and can creep close before attacking. A hidden hunter going after easy-to-see prey should succeed more often, which deepens the puzzle about how zebras survive.'),
57	('65b2a7ca-2c58-4157-9cb4-d54c71f2cf74'::uuid,'f7c9225a8d5d6bd183991ab12a4c3864','D is about what lions do after a kill. Sharing the food doesn''t change how often lions bring down a zebra, and it has nothing to do with the stripes. The puzzle about surviving with vivid markings is untouched.'),
58	('e46b86bc-383f-4018-89f9-4eb554fc7f2f'::uuid,'0e87697392ef4451515010a7d82cfd5f','E gives the stripes a job other than hiding. Zebras generally run in a group when danger comes, and in a running group the stripes make it hard for a predator chasing one zebra to discern its outline. A lion can spot the herd easily but struggles to keep track of the one zebra it is chasing.
59	
60	That resolves the puzzle. The stimulus showed the stripes don''t help a zebra hide. E shows they help it escape. Being seen and being caught are two different things, and E works in that gap.
61	
62	The move to repeat: when the stimulus rules out the obvious benefit (here, camouflage), look for an answer where the same feature helps in another way.'),
63	('f6f341d7-2b02-40f0-bfca-1a390be7a6bc'::uuid,'36564e534c56aecb53385133655921aa','A explains why the rain''s diluting effect would be tiny: there isn''t much rainwater compared with the bay. A tiny dilution means pollution should stay about the same. But the pollution goes up, to its highest levels. A explains why the rain doesn''t help, not why pollution rises.'),
64	('003048d4-686d-424f-a90f-b313836a70bc'::uuid,'554010ecb46e56f5b13d4fb63400729a','B gives the connection we were looking for. Most of the rainwater that reaches Crystal Bay first falls on pesticide-treated fields. It picks up pesticides there and carries them into the bay. A heavy rainfall means a lot of runoff and a lot of pesticide arriving at once, so pollution peaks shortly after.
65	
66	The move to repeat: this paradox quietly assumed the rain goes straight into the bay. When a fact seems to point one way (pure water should dilute), ask what happens between that fact and the result. Here the rain picks up pollution on the way.'),
67	('889a07ef-854a-4956-9c3f-ad86c48b8177'::uuid,'ba3493aadf8fd8bf320abcd2b329ebf6','C is about where the water in rain clouds comes from. Whatever its origin, the stimulus tells us the rain is almost totally pure. Where the water started gives no way for heavy rain to add pollution to the bay.'),
68	('54d91e1c-005a-4966-8f74-4f32c0c91758'::uuid,'1d17be1f0b354a92690ed4cc86f3d6f9','D names the bay''s leading pollution source, beachgoers'' trash that blows into the bay. But nothing in D ties that trash, or the wind that carries it, to rainfall. A pollution source with no stated link to rain can''t explain why the peak comes shortly after a heavy rainfall.'),
69	('e78d8afc-4e17-4531-8a75-7c639b296ff3'::uuid,'c0773d50d2c2802df2fda27cc1d55ed9','E says nearby ocean areas show an extremely similar pattern of pollutant increase and decrease. Suppose that pattern includes the same spike after rain. Then the puzzle has spread to more places, and we still don''t know why rain raises pollution anywhere. A repeated pattern is not an explanation of it.')
70	) v(id,ob,nb) where t.id=v.id and md5(t.body)=v.ob returning t.id;

Negate A: a dangerous operation can be ethically justified even when the condition it treats is not more dangerous. The researcher can accept that and still say some of these polyp removals were not medically necessary, so the argument survives.'),\n('e67dd86c-ba1d-401c-ba7a-3776c1f4d704'::uuid,'b68bd82bbd7e369a41dae6fe4afde755','The evidence says some removed polyps turn out not to be malignant. The conclusion says some of the operations were not medically necessary. B is the bridge between those two terms: removing a nonmalignant polyp is not always medically necessary.\n\nNegate it: surgical removal of nonmalignant polyps detected by the test is always medically necessary. Now every operation the test prompts was needed, malignant or not, and the conclusion has nothing left to stand on. The negation wrecks the argument, so the argument requires B.\n\nNotice the soft wording. \"Not always\" only asks for some unnecessary removals, which is exactly as much as \"can prompt\" in the conclusion needs. That only works if historians don''t already place Sumerian literature earlier than the tablet.\n\nNegate C: historians generally believe the Sumerians did create literature earlier than 3300 B.C. Then the Egyptian tablet comes second on the historians'' own timeline, and it challenges nothing. 2	('0784c1a8-17e4-4f09-b84d-9d2771c21dbe'::uuid,'0a5549b12e260e6a2e30f9584705c77a','Chain the first two premises: `accepted → distributor buys → recoup`. So acceptance is one way to guarantee the backers get their money back.
3	
4	Now look at the fact we''re given: this film was not accepted. That negates the very first condition in the chain. What does a rule tell us when its trigger is missing? Nothing. The rule describes films the committee accepts. It is silent about films it turned down.
5	
6	How could the backers still recoup? A distributor could find the film somewhere other than this festival, or the film could earn its money back some other way. Nothing in the premises rules that out.
7	
8	So the author has taken `accepted → recoup` and concluded `~accepted → ~recoup`. That''s an illegal negation: denying the sufficient condition and then denying the necessary condition too.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
9	('644c3ff2-f372-4a52-b5df-e2ac4855c463'::uuid,'eebbedac3583625007c8edba445011d1','Because the stimulus is built from conditionals, we can match structure without arguing about content. We want this recipe:
10	```
11	P1: A → B
12	P2: B → C
13	P3: ~A
14	Conc: ~C
15	```
16	Two rules that chain, a fact that negates the first condition, and a conclusion that negates the last outcome. Any answer that runs a chain correctly (forward from A, or backward from ~C) is valid, so it can''t be our match.','Goal','Goal'),
17	('3b09f457-6f4e-41a2-a1ad-30dcd8e3b300'::uuid,'5b78f50ee91302cc26382767b9f9509e','Devan does not meet any of these basic criteria for friendship: Devan has never bothered to be kind to the speaker, and has never offered help or companionship.','Evidence (since)','Evidence (since)'),
18	('d26f253b-a72f-40df-8a3f-8c40a85aad70'::uuid,'4d5ad7e884609949410a1ce8960bcbf9','How would we object to this conclusion? Given that Devan has never been kind, never offered help, and never offered companionship, how could we argue that Devan is not the speaker''s enemy?
19	
20	Easily. Failing the test for "friend" doesn''t put someone in the opposite category. There''s a lot of room between friend and enemy: a stranger, an acquaintance, a neighbor who never thinks about the speaker at all. An enemy is someone working against you. Nothing in the evidence says Devan has done anything against the speaker.
21	
22	So the author treats two opposites as if they were the only options. That''s a false choice: the evidence shows Devan is not at one extreme, and the conclusion puts Devan at the other.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
23	('09a4986f-7a40-41a5-a887-eecf63025b43'::uuid,'b8edb21a2dfcb4227ab12ffa5677daeb','Let''s look for an argument that shows something lacks the marks of one extreme, then concludes it belongs at the opposite extreme, skipping the middle ground. For example: Jim meets none of the criteria for best employee, so Jim is the worst employee.
24	
25	The direction can flip (no sign of the bad extreme, so the good extreme) and the topic will change. The quick test for each answer: is there a sensible middle option that the conclusion ignores?','Goal','Goal'),
26	('8504a9b1-f245-4975-8778-7556d38957de'::uuid,'265c99b04f5aa41afc01e9a27c86509f','Start with what the premises do prove. Some freelance journalists sell to magazines with lax standards. That gives us: some freelance journalists are not self-respecting writers.
27	
28	The author flipped it: some self-respecting writers are not freelance journalists. That''s a different claim, and the evidence doesn''t support it. 31	('2fd14b45-5190-46f6-9dd3-a188aa5c3469'::uuid,'fdfdbe005367c1702f5368357ccea955','Let''s look for something with this formula.
32	```
33	Premise 1: Some A''s are B.
34	Premise 2: No C''s are B.
35	Conclusion: Some C''s are not A.
36	```

38	('3af3fb66-9fbb-4a9f-8969-596fe0678c0d'::uuid,'6fc0f7f9fa7c90db3a8a7ad0e92e4245','Because there are quantifier and conditional words like "Every" and "no", it makes sense to think about diagramming this argument somewhat algebraically.
39	
40	There are also overlapping ideas (well-behaved is in all three claims, training is in two, Labradors are in two), which also argues for an algebraic approach.
41	
42	With a strong structural recipe, we might find the correct answer just by matching parts. But this conclusion is causal, so let''s be clear about why we object to it.
43	
44	How could we argue with the conclusion? We know training is required for good behavior. But required doesn''t mean it''s the whole story. Couldn''t a Labrador''s genes also play a role? A trained dog with a calm temperament might behave well, while a trained dog without one might not. 45	('07295199-3b8c-4852-a42b-7a1b932528e6'::uuid,'259c70f57f955bc6e0800ea47dffe4f4','Look for the same valid move: a rule with two necessary conditions joined by "and", a fact confirming one of them, a fact denying the other, and a conclusion that the sufficient condition fails.

53	('1c56b3ae-ebf1-4678-8be1-fa0edbd01ed0'::uuid,'671deccbfa8dfcec815cf539360c7a91','The proportion of full-length science-fiction films that are commercially successful is higher than the proportion of short documentary films that are commercially successful.','Conclusion','Conclusion'),
54	('30307406-fc89-436d-8539-c1da8d142d60'::uuid,'f75cce7a120f24f3d887808fae28ce65','Let''s take notes: `# succ short doc < # succ FL sci-fi`, `# short doc > # sci-fi`, therefore `% succ FL sci-fi > % succ short doc`.
55	
56	The evidence talks about numbers, and the conclusion talks about proportions. That shift often signals a flaw, but here it works. Short documentaries have fewer hits and more films. Fewer successes spread over a bigger group has to be a smaller share. Try numbers: 100 short documentaries with 5 hits is 5%; 50 science-fiction films with 10 hits is 20%.
57	
58	Now notice a modifier shift. The first premise and the conclusion say "full-length science-fiction films," but the middle premise says only "science-fiction films." That''s harmless too: if short documentaries outnumber all science-fiction films, they also outnumber the full-length ones.
59	
60	So the argument is valid. We need an answer with the same valid shape: fewer successes in the larger group, so a lower proportion in that group.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
61	('47672b3d-99ba-4d1d-8cf3-8d7d7f683885'::uuid,'7c43688ac55fbfa1fb9b1bbde101983b','Look for an answer with these pieces in these roles:
62	```
63	P1: Group X has fewer successes than Group Y.
64	P2: Group X is larger than Group Y.
65	Conc: Group Y has a higher proportion of successes.
66	```
67	The two premises must point in opposite directions (fewer hits, more members), and the proportion claim must be the conclusion, not a premise. 90	('2b6dd56f-9b93-4a93-96e2-24aa919cf549'::uuid,'18645c6a00aafbfc2b2fc23c78d68a67','Look for this recipe:

98	('dae977ee-437c-422b-92e2-77b07b511064'::uuid,'ed0d47ac395779a1e4d45432e3818bf8','This is a reasonable argument, built on a dispute between two sources.

102	The author doesn''t claim to settle it. The conclusion is modest: we should be suspicious of the reporter''s claim. Why lean toward the inspector? 103

13	('2f36e995-a397-4279-b070-de3509a8a40f'::uuid,'dcbb3403397f21882e727e9c3f5a2d43','This is a case, and the stem wants the general rule it illustrates. So strip out the specifics and keep the moving parts.

23	('56f863a7-167b-4c61-a12f-5bbf77c82d7e'::uuid,'1cde477671d3a063d92f0ea4a055fb93','This isn''t an argument. Nothing here is offered as proof of anything else. It is a description of a tradeoff, and the stem asks for the generalization it fits.
24	
25	Taylor''s methods did two things at once. They raised efficiency and productivity, and that raised most workers'' standards of living: a material gain. They also made jobs routine and repetitive, which took away some of the work''s intrinsic worth: a loss in what the work itself is like.
