2	('502b30bb-33b7-433b-9333-2980364a57dd'::uuid,1,'Evaluate','Line the analysis up against the coat. The coat buyer gives up warmth, which is comfort. The coat buyer does it to look sophisticated, which is appearances.
3	
4	So the analysis has two ingredients, and a matching situation needs both:
5	1. A real sacrifice: the person picks something that feels, tastes, or works worse for them.
6	2. A reason about how they look to others.
7	
8	A choice with only one ingredient doesn''t fit. Someone who sacrifices comfort for the planet fails the second. Someone who wants to impress but gives up nothing fails the first.'),
9	('502b30bb-33b7-433b-9333-2980364a57dd'::uuid,2,'Goal','Look for a person who knowingly takes the less pleasant option so that other people will be impressed.'),
10	('02878155-9b61-4c9e-91c7-2a55dc07b72f'::uuid,1,'Evaluate','Describe what happened in general terms, since the right principle won''t mention stairs or ladders.
11	
12	How did the children learn the word? By walking up and down the stairs, so they learned it through how the object is used.
13	
14	What did they do later? They called a ladder "stairs." A ladder is a different object, but it is used the same way: you climb it.
15	
16	So the study shows children stretching a word from the object they learned it on to a different object with the same use. Notice what the study does not show. It doesn''t compare teaching methods, so it can''t tell us how children learn "best." And it has one group at one age, so it can''t tell us anything about age.'),
17	('02878155-9b61-4c9e-91c7-2a55dc07b72f'::uuid,2,'Goal','Something like: children who learn a word through how an object is used sometimes apply the word to a different object that is used in a similar way.')
18	) v(e,p,l,b) where not exists (select 1 from lr_explanation_steps x where x.explanation_id=v.e and x.position=v.p) returning id;

1	update lr_explanation_choice_notes t set body=v.nb from (values
2	('c8e1214f-182c-45d9-970c-7cd03c222039'::uuid,'f77e95c762f9f0a40e73ee171fd58769','Roger won''t buy the expensive vacuum because Roger is frugal and would never forgive the spending. "A penny saved is a penny earned" is the frugal person''s motto, so the story illustrates it and the phrase is used properly.'),
3	('25c2f540-0a00-41b4-be44-924f3db1b5f9'::uuid,'735758e779bc487d92d996be0a35c308','Check both ingredients. The sacrifice: the couple passes over their favorite wine, which tastes better, so they give up pleasure. The reason: they think the other wine "will impress their dinner guests," which is appearances. That is the coat again: a worse experience in exchange for a better image. The "less expensive" detail is extra; the taste is the pleasure being given up.'),
4	('d8c733e7-9bb7-4638-88c7-0d6cdffa8ac9'::uuid,'43ca5ca7a8622caa9b5a385c6abb28f4','C is about how early in life a child meets an object and how easily the child learns not to misuse the word. The study has one group of young children and never compares ages. It also shows the children misusing the word, not learning to avoid misuse, so neither half of C has an example here.'),
5	('cb01788e-5b7d-4580-876b-8530c8be03aa'::uuid,'b22baecbde4242675f47c00501278f73','Match D to the study piece by piece. "learn a word by observing how the object denoted by that word is used": the children learned "stairs" while walking up and down stairs. "sometimes apply that word to a different object": they called a ladder stairs. "that is similarly used": both are things you climb. Every part of D has a matching fact, and D stays modest with "sometimes," which is all one study can illustrate.'),
6	('a0dabe1a-8844-44c7-b890-aaf04db0c502'::uuid,'1c249c5f5dab1f6fa20c404693baf123','A contrasts who really has the most power with who the public thinks has the most power. The case is about power people feel they have over a figure, not how powerful a figure seems to be. It never says the public misjudges who is most powerful, so A''s contrast has no example here.'),
7	('f1300a61-c45e-4816-b53d-112537638812'::uuid,'1387ad86ba27450163a48df80f37c640','B ties familiarity to how much power people ascribe to someone. The stimulus sets familiarity aside as not the main reason for blame, and never says familiarity changes how powerful anyone seems. B also leaves out blame, which is the behavior the whole case describes.'),
8	('6fd26bd8-e5d9-4c4c-b2dd-4e2cdb59ede4'::uuid,'a9d3b50a25c74c69777e6edcf517f40d','C is the tempting one, because politicians are well known and they do get blamed. But C makes being well known the reason for blame, and the stimulus says the blame is "not primarily because politicians are more familiar." The case illustrates a different cause, felt power. An answer that adopts the explanation the author rejects can''t be what the case illustrates.'),
9	('39743271-aedf-4cc7-ae43-350d50350193'::uuid,'646ab37c47df644419f5c82f9699c92b','D is about whether public figures are blamed enough for the problems they cause. The stimulus never judges whether the blame is the right amount; it explains why one group gets more blame than another. If anything, politicians get more blame than figures who are at least as responsible, which points away from "not held sufficiently responsible."'),
10	('d900629c-87dd-4d7f-acf8-b61fbcf0ea8b'::uuid,'da12530b5532dcce367b4b59f55c4913','Match the parts. "a publicly known person" covers politicians. "someone over whom they feel they have power" is the author''s own reason. "more inclined to blame" is the behavior in the case. E turns the case into a rule by swapping the specific group for a general category while keeping the cause the author endorses. Test it by plugging the case back in: people feel power over politicians, so they blame politicians more. That is the stimulus.'),
11	('9901c3d7-142b-4104-9488-80a979c2869e'::uuid,'3200021689453af4bbc0648392e8c99f','A ties precision to how detailed and complete the evidence is. The stimulus never describes the evidence behind the music or jazz predictions, let alone says it is more or less detailed. The only thing we see change is the target, from professors to music professors to jazz studies professors. A case that never shows the evidence varying can''t illustrate a rule about evidence.'),
12	('beeeaf67-2e21-4f2f-a80e-48e500bf8ab2'::uuid,'55a6d151b8bd2424891af063e8db8489','Line up the three predictions. All professors: reasonably accurate. Music professors, a narrower group: less accurate. Jazz studies professors, narrower still: less accurate again. Each step down makes the prediction more specific and less accurate, which is B read in reverse: the more general the level, the more accurate. On illustrate questions, name what changes across the case and what changes with it, then find the answer that links those two things.'),
13	('a1cf05f6-2b77-488b-b0ae-b5f276185dff'::uuid,'ed62da888831c469940ed2786127a109','D has A''s problem with a different outcome word: confidence instead of precision. Nothing in the stimulus says the evidence for one prediction is more detailed or complete than the evidence for another, so the case shows no example of better evidence earning more confidence. What changes is how specific the prediction is.'),
14	('5a34b232-1c82-4c9b-8614-148e78cabbb6'::uuid,'1c80e9d823b43d3c265950c3b892d41c','"It" refers back to efficiency, so A says some measures that seem to boost efficiency actually hurt efficiency. The stimulus says the opposite about Taylorism: it produced "greater efficiency" and increased productivity. The loss in the case is to the work''s intrinsic worth, not to efficiency.'),
15	('c094dc25-7da8-4c72-a463-d554e2589006'::uuid,'dfb8971d233da901043863ed15b92cc0','Match each piece. "Some developments in industry" is Taylorism. "benefit workers financially" is the rise in standards of living from increased productivity. "less rewarding in other respects" is the loss of intrinsic worth when the jobs became routine and repetitive. B keeps both sides of the tradeoff and stays modest with "Some" and "can," which is exactly what one case can illustrate.'),
16	('36de212e-6eda-4dcf-92fe-d243c4dca6b2'::uuid,'e2293dd2b3425df8b2097a2975ffca4d','C swaps in a different loss: workers devoting less effort to their jobs. The stimulus says the jobs became routine and repetitive, not that workers try less, and a repetitive job can take plenty of effort. The loss in the case is the work''s intrinsic worth, which C never mentions.'),
17	('1faf37f7-7be3-4b14-bd74-a5e68f98f1ea'::uuid,'1992591ad8a60006900759e37e002c0a','D is the closest trap because it uses both sides of the stimulus: higher living standards and something like valuing the job less. But D says a rise in living standards "will likely involve" a drop in how much workers value their jobs, as if the first brings the second. In the case, both came from Taylor''s methods; the higher living standard didn''t produce the routine work. D also stretches "some of the intrinsic worth" into how much workers value their jobs "overall," and the stimulus never says what workers themselves value.'),
18	('86362718-da1f-449a-a2d7-7eabf3e112b7'::uuid,'5d83334dca9eef3b51dc56c73b77ee68','E compares two kinds of workers, highly creative ones and average ones, and says the creative ones are sometimes less efficient. The stimulus compares the same jobs before and after Taylorism, not different workers. It never measures anyone''s creativity or says creative workers are slower.'),
19	('c52ddec7-ec2f-49ea-b2e7-2a54d5b9fff6'::uuid,'30b42c62fc8e2eb978c8737a32bfc61d','A is about people who see several ways to reduce a risk and take only the one they think works best. The journalist never mentions people choosing between safety measures. The argument is about protection leading people to take more risks, so both A''s trigger (several measures available) and its outcome (picking just one) miss.'),
20	('bf25f385-b25d-4d8a-bbb5-afde8af02948'::uuid,'dd28740b408db7e6c375f2ad46b6cd30','Set B beside both halves of the analogy. "ways to protect people from the consequences" is the SUV''s lower injury risk and the cancer cure. "behaviors that would normally harm them" is careless driving, smoking, and too much sun. "less careful to avoid such behaviors" is drivers driving less carefully and people smoking and tanning more. B is the Goal in general terms: protection from the downside makes the risky behavior more likely. When the reasoning is an analogy, the right principle is the one rule that covers both halves.'),
21	('f629f96d-2160-4046-ad61-321886f85b96'::uuid,'9d50c3c77bdb256e97737a61e54407ad','C says people take special care with behaviors they think will likely seriously injure them, and none with behaviors they think are harmless. The journalist''s people don''t think careless driving or smoking is harmless; they think the risk is lower or the disease curable. C also never says that reducing a risk makes people less careful, which is the journalist''s whole move.'),
22	('527e3d7c-082e-4d93-abe5-27b16a6b32fd'::uuid,'9d23112d140598ab8bd858dfd2e1efdf','D compares activities with known risks to activities of unknown risk. In the journalist''s examples the risks are known: SUV drivers "correctly" believe the risk is lower, and smoking and sun exposure are "known to increase the risks" of cancer. What changes is how bad the consequences are, not whether the risk is known, so D''s comparison never appears.'),
23	('6071dc4d-6710-40b2-a5cd-3119972d3f6c'::uuid,'e9e1408a5f8744dc9293053a0b6eeed8','E tempts if you reason a step ahead: a cure makes cancer a lesser harm, so other desires win out. But the journalist never sorts harms into serious and lesser and never mentions competing desires. The reasoning runs from more protection to less care. E mentions neither protection nor a change in behavior, so it doesn''t capture the link both of the journalist''s examples rely on.'),
24	('71b7fecc-9c8e-4bab-a960-5281b8994111'::uuid,'8b18e77a7ffae26d479183c6f86df042','A concludes the government is unjustified in interfering with Jerry''s moviemaking. Our principle can only prove that interference is justified. Jerry''s facts (no harm, a motive to benefit the children) show the triggers are missing, but a missing trigger never proves the opposite outcome. The principle simply has nothing to say about Jerry.'),
25	('fb983a5a-200b-456e-b16a-e28af79aa6c1'::uuid,'871aab9c62ebba0365ce53dcc9f79e8b','B has the right kind of outcome, a city council justified in acting, but the harm is aesthetic: a property is "less pleasing" to look at. The principle needs an increased likelihood of physical harm to others, and an unmowed lawn doesn''t make anyone more likely to get hurt. With the first trigger missing, the neighbor''s motive never matters.'),
26	('988fc8a3-804f-4bcb-9871-bdd77a802fe1'::uuid,'e0b8a2a0fb48d203f1cc49dc01520cf2','C is tempting because it involves physical injury and a government rule. But ask who gets hurt when a rider skips the helmet: the rider. The principle requires harm to others, so the first trigger fails. C also says nothing about the rider''s motive, so the second trigger is never established either.'),
27	('5978fe37-f39b-4f52-b14c-7d076a311670'::uuid,'28ed6cd3dc3246ec3431a9c32ba870b6','D gets the second trigger: Zabziew''s research is motivated by profit, "not by the desire to benefit customers." The first trigger fails. Being "of little help to people suffering from serious illness" is not increasing the likelihood of physical harm to them. Failing to help someone isn''t harming them, so the principle never fires.'),
28	('711c3689-a7e1-4279-814f-7a9c55a14617'::uuid,'cb0bf19b6f8be42face5cb89e01a6b23','Check both triggers against the facts. Physical harm to others: the speech "would most likely have caused a riot and people would have gotten hurt." Not motivated by a desire to help others: Jill''s aim was to further Jill''s own political ambitions. Both are established, so the rule delivers its outcome, and E''s conclusion matches it: the government was justified in preventing the speech. That is the move for every conform question with a conditional rule: confirm each trigger with facts in the choice, then make sure the conclusion is the rule''s right side.')
29	) v(id,ob,nb) where t.id=v.id and md5(t.body)=v.ob returning t.id;

2	('f23671f1-a452-49dc-b932-5172e154f330'::uuid,'4b44f027948580f8db31ed44576c2842','Rain is the only effective check on grass and brush fires.
3	When rainfall stays below normal for an extended period, there are many more of these fires.','Given That','Given That'),
4	('c8a11028-e252-4971-a598-7046817c23c7'::uuid,'9fbe49fd4a4558fb6472aa3131a6e932','Line the two periods up side by side:
5	```
6	Severe Drought        vs.   Normal Rain
7	many more fires             fewer fires
8	less $ damage               more $ damage
9	from fires                  from fires
10	```
11	Total damage is the number of fires times the damage each fire does. Drought brings many more fires, so if the drought total is lower, the average drought fire must be doing far less damage than the average fire in a normal year.
12	
13	So ask: what is different about a fire in a wet period that lets it do more damage? Rain does more than put fires out. Rain also grows plants, and plants are what these fires burn. A long drought leaves less to burn.
14	
15	Goal: look for an answer that makes each normal-rainfall fire bigger or costlier, or each drought fire smaller. Be suspicious of any answer that is equally true in drought and in normal rainfall. A fact that does not change between the two periods cannot explain a gap between them.','Evaluate / Goal','Evaluate / Goal'),
16	('dfd0a1a1-b154-4f26-8541-e0651f776943'::uuid,'0a8e2efad8169cce719f06af1b8dcd38','Since we know rescue squads save the lives of climbers, how would getting rid of the rescue squad lead to fewer climbing deaths and injuries?
17	There must be something else different in a world without rescue squads that would lead to fewer climbing deaths and injuries. Maybe having a rescue squad emboldens people to take risks they wouldn''t otherwise take. It''s like if you take away the safety net from a trapeze, a lot fewer people are going to attempt the trapeze, and so maybe you get a net reduction in trapeze injuries.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
18	('6138ce7b-e290-43db-ab1d-8ffaf0fe97c8'::uuid,'3850bfb9bab87c73f99281431b1cd921','Look for something that would be different in a world without rescue squads, something that would put fewer climbers in danger in the first place. The likeliest shape: the squads change who climbs, or how carefully they climb, by making the mountains feel safer than they are. If the squads draw enough extra people into danger, removing them could cut the toll even though each rescue saves a life.','Goal','Goal'),
19	('c7a81d9b-e963-497e-8042-2e432a697a8f'::uuid,'24515d00c53f27365475d2b46db18137','Jimmy replaced the old gas water heater with a new, pilotless, gas water heater that is rated as highly efficient. After that, Jimmy''s gas bills increased.','Apparent Paradox','Apparent Paradox'),
20	('a6a23aa9-aaaa-4593-b1bd-99de298dc8b6'::uuid,'f981f7fe9de480f9de00d9c7462d296d','This is less a paradox than a surprise. A highly efficient heater sounds like it should lower the bill. But the bill depends on two things: how much gas the whole household burns, and the price of each unit of gas. The water heater is only one of the things in the house that burns gas.
21	
22	So the bill can rise, even with a better heater, by two routes.
23	
24	Route one: more gas used somewhere in the household. More people, a new gas appliance, more heating.
25	
26	Route two: a higher price for each unit of gas.
27	
28	The new heater''s efficiency only shrinks the heater''s own use. It does nothing about the rest of the house or the price.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
29	('64c64245-41ef-40e8-93d3-dc2e23e5b14f'::uuid,'e619346b426a76a08ea7cabd62d0c472','Notice what the stimulus measures: the retail profit margin, meaning how much profit stores keep out of what they take in on PC sales. Rising demand might make us expect fat margins, since stores could charge more and still find buyers. But demand is only one input. A margin depends on the price the store charges and on what it costs the store to make each sale.
30	
31	So there are two routes to a thin margin.
32	
33	Price is held down: heavy competition, or stores choosing to keep PC prices low on purpose.
34	
35	Costs are pushed up: expenses that come with selling PCs in particular, such as extra staff time or stock that loses value.
36	
37	The stimulus also compares PCs with other popular high-tech items, so the strongest explanations hit PCs harder than those items.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
38	('2ecfc5bb-81ac-4888-9b83-615ca55fdd7d'::uuid,'9e668710e36356fca16d64f0f04fd02f','We need to find four reasons why PC''s have a lower profit margin (or why other popular high-tech items have a higher profit margin). Each one should either lower what stores can charge for PCs or raise what it costs stores to sell them. The exception will do neither. Watch for an answer that is about PCs and their buyers but never touches the store''s price or cost.','Goal','Goal'),
39	('847bb3f5-435f-48a5-9ebd-c3907c2d2900'::uuid,'86a3f4c443e9560696900460c515719d','This is less a paradox than a result to explain. We might expect bottling up upsetting feelings to backfire, yet the repressors come out ahead on every measure: less shy and anxious, better frustration tolerance, better social skills, higher grades, more self-esteem.
40	
41	An answer contributes if it gives a reason for any one of those advantages. There are a few ways in.
42	
43	Something about repressing helps directly: it keeps repressors focused, or keeps them from pushing people away.
44	
45	Something about sensitizers drags them down. The finding is a comparison, so a sensitizer disadvantage explains the gap just as well.
46	
47	Something outside the students treats repressors better.
48	
49	So we eliminate four answers that give a reason for at least one advantage. The exception will explain something else, such as why repressors repress in the first place, rather than why they have the advantages.','Evaluate / Goal','Evaluate / Goal'),
50	('6ea0a928-0732-4f7d-8489-f6b316a10c6f'::uuid,'230d5e9f0cc2da5424470d1b016b55a4','Premise: People who have never been asked to do more than they can easily do never do all they can.
51	(Never pushed → never does all they can.)
52	Premise: Alex has not done all that Alex is capable of doing.
53	Conclusion: No one has ever pushed Alex to do more than what comes easily.','Original Argument','Original Argument'),
54	('2e179b89-b749-4bf4-8adb-9d1284ecddf1'::uuid,'db028c37a4f47d3b7e079f87ebd04fd1','The flaw is affirming the consequent, also called mistaking a necessary condition for a sufficient one. The rule says: never pushed → does not do all they can. The argument sees the right side (Alex is not doing all Alex can) and concludes the left side (Alex was never pushed).
55	
56	But the rule only runs one way. Someone who was pushed hard might still fall short: laziness, illness, bad luck. Falling short is necessary for being never pushed (everyone never pushed falls short), but it is not sufficient to prove it. The argument treats Alex falling short as enough to prove Alex was never pushed.
57	
58	In plain shape:
59	All A are B.
60	X is B.
61	So X is A.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
62	('24c39abf-6eb6-48c7-88c3-ba3de8524ecf'::uuid,'b4cd3e00959a193e04eb74dd221af45a','Find an answer with the same shape: a rule (A → B), a fact that something has B, and a conclusion that it has A.
63	
64	For each answer, diagram the rule, then ask two questions. Does the evidence land on the rule''s right side? Does the conclusion land on its left side? Expect two kinds of traps: an answer that negates the left side instead (a different flaw), and an answer that runs a valid contrapositive (no flaw at all).','Goal','Goal'),
65	('29df0386-d9ee-4487-bccc-5ed11a66c7be'::uuid,'58028f141b637437941ea97925e444f7','The evidence is a comparison between two groups: people who use a tax preparation service get refunds about 50 percent higher, on average, than people who do not. The conclusion turns that into advice: use a service to get a large refund. That move assumes the service causes the bigger refund.
66	
67	How else could the gap arise? Maybe the people who hire a service are the ones with complicated returns, more income or more deductions, and they would get big refunds whoever did the paperwork. The big refund might be the reason they paid for help, not the result of it.
68	
69	This is a causal flaw: a correlation between two groups treated as proof that one thing produces the other, then used to recommend it.','Evaluate','Evaluate')
70	) v(id,ob,nb,ol,nl) where t.id=v.id and md5(t.body)=v.ob returning t.id;

The correct answer will do neither. A good place to look: an answer about the water heater itself, since the stimulus already tells us the heater is efficient, which points toward less gas, not more.'),
3	('c55f58b1-63cc-446d-9615-85cc6834668a'::uuid,3,'Goal','Look for an argument with the same recipe:
4	People who do X have more Y than people who do not.
5	So if you want Y, you should do X.
6	
7	The evidence must be a bare comparison between groups, not a stated cause. If an answer''s evidence already says X produces Y (it enables Y, lowers Y, helps with Y), then recommending X is reasonable and the flaw is gone.')
8	) v(e,p,l,b) where not exists (select 1 from lr_explanation_steps x where x.explanation_id=v.e and x.position=v.p) returning id;

2	('639264bc-735b-463a-881c-f12c4be3e025'::uuid,'89653a512c7360fedea8e508439e98ea','A pushes the wrong way. 3	('c16b668d-57be-45c5-8d84-533ce521336a'::uuid,'39ac34922ff4005ed1e24d83d0ffb2d0','B compares places, not periods. It says fire-prone areas are less densely populated than areas with few fires. 4	('d30c5889-77cc-4ea4-85bf-71c8445103de'::uuid,'e0941303e9094338cb1e3f4927dcd3d7','C gives us the difference-maker. 5	
6	Now both facts fit. In a drought, fires start easily, so there are many more of them, but there is little fuel, so they stay small. 7

10	('c55a4068-20ef-428c-a31f-0a7159c0eebf'::uuid,'b25b3e19502109ba27a89c6c7ffef579','E is the vegetation trap. It talks about fuel, which is the right topic, but it does not help. 20	('bc1e9cd3-871c-463a-ae9e-14108e66a53e'::uuid,'6963688863a9f4b1bd18e4caa6760554','A takes road 1. If the wastewater draws in fish that prey on bass, more bass get eaten and fewer are left downstream to catch. That explains the drop in bass caught, so A is out.'),
21	('09715b96-d8dc-43ac-9da7-8df2738d6c9d'::uuid,'36b237f8f43a4e352d60291924071fac','B also takes road 1. The warmer discharge sends bass off to find cooler water elsewhere. Fewer bass stay downstream of the plant, so anglers there catch fewer. That explains the drop, so eliminate B.'),
22	('a7363b92-0e04-4d9f-92f5-559a26c2300a'::uuid,'fb4ffc92331aa08bc7ea696c80dc24a9','C pushes the other way. Better access brings more anglers fishing for bass downstream. More people fishing should mean more bass caught, not fewer, so C cannot explain the decrease.

25	('96597a73-05b1-4189-b7a8-85bb2b514718'::uuid,'90bdfbd1dad314b7f2d5b66d4843b515','D is the road 2 answer, and it is easy to throw out as off topic because it is about anglers, not bass. 26	('6b186f39-db7c-4cdb-811b-9d07def23aa5'::uuid,'c2f7a9c6eba2c67409143ebb32cb2fc9','E is road 1 again. Turbulence from the wastewater disrupted the river vegetation and destroyed some of the bass''s habitat. Less habitat supports fewer bass downstream, so fewer get caught. E explains the drop.'),
27	('dfc41b19-dd36-46d8-b6cb-a4e8fae00a46'::uuid,'a3882a896e36bbc6cff3522ebce636ed','A explains nothing. It says the new heater uses a smaller percentage of the household''s gas than the old one did. 34	('59ef34b9-9fb1-479a-a40f-25c01c9e601b'::uuid,'a0cc43cc39943a9b72b7072f34156d6a','A is the cost route. When computer technology changes fast, unsold stock is more likely to become obsolete. 36	('a896e35d-6599-48a6-8f65-b37a66ffc9b0'::uuid,'09d413adfe423533da37617773a6b769','C is the cost route, with the comparison built in. 37	('b4dc49ba-f562-409f-a103-72ef40f95db8'::uuid,'b569be71c6aebfd306c8dbe2ee88bcda','D is the price route, chosen on purpose. Figoria has conserved, and nobody has shown that its development is hurting anything.
12	
13	So the fight is over timing. Should Figoria regulate in advance, based on what happened in other nations, or wait until harm is shown in Figoria? A principle that says regulation has to wait for demonstrated harm would settle that fight in the Development Commission''s favor.
14	
15	Also watch the direction of the stem. We need a principle that helps the Development Commission against the Wildlife Commission. An answer that supports protecting wildlife, however reasonable it sounds, is on the wrong side.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),

43	('1839d06e-b7a9-4805-b5bd-057cfc7b1c4c'::uuid,'4909310c79c592df259f56840c554816','E is the most tempting wrong answer. And E says James thought "a different one might work better," which suggests James still wanted a camera for future filming. The intended use was not finished.'),

53	('d9991a7a-df28-48cf-a60b-fe1e8d39796b'::uuid,'120a2368c553be0115232d05bf56f271','C is about when governments should pay: government required to pay → manufacturers also required. 54	('b034f92e-7340-4eca-9a8a-6547f6eeb6ff'::uuid,'902d0c7d7bc21268d81e54192cd7b1ca','D says: an industry whose product''s use contributes to costly damage for others → that industry is liable for the damage. Outcome: the industry is liable, which covers "help pay."

56	D''s outcome is a little stronger than Mateo''s conclusion (liable for the damage, not just help pay). That is fine on a justify question. A principle can prove more than the conclusion needs; it just cannot prove less.'),
57	('c6d51b0b-d733-4c17-b7dd-50fed53d9f42'::uuid,'50ab7a19af949c53f00c4a9fb44ef285','E''s "only if" makes the general obligation a requirement: required to pay for specific damage → general obligation to pay for all damage produced by global warming. 58	) v(id,ob,nb) where t.id=v.id and md5(t.body)=v.ob returning t.id;

2	('c98f53e7-554d-45c9-860b-0fc7af5b9a5c'::uuid,3,'Goal','Look for a principle whose condition is met by the evidence and whose outcome says something about all commitments:

2	('b2723059-9d7e-4017-a4a1-29ec80e7550d'::uuid,'2f5efd746d29408eb925cad8dd954af5','The builders won''t finish the Glen Veil complex unless a road connecting it to Sierra is built. So the road is required for the complex.
3	
4	If the complex is completed, it will strengthen Sierra''s economy, and a stronger economy would benefit every Sierra resident.','Evidence','Evidence'),
5	('3310ea29-a41b-4cd6-b66c-e5c17902eed8'::uuid,'29989d5a0b25a5447c081a3578261e6c','Line up what the premises give us against what the conclusion asks for.
6	
7	The premises are all about benefit. The complex is waiting on the road, the finished complex strengthens the economy, and the stronger economy helps every resident.
8	
9	The conclusion is about duty: residents should vote for a tax. Nothing in the premises says that benefiting from something means you ought to vote to fund it. That''s the new idea the conclusion brings in, and it''s the gap.
10	
11	There''s also a cost the developer never weighs. A tax costs every resident something too. The developer simply treats the benefit as enough to settle the vote. A principle that justifies this reasoning has to make that move for us.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
12	('96a7eb1b-8852-45ed-8fc6-c64b3d76f940'::uuid,'fea6c5627a60adea7d8a16f88a4dc7a9','On a justify-the-reasoning principle, the answer usually has the shape If Evidence, then Conclusion, written in general terms. 13	
14	would benefit from a construction project → should vote for a tax that funds it
15	
16	The right side has to say residents should vote in favor. A principle that only tells us when not to vote for a tax, or who should pay one, can''t deliver that conclusion.','Goal','Goal'),
17	('5de67afa-c920-4f55-a9ab-7675f95e9ea6'::uuid,'23fa8aa6b1557b7cfd80dedab9dafeff','We should not be persuaded by Graham''s argument.','Main Conclusion','Main Conclusion'),
18	('5b95a90f-0d10-4886-b6cb-159da16407ac'::uuid,'6f19c58fdef23cd4411360a2cd595c3c','The best life is a life that is full of activity.','Opposing Point','Opposing Point (Graham''s conclusion)'),
19	('b65862a4-6b68-4ac1-b554-6d99edac9a87'::uuid,'c4825554f2c5f357549ac56770a2133a','A person is truly happy only when doing something.','Opposing Point','Opposing Point (Graham''s premise)'),
20	('21922f05-e8be-427e-85b2-ce475ef19f95'::uuid,'e459c4e7e23956427d75b2614798b0c6','The evolutionary advantage of sexual reproduction is that it increases the range of genetic variation in a species, which is an advantage for the species as a whole. However, an increased range of genetic variation in a species is not advantageous for any individual member of the species.','Evidence','Evidence'),
21	('74fef0de-d608-4bbf-932a-97adf76734dc'::uuid,'4a1559850785178c16855781124bd911','"It follows that" marks the last sentence as the conclusion: the sole reason sexual reproduction became the rule is that natural selection favored some entire species over others.
22	
23	Why should we believe it? The biologist gives two facts that work together. First, the advantage of sexual reproduction is wider genetic variation, which helps the species as a whole. Second, that variation helps no individual member. If the advantage shows up only at the species level, selection among individuals can''t explain why sexual reproduction spread. That leaves selection among whole species, which is the conclusion.
24	
25	Slow down on the "However". It contrasts species with individuals, but it doesn''t turn against the biologist. Both sentences are on the conclusion''s side. The second one actually does the heavier lifting, since it is what rules out an individual-level explanation.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
26	('e781f424-c2e2-4c0a-bee0-c4bc68159971'::uuid,'a5cd1a89dc9078525dea319f5b7a0711','The stem asks about the second premise, the claim that the variation helps no individual. Predict: a premise that supports the conclusion. Expect an answer as plain as a claim offered in support of the conclusion.','Goal','Goal'),
27	('b00f913d-5cb5-4b09-9b98-b9a7d29ba588'::uuid,'38a005370e81160cca1baffd36eb3545','Emotion only seems nonrational because language lacks the ability to convey adequate conceptions of emotion.','Intermediate Conclusion','Intermediate Conclusion'),
28	('4b34d9dd-e6f5-4bd6-93cb-1ce9ec475561'::uuid,'09b1e356a652e7c3734f29045abbcc1c','The words we use to refer to emotions name only very general kinds of inner experience, such as excitement, calm and joy.
29	
30	Illustration of that: there is no language for describing just how one joy differs from another.','Evidence','Evidence'),
31	('3dca010a-1ca5-4cfa-a0e7-ff601025c577'::uuid,'af55122d05b81512bdd3158649ccd1df','Role and Main Conclusion arguments often put the conclusion right after a pivot that pushes back on someone''s view. Here the philosopher opens with how philosophers usually treat emotions, as nonrational, then pivots with "But": emotion is not nonrational. That''s the main conclusion.
32	
33	Everything after it is support, in layers. Why believe emotion isn''t nonrational? Because it only seems that way, since language can''t convey adequate conceptions of emotion. Why believe language falls short? Because emotion words name only very general kinds of experience.
34	
35	Then the last sentence opens with "Thus, for example". Two signals that seem to fight. "Thus" usually marks something that follows; "for example" marks an illustration. Both fit. If emotion words are only general, they can''t separate one joy from another, so the last sentence follows from the general claim. And it is offered as one concrete case of that general claim. It isn''t where the argument is headed. It is a picture of the evidence.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
36	('a9eb97e3-cf7b-4a59-a97b-4b8d2fa34fff'::uuid,'6f2fa550bf2a33c2d8cc86f2131a1fdd','The target claim is a specific case of the general claim about emotion words, and that general claim supports the main conclusion through the middle step about language. Predict an answer that calls it an example or illustration of a supporting claim, with only an indirect link to the main conclusion.','Goal','Goal'),
37	('fdd643c6-3726-49f1-8a6a-62029db0a774'::uuid,'1ebeae12df740e4efd3b53b08d7a376a','Start with the indicator. "Thus" opens the last sentence, so that''s a conclusion: groups that switched to agriculture were likely motivated by benefits of settled life.
38	
39	Now test the first sentence the way we test any candidate: why should we believe the transition was traumatic? The second sentence answers. More disease and injury, and a diet lacking vital nutrients. So the first sentence has support of its own.
40	
41	Does it support anything? Yes. Why think the groups were drawn by benefits like wealth? Because the switch was traumatic, and the argument''s thought is that groups wouldn''t accept that kind of hardship without something to gain. So the traumatic claim is supported by the second sentence and supports the last one. That makes it an intermediate conclusion.
42	
43	The first sentence looks like a classic first-sentence conclusion. It is a conclusion, just not the main one. "Thus" settles which one is main.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
44	('76ef4fb8-1fec-4f04-8aee-3f4e268e01bf'::uuid,'6b43e421ab74166d8d232f87a7cc8c3b','A successful legal system prohibits only those few behaviors that citizens find absolutely intolerable.','Conclusion (Therefore)','Conclusion (Therefore)'),
45	('b4bbfe52-39ce-4c25-af44-b5f393dff913'::uuid,'b7e19e2c46033d0cb36c3701a7858588','On Role and Main Conclusion, it pays to check the first sentence and any pivot before trusting the end. Here neither holds up. The first sentence, about the purpose of a law, gets no support from anything else. The "But" sentence, about the odds of being caught dropping as prohibitions multiply, isn''t supported either. A claim with no support can''t be a conclusion.
46	
47	That leaves the "Therefore" sentence, and this time it really is the main conclusion: a successful legal system prohibits only the few behaviors citizens find absolutely intolerable. Why believe that? Laws work by threatening punishment. The threat works only if people think they''re likely to be punished. And the more kinds of acts are prohibited, the less likely punishment becomes. Keep the list short, and the threat stays believable.
48	
49	The first sentence is the starting point of that chain. Nothing supports it, and it supports the conclusion.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
50	('6919ad1a-3684-47e2-8849-c8c87ebe5896'::uuid,'82480d0f39fb3f061f8e580b00df657c','The target is the first sentence. It supports the conclusion and has no support of its own. Predict: a premise.','Goal','Goal'),
51	('8b4c7808-551e-4002-a35e-98c711a9ad06'::uuid,'f4665fe621eaa0d45e9e16b340f7b8f4','On Main Conclusion and Role, the conclusion is usually found earlier than the support, but in this case it was the final sentence, signified by "Hence". Because this is Role, we want to be highly alert for whether that "Hence" is actually just an Intermediate Conclusion, but in this case we can tell it''s the main conclusion because the 1st and 3rd claim combine to support this 4th claim. There are four claims in this argument, and structurally they go in this order:
52	    1. Premise
53	    2. Counterpoint (although)
54	    3. Premise
55	    4. Conclusion (hence)
56	    We''re being asked about the first sentence, which was one of the two premises for the conclusion in the final sentence.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
57	('590aeacf-663b-4031-8953-c7c6fe3e9d29'::uuid,'99975be4383a4e1465899b7551190657','The stem asks about the first sentence, one of the two premises. Predict: a premise that supports the conclusion that a widespread grassroots push for stricter air pollution controls is unlikely right now.','Goal','Goal'),
58	('d42ea42a-23c0-465d-a5ca-6a5a43183410'::uuid,'fb01e37436b1a9057b36ce716c998932','On Role and Main Conclusion, the conclusion very often sits in the first sentence or right after a pivot. So hear the first sentence as a possible opinion: our mastery of Latin and Ancient Greek is "at best imperfect." If the rest of the passage supports it, it''s the main conclusion.
59	
60	It does. The second sentence sets up a contrast. On one side, the best students of a modern language can immerse themselves where it is spoken and get close to perfect knowledge. On the other side, you can''t spend a year abroad at Plato''s Academy. Immersion is open for living languages and closed for ancient ones. That contrast is why the classicist thinks mastery of the ancient languages falls short.
61	
62	Notice what the Plato''s Academy line is. It isn''t a general statement that ancient immersion is impossible. It is one vivid case that makes the point.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
63	('d1b5c182-d05e-4fe3-9bca-613753f99083'::uuid,'0226cdf72604b474d28c9bc224855808','The target claim is the second half of the contrast, given as a concrete case. Predict: support for the first sentence, possibly described as an example or as one side of a comparison.','Goal','Goal')

2	('54578ff4-38db-4c40-a9a5-21b0d21c86b9'::uuid,4,'Evaluate','Two arguments are stacked here. Graham''s: a person is truly happy only when doing something, so the best life is full of activity. The philosopher''s: we shouldn''t be persuaded by Graham''s argument, because people are sometimes truly happy while sleeping, when they aren''t doing anything.
3	
4	Which part of Graham''s argument does the sleep claim hit? Graham''s premise is a conditional:
5	
6	truly happy → doing something
7	
8	A sleeper who is truly happy while doing nothing has the left side without the right side. That''s a counterexample to the premise.
9	
10	Notice what the philosopher does not claim. The philosopher never says the best life isn''t full of activity. The conclusion is only that Graham''s argument shouldn''t persuade us. Knocking out a premise is enough for that, because an argument with a false premise doesn''t establish its conclusion, even if the conclusion happens to be true.'),
11	('54578ff4-38db-4c40-a9a5-21b0d21c86b9'::uuid,5,'Goal','The claim in the stem is the philosopher''s premise, and its job is to show that Graham''s premise is false. Look for an answer that names both pieces: an example, aimed at Graham''s premise rather than Graham''s conclusion.'),
12	('c455f175-2763-4d8b-972a-a61f7a8224a2'::uuid,4,'Goal','The quoted claim is an intermediate conclusion, but the answer may not use that phrase. It might call the claim a premise that has support of its own. Look for an answer that says the claim is supported and also supports the main conclusion.')
13	) v(e,p,l,b) where not exists (select 1 from lr_explanation_steps x where x.explanation_id=v.e and x.position=v.p) returning id;

56	('7674ffe2-0c4d-4aa2-801b-6ffac58f9777'::uuid,'6f7e8559a74753d6faa07045b34fd632','B describes the claim''s job piece by piece. 60	('7745c34e-bc87-45bb-ad27-c20d86e952be'::uuid,'e481e43a10b6178045a4032d096a311c','D starts well, because the claim is support. The problem is "guarantees the truth". 61	('9625d1bf-cd58-4e5a-b56d-3612b62f0c42'::uuid,'cfa12194c7ab1401a82d5852a8c0547a','An ancillary conclusion would be a claim the argument supports on its way to the main point. Graham''s: a person is truly happy only when doing something, so the best life is full of activity. The philosopher''s: we shouldn''t be persuaded by Graham''s argument, because people are sometimes truly happy while sleeping, when they aren''t doing anything.\n\nWhich part of Graham''s argument does the sleep claim hit? The conclusion is only that Graham''s argument shouldn''t persuade us. Knocking out a premise is enough for that, because an argument with a false premise doesn''t establish its conclusion, even if the conclusion happens to be true.'),\n('54578ff4-38db-4c40-a9a5-21b0d21c86b9'::uuid,5,'Goal','The claim in the stem is the philosopher''s premise, and its job is to show that Graham''s premise is false. It might call the claim a premise that has support of its own. 2	('00e40578-bc91-4a71-8b9f-67df69fbcf56'::uuid,'6ebd0e6dcdb28bb6af21f515460594da','On a Role question, find the conclusion first, then ask what the named claim does for it.
3	
4	The conclusion carries the opinion word: the medical establishment should "announce only conclusive results". The next sentence opens with "After all," and that phrase hands us a reason for the claim right before it. So the fire drill sentence is support for the conclusion.
5	
6	Now look at what kind of support it is. Fire drills have nothing to do with food studies. The physician pulls in a situation from a different area of life because it works the same way: people hear a signal over and over, the signal rarely means anything, and they stop reacting. Constant tentative warnings are the fire drills. A health warning that finally matters is the real alarm. That is an analogy.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
7	('88d2713b-fc3b-4661-bf77-db6938b0e762'::uuid,'85a4009d9a50141df4c269260ff5696e','We''re asked about the last sentence. Prediction: it''s an analogy offered as support for the main conclusion, the claim that the medical establishment should announce only conclusive results.
8	
9	Any answer that calls it an example of the health warnings themselves, an objection, or decoration is out before we read the details.','Goal','Goal'),
10	('47320945-1608-4997-8a8d-2553ef76b2c0'::uuid,'0ea35382176ad5a255d74089f0c0e2f4','Among 100 first-graders who got handwriting lessons, those whose composition skills had improved the most were the ones who had learned to write letters the most automatically.

12	Notice the mismatch: the composition half is about improvement, while the handwriting half is about how automatic the kids ended up.','Evidence','Evidence'),
13	('cf84d2b1-9d6f-44a8-b234-abc41fd3c429'::uuid,'4de4c24d06fc48a08c438fe20146ba7d','This is a study that hands us a correlation, and the author reads a cause into it.
14	
15	CURIOUS FACT: Why were the kids with the biggest composition gains the same kids who wrote letters most automatically?
16	
17	AUTHOR''S EXPLANATION: Handwriting lessons made writing automatic for some kids. Once forming letters stopped taking effort, those kids had attention left over for what they were writing, so their composition improved.
18	
19	Now argue with it. How could we explain the same data without the author''s story? Maybe some kids were simply stronger students from the start. They could already write letters automatically before the lessons, and they also picked up composition faster, with no help from automatic handwriting. The evidence doesn''t rule that out, because it never tells us whether automaticity changed during the lessons.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
20	('7c43a239-ae68-4b6e-8e8c-c8baf632e8ec'::uuid,'03bb0458011b26fc7f9e793f4cf0a51d','Strengthen answers for a curious fact usually do one of two things: make the author''s explanation more plausible, or rule out an alternate explanation.
21	
22	The best target here: show that the kids who gained the most automaticity during the lessons also gained the most in composition. Change tracking change is what we''d expect if automatic handwriting frees up attention, and it shrinks the room for the stronger-students-from-the-start story.','Goal','Goal'),
23	('dfe89858-b232-4a53-b9da-12973ec59c10'::uuid,'7438b726b97146fe8aab2d9540a350eb','The conclusion follows a process of elimination. M can''t be a soft-gel, because the company "does not have soft-gel manufacturing technology" and makes everything itself. Capsule is what''s left.
24	
25	But look at who the first rule covers: only medications with an unpleasant taste. Nothing tells us M tastes bad. If M tastes fine, the rule never applies, and M could come in a liquid, a powder, or anything else. The elimination only works if M is in the group the rule covers.
26	PT → (T or C or SG)
27	~T
28	~SG
29	missing: PT','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
30	('75c4f679-6d2a-401c-938d-59a4bf0c3e64'::uuid,'44707bda1a062188817b66cfae608ca5','In ancient Greek courts, witnesses were not cross-examined, and the jury, "selected from the citizenry," "received no guidance on points of law".

32	('bac48c6b-a834-48b0-82d2-9d1b65a21402'::uuid,'1e41c824566089cf373502c4545dd4fd','The evidence tells us litigants worked hard to impress jurors. The conclusion jumps to something else: that their speeches show what ordinary citizens thought was moral.

48	
49	How could we argue they weren''t? Maybe the sharpened poles were for fending off predators. Maybe the horses died on their own, and the precursors used the flint and poles to cut up and carry away the carcasses. Either way, the find fits a group of scavengers just fine.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),

51	('5255bdef-38f2-4903-8b12-a8ead7021a4d'::uuid,'27fbaa7298362c107251c4eb0d7ccfc1','Profit is what you take in minus what you spend. The evidence says organic and conventional orchards cost the same to run and produce the same amount. 52	
53	How could we argue against that? Maybe buyers don''t care about taste. If people buy apples by price or by looks, better tasting apples sell no better and earn no more. Then equal costs and equal output mean equal profit.
54	
55	The argument needs better taste to turn into more money: higher prices, more sales, or both.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),

57	('1316bb8b-f740-422a-9ab1-94498a72113c'::uuid,'84470016873c69b4ab8364767e3ca902','First-born children in the study consistently showed "less cognitive plasticity than did their siblings." Cognitive plasticity is the willingness to accept new ideas.

59	('fba4670a-559d-475c-83e6-f8f64bafea7e'::uuid,'39cfba36a361a2ba1f310ab596c114e5','The study only measured one thing: openness to new ideas. The conclusion is about something else: being adventurous. The psychologist bridges the two with a premise that is just "reasonable to think".

1	update lr_explanation_steps t set body=v.nb, label=case when v.nl='' then t.label else v.nl end from (values
2	('60b131b6-a973-463f-aafe-09362438b040'::uuid,'1fa2b7bed1f7c7ff676682ad74491c4c','This is a curious fact with two competing stories. The fact: this society burned large areas of land. The rival story: the burning cleared ground for planting, so the society was turning to large-scale agriculture. The author''s story: the society was still hunting and gathering.
3	
4	The author''s only support is an absence: little evidence of cultivation after the fires. That is a fair point against the farming story, but it leaves a hole. If these people were hunter-gatherers, why were they burning large areas of land at all? Right now the burning has an explanation under the farming story and none under the author''s.
5	
6	Given that the society burned large areas of land, how could we still argue that it was farming? We could say crops were planted but left little trace, or that the land was burned for some other farming purpose. Nothing in the argument answers the basic question: what would hunter-gatherers want with a big fire?','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
7	('3d637c76-8c6a-4650-9ad8-8fa720de43bd'::uuid,'75db097a9839b538c6dcc71607b175ae','Look for an answer that gives hunter-gatherers a reason to burn large areas of land. That turns the burning from evidence for farming into something the author''s story expects. A second acceptable shape: more evidence that the burning was not done to clear ground for planting. Answers about small fires, or about farming in other societies, will not do this work.','Goal','Goal'),
8	('bba7ef62-0a16-4a9f-ade3-0a0b759dd2ba'::uuid,'ca9e52dd1b063c3b6779b3f539ab4710','The premise is about problems: most daily-life problems need knowledge from more than one discipline. The conclusion is about courses: schools should require interdisciplinary courses instead of single-discipline ones. The gap is the jump from what problems need to how courses must be built.
9	
10	Given that most daily-life problems need more than one discipline, how could we still argue that schools should keep single-discipline courses? Easy. Students could take several single-discipline courses and then combine what they learned when a real problem shows up. If students can do that combining on their own, interdisciplinary courses are not needed.
11	
12	So the educator is assuming that students in single-discipline courses will not put their knowledge together on their own.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
13	('a9b995df-a258-4b59-bd78-4ed1b9edaf72'::uuid,'354350dfedf7be45f7be72dd9ccf084c','Look for an answer that shuts down that objection: students who take only single-discipline courses do not, or cannot, combine what they learned. A second acceptable shape links premise to conclusion directly: if daily-life problems need several disciplines, schools should teach across disciplines. A strengthener does not have to prove the conclusion. It only has to make it more likely.','Goal','Goal'),
14	('e4f2e465-fe3c-43e5-88ed-ac3bb4c78929'::uuid,'f3ef18453d82d6c84053e7a2fe04438e','The psychologist presents a correlation:
15	```
16	more stressed by speaking (introverts)  ||  bigger blood pressure rise
17	```
18	Then the psychologist concludes that one causes the other: the stress of communicating drives the rise, not the physical work of producing speech.
19	
20	That is a Curious Fact → Causal Explanation argument, so we check two things:
21	1. Is there an alternate explanation for why introverts'' surges are bigger?
22	2. How plausible is the author''s explanation?
23	
24	Given the correlation, how could we still argue that physical exertion causes the rise? Maybe introverts and extroverts differ in some physical way when they talk, or in some health factor that changes how much their pressure moves. The bigger problem: whenever someone speaks, communicating and the physical act of speaking happen together. The argument never pulls them apart.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
25	('179a492d-c909-420b-b1ca-629f60a75a89'::uuid,'e54656de8271afd4bf8884adf13fbdf7','Look for an answer that separates communication from the physical work of speaking and shows blood pressure following communication. The ideal case: communication without vocal speech, or similar physical effort without communication. A second acceptable shape rules out an alternate explanation for why extroverts'' surges are milder.','Goal','Goal'),
26	('709e28bc-36a1-4abe-aa2a-c5b77ae40e96'::uuid,'d51297a607323439f52baf4042d74aba','This premise is conditional. By contrapositive, it tells us something about every frying pan that comes with a warranty.
27	```
28	manufacturer offers a warranty  →  manufacturer does not expect to reimburse many customers
29	```
30	So the author says we should only buy pans with a warranty, because a warranty means the manufacturer is not worried about paying out a lot of claims.
31	
32	The author assumes the manufacturer is not worried because the pan is good: it is not expected to fail for many buyers.
33	
34	But maybe the manufacturer is not worried for a different reason. It might expect plenty of pans to fail and still bet that few customers will bother to claim.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
35	('c11586d4-6ad8-4cf4-bd8b-acd63bc0cd8b'::uuid,'7aff3cf06d16ac1c285c729fa13f2546','Look for an answer that closes that gap: a pan that does not work well or last long really would cost its manufacturer, because many buyers would seek reimbursement. Then a warranty can only sit on a pan the manufacturer expects to hold up.
36	
37	Notice who the conclusion is talking to: a buyer who would never bother to claim. So the answer has to be about other buyers. Their claims are what make the warranty mean something.','Goal','Goal'),
38	('19040624-732b-4a02-93a5-00bc449fc4b1'::uuid,'1da894e9961221f7d72f7ac853691554','There is no evidence here, just one claim. So our job is to find reasons to believe it.
39	
40	Think about how a longer prison term is supposed to work. It deters only if a would-be robber knows the penalty, expects it to apply, and weighs it before acting. So the claim gets support from anything that breaks that chain: robbers who do not know the sentence, robbers who do not expect to be caught, robbers who are not weighing costs at all. It also gets support from a similar case where a longer term made no difference.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
41	('d0bb375a-3648-4bd9-a02b-6fb47fef2005'::uuid,'d1a9ac878bfd22657a7ac15c7cdedb18','Four answers will give one of those reasons to believe a longer term would not discourage robbery. The answer we want gives none. Expect it to have no clear impact on what a longer term would do, or to cut against the claim.','Goal','Goal'),
42	('a6cc6932-a37b-44fd-8e4c-ab06d99aef6d'::uuid,'433ee42bc32ebb5505515ddc93f0439b','The evidence counts fatal accidents: in each of the last ten years, more happened during the day than during the night. The conclusion is about risk to "an individual": driving by day is more dangerous for each driver.
43	
44	Given that more fatal accidents happen by day, how could we still argue that night driving is just as dangerous? Count the drivers. If far more people drive during the day, the day could have more fatal accidents and still be safer per driver. A bigger total is not a bigger rate.
45	
46	So the argument needs a reason the danger itself is higher during the day: something about daytime driving that raises the risk for each driver.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
47	('d5fd6170-1471-444c-b0a0-ed19be5c4538'::uuid,'47b6a1649fa355a8e179c25143131710','Four answers will strengthen by giving a day-specific risk: something that makes each daytime trip more dangerous, or each nighttime trip safer. The correct answer will not. Expect it to show no day-versus-night difference at all, so it cannot explain why the day is more dangerous.','Goal','Goal'),
48	('db6c1efe-c0d1-456f-ad76-549a53a60d6a'::uuid,'5fc6e19a861f9c46291ae21afa949b47','Those persons who are perceived as forming opinions of others only after cautiously gathering and weighing the evidence are generally resented.

51	AP → R','Evidence','Evidence'),
52	('82c7591b-dce5-49e2-8b20-53233f5721ef'::uuid,'7ddd6f1e241fe30a76d4cac1f8ed8689','It is imprudent to appear prudent.
53	AP → ~P
54	
55	Here ~P means not prudent.','Conclusion','Conclusion'),
56	('e81ea5ed-4f01-491d-9945-b76f6fc53393'::uuid,'b30e3f786835b3e3aa530a8469ad8ed9','Line the two up. The premise starts at appearing prudent and ends at being resented. The conclusion starts at appearing prudent and ends at imprudent. Same start, different finish. Being resented shows up only in the premise, and imprudent shows up only in the conclusion, so the missing piece has to connect them:
57	R → ~P
58	In words: causing people to resent you is imprudent. Add that and the chain runs
59	AP → R → ~P
60	which is the conclusion.
61	
62	The first sentence, that people want to be instantly and intuitively liked, explains why cautious people are resented. It is background. It never reaches the conclusion''s new idea.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
63	('3d1ff9f9-4099-40e6-9e1e-86fcaf485884'::uuid,'852d0958abb0efb920df32145377a603','Both premises use without. A sentence of the form no X without Y means X needs Y: X → Y.
64	```
65	IF → SI
66	GL → SI
67	```
68	Individual freedom requires social integrity. Pursuing the good life requires social integrity.','Evidence','Evidence'),
69	('74c50797-a803-4897-ad50-3044f024d32d'::uuid,'dd20859981dbcefaa2255fae635ac5ac','```
70	IF → RL
71	```
72	Individual freedom requires the rule of law. The rule of law appears only here. No premise mentions it.','Conclusion','Conclusion'),
73	('9560d25c-6fa3-40ec-ac88-b074d3779532'::uuid,'512fc7dee4d211b751eb303aa9c5a9af','Start from the conclusion''s trigger, IF. The first premise takes us from IF to SI. Then we are stuck: nothing takes us from SI to RL. Supply that link and the chain runs

75	IF → SI → RL
76	```
77	which gives IF → RL.
78	
79	The second premise, about the good life, is a distraction. GL also points to SI, so two arrows lead into SI and none lead out. The good life never connects to individual freedom, so it cannot help.','Evaluate','Evaluate')

2	('1f09730b-aa9b-4b7e-b943-461b5db1c335'::uuid,'beba3bee5f9c8203d4498abddb6fbc97','A says that in many ancient cultures, agriculture came first and fire-clearing came later. That says nothing about why this society burned its land. If anything, it hints that a society clearing land with fire already farmed, which leans the wrong way. It gives no hunter-gatherer reason for the fires.'),
3	('8980f5f9-efad-4832-b05f-632bf82a814e'::uuid,'942968786756f6c79115f4d225d04053','Cooking and heat explain campfires, not the burning of "large areas of land." Farmers cook and keep warm too, so this use of fire fits both stories equally. A strengthener has to explain the large-scale burning in a way the hunter-gatherer story predicts and the farming story does not.'),
4	('e5cf4e7f-0af4-4f90-98b2-00502ec1cb44'::uuid,'72f2b7b1048725b61b3b6ca5dd051966','C says fire releases the seeds of certain plants. That is a fact about plants, not about why this society burned land. The seeds are "inedible," so it does not give foragers a food reason to burn. And if fire helps plants spread, it might even suggest a planting motive. No link to hunter-gatherers, so no strengthening.'),
5	('1719a8e0-8f29-49c6-bc52-2ff43f0ea6b8'::uuid,'f0cfc2dbd343290440bcc6e0dcc53b35','D supplies the missing reason. Hunter-gatherers are known to burn land to move animal populations from one area to another. Now the fires have an explanation that fits the author''s story, and the lack of cultivation afterward is exactly what we would expect: the fires were for hunting, not planting. The burning stops counting as evidence for farming.
6	
7	The move to repeat: when an argument picks one explanation for a fact over a rival, look for an answer that explains the fact under the author''s story. A fact only the rival story can explain is a liability until an answer like D removes it.'),
8	('d222714c-739f-40ce-9fdf-43712069449c'::uuid,'73113ade47524e58221e690bfec86bc2','E undercuts one possible farming motive: burning to enrich the soil. But the farming story in the stimulus is about clearing ground for planting, not adding nutrients, so E leaves it standing. 9	('0202d8c0-b410-4b0e-aa2d-42044621f900'::uuid,'7676e800adba17c3f6103dcffd91ac4d','A says common sense usually solves daily-life problems. 10	('7799cd57-36fa-4da9-8fc9-9ee1424424d1'::uuid,'002ceb480561c724e1bc0fbd854a30b6','B gives a reason to keep the current system: most teachers do a better job with single-discipline courses. 11	('931c94e9-77fe-45ff-8308-696b53363bdd'::uuid,'3cf43a0cabb0c14331f7ff868c046251','C answers the objection we built. 12	
13	The move: when a recommendation is built on a need, ask how the current approach might already meet that need. The answer that says it does not is the strengthener.'),
14	('e4b87a42-1013-4f48-b7a9-4f263d4945a7'::uuid,'d560010ec62b8b2235efa60f05b2a214','D says most students in single-discipline courses "can effectively solve many problems faced in daily life." 15	('36af108a-ee4c-430d-8b59-948d7a6a54d8'::uuid,'0e9bbe87c94b5b34ceb46ee1fff3aaa6','E says most interdisciplinary courses are not designed to teach daily-life problem solving. 16	('69112128-691d-47b6-a008-628b3a139085'::uuid,'313a536ec01b92875d36ed41510c33fc','A says blood pressure medication does not stop the rises during speech. That tells us the rise is hard to block, not what causes it. A rise driven by stress and a rise driven by physical exertion could both get past medication, so A favors neither cause.'),
17	('4b9fdb27-d274-4df2-99c9-49b443c128de'::uuid,'816b0d0d54abab344d7c943aa9e854fd','B links a person''s typical blood pressure to how much it rises under stress. 18	('2bbcd858-e618-42a4-b6bb-4ec8a4c1bb13'::uuid,'355c015c595284ba2bf7fad0103f38cd','C says introverts often sense the rises when they talk. Noticing a change says nothing about what caused it. 19	('89f3a439-df4b-456a-bd8c-dc1d2f79ee48'::uuid,'0323b847eb16c406d901b96ace9d9992','D builds the test we wanted. Signing is communication with no vocal speech production. With the physical effort held roughly constant, only communication changes, and blood pressure follows communication. That cuts down the physical-exertion explanation and supports the stress of communicating.
20	
21	The move: when an argument picks between two causes that always show up together, the strongest support finds a case where they come apart and shows the effect tracking the author''s cause.'),
22	('0ed5b5cd-0c23-4dde-aa4d-c486b504d77f'::uuid,'5679bbe9484249e43d72d33cdb3e7581','E looks relevant because it is about extroverts and blood pressure, but it weakens. That is an alternate explanation for the very difference the psychologist credits to stress.'),
23	('926ede8d-cc27-4508-a22c-d276094388d5'::uuid,'76f29fdb5c3bd336a2bb54c5b32a5a38','A says most people who buy a pan with a warranty "would seek reimbursement" if it failed. Now follow the chain. If the pan were bad, many buyers would claim, the manufacturer would have to reimburse many customers, and by the premise it would not offer the warranty. So a pan with a warranty is one the manufacturer expects to work well and last. That is why even a buyer who would never claim should buy it.
24	
25	The move: when a premise says a party avoids a cost, check what makes the cost real. Here the cost depends on buyers actually claiming, and A supplies that.'),
26	('a8655c27-9884-4436-8064-4aa63507a69f'::uuid,'de9239a83fe30df3c5d1af8f43ac1dda','B compares pans only "at the time of purchase." B also says nothing about why manufacturers offer warranties, so it does not connect the premise to the conclusion.'),
27	('500d8893-bc1c-41bb-b6c1-a0157417e472'::uuid,'fd1cb5113567a6d71109bd042baa6a5e','C ties price to warranties. It does not show that a warranty means a good pan. The conclusion already accepts paying more, so learning that pans with warranties tend to cost more adds no reason to buy them.'),
28	('d3817786-71a8-4beb-babd-7fff4c5458c4'::uuid,'2c22b07bf176a54c33271dbfe743dba0','D ties price to quality. The conclusion says to buy pans with a warranty, not expensive pans. 29	('513c2131-a3bf-416d-b267-cd5c95fcfeff'::uuid,'2c1f0a61b920f1fbe0d33b6025afc0f7','E says most warranties "provide for full customer satisfaction." That describes what a claim gets you. 30	('65750e5e-9b29-4c54-83ed-64e151e80a0d'::uuid,'f960180b6db13b01bd9ba8814655aa5c','If many robbers are driven by "thrill-seeking and risk-taking," they are not carefully weighing costs, and a longer sentence may even add to the risk they enjoy. 31	('928882e6-b545-40eb-98d5-ebd431a15301'::uuid,'7a73e59e85e06ff4cf2f1e8110cd891c','B is an analogy. A longer prison term for embezzlement did not change how often that crime was committed. 32	('8fe2f2a7-a4bb-476a-89dc-5bb4d29062b2'::uuid,'470919646f36126e338e1f769bb00305','C is about the past: robbery terms "have generally decreased in length recently." 33	
34	The move on Strengthen EXCEPT: list the kinds of support before reading the choices. Here that list was robbers who do not know the sentence, do not expect to be caught, or do not weigh costs, plus a similar case. The answer that fits none of them is the one to pick.'),
35	('a0d5bed2-5993-4708-a4b1-e0910d43ca8a'::uuid,'c9496830f78d31f5af13cad7ee6eac6a','If most robbers believe "they will not get caught," they do not expect any sentence to apply to them. 36	('b8247c03-271a-4dac-98bb-02dec610ed00'::uuid,'eedc4ae9e034061aaae1ec59f288d8a5','If most robbers "have no idea what the average sentence for robbery is," they would not notice a longer one. A penalty you do not know about cannot deter you. That supports the claim.'),
37	('a9ad1aad-ad09-4492-9333-23ced104dce8'::uuid,'563932e34a3fa50032e38384847b77e3','A gives a daytime-only hazard: only during the day do unsafe vehicles outnumber safe ones. 38	('1351a44c-5b03-490f-8c56-5315ac1401ea'::uuid,'eba06efa2509c52609d3610317ad1f08','B says there is less law enforcement during the day. 39	('5b35563d-8f14-485f-b9d9-90cf2fec3c8d'::uuid,'1e588ab8dc90138ac9b4f54a61843721','C says people drive more cautiously at night. That makes each night trip safer than a day trip, which explains the extra daytime fatal accidents with something other than traffic volume. It strengthens.'),
40	('df83e2aa-29d5-49f2-b7b5-b2dd4836b084'::uuid,'062b8a6ca66c90a399577a7617d04174','D is the exception. More travelers per vehicle over the past ten years is a trend across day and night alike. 41	
42	The move on a Strengthen EXCEPT built on a comparison: each strengthener has to favor one side of the comparison. An answer that applies equally to both sides cannot help.'),
43	('5a57d2c0-480d-498d-8004-5e02b9025d8c'::uuid,'ea7807e43ea033731ba1eca91c7b0866','E says people drive faster during the day than during the night. 44	('22ea66a2-1b49-4d4a-9e6b-06db83e87cc6'::uuid,'152c6a8815cd02652af588e33c6fad9f','A says people who act spontaneously are well liked. The gap is between resentment and imprudence, and A touches neither side of it.'),
45	('d3bfaf37-b722-48ff-8344-0335eec1d047'::uuid,'ff102199a9569a00e732d6763be8a653','B starts from imprudent people:
46	~P → acts instantly and intuitively
47	That puts imprudent on the trigger side, but we need to prove imprudent, so it has to be on the outcome side. B also talks about how people act, while the argument is about how they appear. It cannot finish the chain.'),
48	('0a252cd3-c2c0-4c71-9d51-5fca62ff3efa'::uuid,'3921673794a324aa44f7a97f54a885e3','C says people resent those less prudent than themselves. It never says that being resented is imprudent, so the conclusion still does not follow.'),
49	('22cc2a02-2e4b-4448-a2ae-b5104d4db920'::uuid,'f828fc07d531089f4c239c65bf4445d8','D is about whether intuitive people know instantly when they like someone. 50	('f533f925-38b7-477d-8ab3-151992ee45fe'::uuid,'2200e0544bcbb4cd2bdb1caae40d8974','E says it is imprudent to cause people to resent you:
51	R → ~P
52	Chain it to the premise: appearing prudent gets you resented, and causing resentment is imprudent, so appearing prudent is imprudent.
53	
54	The move on Sufficient Assumption: find the idea in the conclusion that no premise mentions (imprudent), find the premise idea that never reaches the conclusion (resented), and pick the answer that joins them in the right direction.'),
55	('042aef57-bc70-4eec-9d97-b1e39ee1c248'::uuid,'a2d03d4de07ce72f28dee1bee656940c','A says there can be no rule of law without social integrity:
56	```
57	RL → SI
58	```
59	That is the link we need, backwards. With IF → SI and RL → SI, both arrows end at SI, so nothing carries us from IF to RL. Watch for this reversal on any chain question.'),
60	('ef210e79-2019-4dc6-b357-a516021df7fd'::uuid,'fff7ed88b89040264c2c88dd3467997f','B says there can be no social integrity without the rule of law:
61	```
62	SI → RL
63	```
64	Hook it onto the first premise: IF → SI → RL, so IF → RL. That is the conclusion.
65	
66	The move: when the conclusion has a term no premise mentions (the rule of law), the assumption must run from the end of the premise chain to that new term.'),
67	('2537095c-c154-420b-815c-fd855119d919'::uuid,'c49587d45f4884ad4d8ea9714661096c','C says one cannot pursue the good life without the rule of law:
68	```
69	GL → RL
70	```
71	That helps only if we can get from IF to GL, and we cannot. The premise gives GL → SI, and nothing leads into GL. C would work only if the good-life premise were reversed (SI → GL).'),
72	('dfac5e14-f75c-471d-ae82-62ace6cd97fd'::uuid,'6daae033e99c3efd86e22ac9973d909f','D says social integrity is possible only if individual freedom prevails:
73	```
74	SI → IF
75	```
76	That reverses the first premise. It points back toward IF, and RL never appears, so the conclusion''s new term is still out of reach.'),
77	('dc8d503e-f9f3-4b83-a1ff-c57a13053453'::uuid,'2637a8b68a991254bb4cd76a4228b4ca','E says there can be no rule of law without individual freedom:
78	```
79	RL → IF
80	```
81	That is the conclusion reversed. Assuming the reverse of what we want to prove does not establish it.')
82	) v(id,ob,nb) where t.id=v.id and md5(t.body)=v.ob returning t.id;

2	('fb8ddc3c-c341-45cf-99e1-83bd347de5f2'::uuid,3,'Goal','Look for an answer that says being resented, or causing resentment, is imprudent. Reject answers that start from imprudent (a reversal), or that talk about acting instead of appearing, or being liked instead of being resented.'),
3	('76988d38-839f-4b5e-a212-48d3dece30c8'::uuid,3,'Goal','Look for SI → RL: there is no social integrity without the rule of law. 4	) v(e,p,l,b) where not exists (select 1 from lr_explanation_steps x where x.explanation_id=v.e and x.position=v.p) returning id;

2	('e8c85123-28f1-4b94-801f-fcc6fe3a8a11'::uuid,'ae2c3d494dcd88b3dea773bb0fa9ccf6','We know the first claim is the conclusion because the other two claims are clearly built to work together. Connectors like and, but, and on the other hand show two claims interacting to move the argument forward.
3	
4	Each conditional premise has TWO outcomes, and one of them is decreasing unemployment. I didn''t bother writing out the other half of each outcome, because all we care about is proving that unemployment will decrease.
5	
6	At first, this argument seems pretty reasonable. It looks like an *Either Way You Slice It* argument: whether spending increases significantly or decreases significantly, we end up with lower unemployment, so either way unemployment goes down.
7	
8	But an argument on Sufficient Assumption can''t *already* be airtight. There has to be a gap, so that the correct answer can close it.
9	
10	So let''s argue with the economist. How could unemployment *fail to decrease*?
11	
12	Spending doesn''t have to go significantly up or significantly down. It could stay about the same. Then neither rule is triggered, and the premises tell us nothing about unemployment.
13	
14	The economist is presenting a *False Choice* (a false dichotomy), treating a big increase and a big decrease as the only two options while ignoring the middle ground where spending barely moves.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
15	('0cf755b5-c56e-473b-8db9-5095d3dd3436'::uuid,'dfc69dc9be2714a1ba355f1f51d1c098','We need to rule out the middle ground. Predict an answer saying that next year government spending will either significantly increase or significantly decrease.
16

18	('85a2d1a6-42aa-4496-adf4-0d1642958629'::uuid,'20cf85bc6f33097591b75bec53cd2596','Most children under six are egocentric and selfish in their attitudes toward animals.

21	('472a536c-d84c-49b2-aad8-6e30ad1e0350'::uuid,'0c63806a78ba133caef1c74de26105f6','Look at the conclusion''s key word: "should." The evidence only describes what young children are like. The conclusion tells us what ought to happen. That "should not have pets" idea is a new concept in the conclusion, and on Sufficient Assumption the correct answer almost always has to supply it.
22	
23	Let''s argue with the psychologist. Given that most children under six don''t yet understand that animals have their own feelings and needs, how could we argue that they should still have pets? Easy: maybe a child doesn''t need to understand that to have a pet. A parent could do the caring, and the child could learn along the way. The argument never rules that out.
24	
25	We can sketch it with arrows, as long as we remember the premise says "Ordinarily," so it is a "most" claim, not an "all" claim:

65	('278cae2d-f407-4a3e-bdb0-c3fd23a744a5'::uuid,'374bd576a1158fccf8be521762d83ee3','On Sufficient Assumption, once we''ve found the conclusion, we ask whether it contains a New Concept. If it does, the correct answer almost always brings that concept in.

76	('c1b89a6b-a22e-4291-b0ec-fb8a90405b87'::uuid,'28ac8855bcc377cfaabeaec0d2e48295','A classic missing link correct answer would say that if the artistic decisions made in creating a film are affected by the need to make profits, then the film doesn''t have absolute integrity as a work of art. 77	('aa629d31-a0a0-420d-a245-fe69cf370cd6'::uuid,'a4e3f8ee187caf32ef83b8673bedfd16','Thriving populations of turtles require conditions that are beneficial to turtles. Wallakim Pond has acidic water.
